abstract: Being able to record the electrical activities of a number of neurons simultaneously is likely to be important in the study of the functional organization of networks of real neurons. Using one extracellular microelectrode to record from several neurons is one approach to studying the response properties of sets of adjacent and therefore likely related neurons. However, to do this, it is necessary to correctly classify the signals generated by these different neurons. This paper considers this problem of classifying the signals in such an extracellular recording, based upon their shapes, and specifically considers the classification of signals in the case when spikes overlap temporally.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the problem of identifying which neuron produced each signal in a recording shared by several neurons. A single extracellular microelectrode can record activity from nearby cells, creating an opportunity to study their responses together. Using that recording requires correctly assigning the observed signals to their neuronal sources.

The proposed basis for classification is signal shape. The paper specifically considers the difficult case in which spikes overlap in time. When signals coincide, the recorded event contains contributions from more than one spike, so classification must account for temporal overlap as part of the interpretation of the waveform.

The motivation is to study the functional organization of real neural networks through simultaneous recordings. Nearby neurons are considered likely to be related, making their joint responses useful subjects of investigation. Correctly distinguishing their signals is therefore a necessary step between collecting a shared electrical recording and analyzing the activities of individual cells within it. The paper focuses on that measurement and interpretation problem.
summary.tldr: The paper studies shape-based classification of spikes from multiple neurons recorded by one electrode, focusing on temporally overlapping signals.

title: Optimal Neural Spike Classification

paragraphs: This paper investigates how multilayer perceptrons trained with backpropagation can classify speech sounds. Its experiments focus on recognizing 16 American English vowels independently of the speaker. The authors use this task to study how network design and training choices affect phonetic classification, reporting results comparable to human performance.

The investigation includes combining heterogeneous information sources, examining learned internal representations, comparing error measures, and choosing initial network settings. It also compares the network with K-nearest-neighbor and Gaussian classifiers. Classification improves as more information becomes available, and the authors describe implementation choices that improve performance and make learning more efficient.

The broader motivation is to connect speech knowledge with a trainable classification procedure. Linguistic and acoustic knowledge can guide the network’s structure, while learning supplies a way to use that knowledge in decisions. The paper therefore treats recognition accuracy and representation design as related questions: what information enters the model, how training organizes it, and which choices allow it to support reliable distinctions between vowels.
summary.tldr: Backpropagation networks achieve human-comparable results on speaker-independent vowel classification while revealing how information and training choices affect recognition.

title: Applications of Error Back-Propagation to Phonetic Classification

abstract: Preliminary results on speaker-independant speech recognition are reported. A method that combines expertise on neural networks with expertise on speech recognition is used to build the recognition systems. For transient sounds, event(cid:173) driven property extractors with variable resolution in the time and frequency domains are used. For sonorant speech, a model of the human auditory system is preferred to FFT as a front-end module.
originalAbstract: Preliminary results on speaker-independant speech recognition are reported. A method that combines expertise on neural networks with expertise on speech recognition is used to build the recognition systems. For transient sounds, event(cid:173) driven property extractors with variable resolution in the time and frequency domains are used. For sonorant speech, a model of the human auditory system is preferred to FFT as a front-end module.

paragraphs: The paper reports preliminary work on speaker-independent speech recognition using multilayer networks and phonetic features. Its approach combines neural-network knowledge with speech-recognition expertise. A central design choice is how the incoming sound is represented before recognition, with different processing proposed for different kinds of speech.

For transient sounds, the system uses event-driven property extractors with variable resolution in time and frequency. These sounds are handled through features organized around acoustic events, with the analysis resolution allowed to vary. For sonorant speech, the authors instead prefer a model of the human auditory system as the front end over an FFT-based representation.

The contribution is a recognition-system design that makes speech-specific processing part of the neural approach. Transient and sonorant sounds receive different front ends because the method explicitly distinguishes their acoustic character. The reported findings are preliminary, so the stated significance lies in this combination of domain-informed feature extraction and multilayer networks for the speaker-independent recognition task.
summary.tldr: The paper combines multilayer networks with speech-specific front ends for preliminary speaker-independent recognition.

title: Use of Multi-Layered Networks for Coding Speech with Phonetic Features

After or during training. a dynamic clustering algorithm extracts the production rules that the neural network has learned.. TIle methods are illustrated by extracting rules from unknown deterministic regular grammars. paragraphs: This paper studies how recurrent neural networks can learn a regular grammar from examples of strings that belong to it and strings that do not. The network must use the sequence of symbols to decide whether a complete string is acceptable. The authors use simple second-order recurrent networks and demonstrate learning and rule extraction for deterministic regular grammars.

Training uses an incremental form of real-time recurrent learning. It computes the complete gradient and updates the network's weights at the end of each string. During or after training, a dynamic clustering procedure extracts the production rules learned by the network, turning its learned behavior into an explicit grammar.

In many of the reported cases, the extracted grammar classifies unseen strings more accurately than the network from which it came. Rule extraction therefore serves more than an explanatory purpose: it can improve the usable result of learning. The approach connects learning from labeled examples with recovering a symbolic description that can itself recognize new strings.
summary.tldr: Recurrent networks learn regular grammars from labeled strings, and extracted symbolic grammars often classify unseen strings better than their source networks.

title: Extracting and Learning an Unknown Grammar with Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Songbirds learn to imitate a tutor song through auditory and motor learn(cid:173) ing. We have developed a theoretical framework for song learning that accounts for response properties of neurons that have been observed in many of the nuclei that are involved in song learning. Specifically, we suggest that the anteriorforebrain pathway, which is not needed for song production in the adult but is essential for song acquisition, provides synaptic perturbations and adaptive evaluations for syllable vocalization learning. A computer model based on reinforcement learning was con(cid:173) structed that could replicate a real zebra finch song with 90% accuracy based on a spectrographic measure. The second generation of the bird(cid:173) song model replicated the tutor song with 96% accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper develops a theory of how songbirds learn to imitate a tutor's song through coordinated auditory and motor learning. The goal is to explain both the acquisition of vocal behavior and response properties observed in neurons across several brain nuclei involved in song learning. This connects a learning algorithm to a proposed biological mechanism.

The central proposal assigns a learning role to the anterior forebrain pathway. This pathway is essential for acquiring song even though adult birds do not need it to produce an established song. The model suggests that it supplies changes at synapses together with adaptive evaluations, allowing syllable production to be adjusted through reinforcement.

A computer implementation reproduced a real zebra finch song with 90% accuracy according to a spectrographic measure. A second-generation model reached 96% accuracy in matching the tutor song. These results show that the proposed framework can generate close acoustic matches. They support its usefulness as a computational account while remaining distinct from direct confirmation of the proposed neural learning mechanism.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning model links a proposed birdsong learning pathway to simulations that closely reproduce a tutor's song.

title: A Novel Reinforcement Model of Birdsong Vocalization Learning

abstract: We are developing special-purpose, low-power analog-to-digital converters for speech and music applications, that feature analog circuit models of biological audition to process the audio signal before conversion. This paper describes our most recent converter design, and a working system that uses several copies ofthe chip to compute multiple representations of sound from an analog input. This multi-representation system demonstrates the plausibility of inexpensively implementing an auditory scene analysis approach to sound processing.

This paper describes our most recent converter design, and a working system that uses several copies ofthe chip to compute multiple representations of sound from an analog input. This multi-representation system demonstrates the plausibility of inexpensively implementing an auditory scene analysis approach to sound processing.

paragraphs: The paper describes specialized, low-power analog-to-digital converters intended for speech and music processing. Their distinguishing feature is that analog circuits model aspects of biological hearing before the signal is converted to digital form. Auditory processing is therefore built into the acquisition hardware itself.

The authors present a converter design and a working system assembled from several copies of the chip. Together, these chips compute multiple representations of the same analog sound input. The use of several representations is central to the system: the hardware produces different processed descriptions of sound that support an auditory scene analysis approach.

The stated finding is a demonstration that such an approach can plausibly be implemented inexpensively. The working system connects biologically inspired sound processing with a concrete hardware realization, while the low-power converter design addresses the practical form that realization can take. Its significance lies in showing how auditory representations can be produced during signal conversion, making the front end an active part of sound analysis.
summary.tldr: Low-power converter chips use analog models of hearing to produce multiple sound representations before digital processing.

title: Silicon Models for Auditory Scene Analysis

abstract: We study here a simple stochastic single neuron model with delayed self-feedback capable of generating spike trains. Simulations show that its spike trains exhibit resonant behavior between "noise" and "delay". In order to gain insight into this resonance, we simplify the model and study a stochastic binary element whose transition probability depends on its state at a fixed interval in the past. With this simplified model we can analytically compute interspike interval histograms, and show how the resonance between noise and delay arises. The resonance is also observed when such elements are coupled through delayed interaction. 1

Simulations show that its spike trains exhibit resonant behavior between "noise" and "delay". In order to gain insight into this resonance, we simplify the model and study a stochastic binary element whose transition probability depends on its state at a fixed interval in the past. With this simplified model we can analytically compute interspike interval histograms, and show how the resonance between noise and delay arises. The resonance is also observed when such elements are coupled through delayed interaction. 1

paragraphs: The paper studies a simple stochastic neuron that generates spikes and receives delayed feedback from itself. Simulations reveal resonance involving the model's noise and feedback delay. The question is how these two ingredients interact to shape spike timing, rather than treating random fluctuations and delayed influence as unrelated effects.

To explain the simulation result, the authors simplify the neuron into a stochastic element with two possible states. Its probability of changing state depends on the state it occupied a fixed amount of time earlier. This reduced model retains the delayed dependence while making an analytical treatment possible.

For the simplified system, the authors calculate histograms of intervals between spikes and use them to show how the resonance arises. They also observe resonance when such elements are coupled through delayed interactions. The work therefore combines a simulated neuron model, an analytically tractable explanation, and observations in coupled elements. Its findings concern these stochastic models and demonstrate a mechanism by which noise and delay can jointly organize spike timing.
summary.tldr: Simulations and a simplified analytical model show how noise and delayed feedback can produce resonance in spike timing.

title: Resonance in a Stochastic Neuron Model with Delayed Interaction

abstract: New functionals for parameter (model) selection of Support Vector Ma(cid:173) chines are introduced based on the concepts of the span of support vec(cid:173) tors and rescaling of the feature space. It is shown that using these func(cid:173) tionals, one can both predict the best choice of parameters of the model and the relative quality of performance for any value of parameter.
originalAbstract: New functionals for parameter (model) selection of Support Vector Ma(cid:173) chines are introduced based on the concepts of the span of support vec(cid:173) tors and rescaling of the feature space. It is shown that using these func(cid:173) tionals, one can both predict the best choice of parameters of the model and the relative quality of performance for any value of parameter.

paragraphs: The paper addresses parameter selection for support vector machines. Choosing parameter values determines which particular model is used, so the selection problem concerns judging alternatives rather than merely obtaining a solution for one fixed setting. The authors introduce mathematical scoring criteria, called functionals, intended to guide that judgment.

These criteria are based on the span of support vectors and on rescaling the feature space. Both connect model selection to the geometry of the representation used by the support vector machine. The proposed functionals turn those geometric concepts into quantities that can be used to assess parameter choices and compare their expected quality.

The authors show that the functionals can predict both the best parameter choice and the relative performance quality associated with any parameter value. These are related but distinct uses: identifying a preferred setting and assessing how other settings compare. The contribution is therefore a basis for evaluating the parameter landscape, providing model-selection information beyond a recommendation of one setting.
summary.tldr: Geometric criteria based on support vectors and feature-space rescaling predict preferred SVM parameters and relative performance across settings.

title: Model Selection for Support Vector Machines

abstract: It has long been known that lateral inhibition in neural networks can lead to a winner-take-all competition, so that only a single neuron is active at a steady state. Here we show how to organize lateral inhibition so that groups of neurons compete to be active. Given a collection of poten(cid:173) tially overlapping groups, the inhibitory connectivity is set by a formula that can be interpreted as arising from a simple learning rule. Our analy(cid:173) sis demonstrates that such inhibition generally results in winner-take-all competition between the given groups, with the exception of some de(cid:173) generate cases. In a broader context, the network serves as a particular illustration of the general distinction between permitted and forbidden sets, which was introduced recently. From this viewpoint, the computa(cid:173) tional function of our network is to store and retrieve memories as per(cid:173) mitted sets of coactive neurons. In traditional winner-take-all networks, lateral inhibition is used to enforce a localized, or "grandmother cell" representation in which only a single neuron is active [1, 2, 3, 4]. When used for unsupervised learning, winner-take-all networks discover representations similar to those learned by vector quantization [5]. Recently many research efforts have focused on unsupervised learning algorithms for sparsely distributed representations [6, 7]. These algorithms lead to networks in which groups of multiple neurons are coactivated to represent an object. Therefore, it is of great interest to find ways of using lateral inhibition to mediate winner-take-all competition between groups of neurons, as this could be useful for learning sparsely distributed representations. In this paper, we show how winner-take-all competition between groups of neurons can be learned. Given a collection of potentially overlapping groups, the inhibitory connectivity is set by a simple formula that can be interpreted as arising from an online learning rule. To show that the resulting network functions as advertised, we perform a stability analysis. If the strength of inhibition is sufficiently great, and the group organization satisfies certain conditions, we show that the only sets of neurons that can be coactivated at a stable steady state are the given groups and their subsets. Because of the competition between groups, only one group can be activated at a time. In general, the identity of the winning group depends on the initial conditions of the network dynamics. abstract: We introduce the notion of kernel-alignment, a measure of similar(cid:173) ity between two kernel functions or between a kernel and a target function. This quantity captures the degree of agreement between a kernel and a given learning task, and has very natural interpre(cid:173) tations in machine learning, leading also to simple algorithms for model selection and learning. We analyse its theoretical properties, proving that it is sharply concentrated around its expected value, and we discuss its relation with other standard measures of per(cid:173) formance. Finally we describe some of the algorithms that can be obtained within this framework, giving experimental results show(cid:173) ing that adapting the kernel to improve alignment on the labelled data significantly increases the alignment on the test set, giving improved classification accuracy. Hence, the approach provides a principled method of performing transduction. Keywords: Kernels, alignment, eigenvectors, eigenvalues, transduction

paragraphs: This paper introduces kernel alignment, a measure comparing two kernel functions or comparing a kernel with a target function. The intended interpretation is agreement: how well the similarities expressed by a kernel fit the learning task. This provides a criterion for choosing or adapting the kernel.

The authors analyze alignment theoretically and prove that it concentrates sharply around its expected value. They also discuss its relationship to established performance measures. These properties support using alignment as more than an informal diagnostic, and the framework leads to simple procedures for model selection and learning.

Experiments show that adapting a kernel to improve alignment on labeled data significantly increases alignment on the test set and improves classification accuracy. The result connects optimization of the proposed criterion with better predictions in the reported experiments. The authors also present the approach as a principled method for transduction. Its central contribution is a task-sensitive measure of kernel suitability, supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical adaptation results.
summary.tldr: Kernel alignment measures task–kernel agreement and supports kernel adaptation that improves test alignment and classification in reported experiments.

title: On Kernel-Target Alignment

abstract: Observer translation relative to the world creates image flow that expands from the observer's direction of translation (heading) from which the observer can recover heading direction. Yet, the image flow is often more complex, depending on rotation of the eye, scene layout and translation velocity. A number of models [1-4] have been proposed on how the human visual system extracts heading from flow in a neurophysiologic ally plausible way. These models represent heading by a set of neurons that respond to large image flow patterns and receive input from motion sensed at different im(cid:173) age locations. We analysed these models to determine the exact receptive field of these heading detectors. We find most models predict that, contrary to widespread believe, the contribut ing mo(cid:173) tion sensors have a preferred motion directed circularly rather than radially around the detector's preferred heading. Moreover, the re(cid:173) sults suggest to look for more refined structure within the circular flow, such as bi-circularity or local motion-opponency.

paragraphs: Moving through the world produces image motion that can reveal heading, but eye rotation, scene layout, and translation speed complicate that motion. Several visual models represent heading with neurons that respond to broad flow patterns. These detectors combine motion information from different image locations to infer the observer's direction of travel.

This paper analyzes those models to determine the precise receptive fields of their heading detectors. The authors ask which local motions contribute to a detector's response. This distinguishes the large-scale flow pattern associated with a heading from the directional preferences of the individual motion sensors supplying the detector.

Most analyzed models predict that the contributing sensors prefer motion arranged circularly around the detector's preferred heading, rather than radially. This challenges the widespread expectation described in the abstract. The results also suggest searching for finer organization within that circular structure, including bi-circularity and local motion opponency. These are consequences of the model analysis and directions for examining receptive fields, rather than reported direct observations of those structures in neurons.
summary.tldr: Analysis of heading models predicts mostly circular, rather than radial, local motion preferences within heading detectors.

title: Receptive field structure of flow detectors for heading perception

abstract: We develop a protocol for optimizing dynamic behavior of a network of simple electronic components, such as a sensor network, an ad hoc network of mobile devices, or a network of communication switches. This protocol requires only local communication and simple computa- tions which are distributed among devices. The protocol is scalable to large networks. As a motivating example, we discuss a problem involv- ing optimization of power consumption, delay, and buffer overﬂow in a sensor network. Our approach builds on policy gradient methods for optimization of Markov decision processes. The protocol can be viewed as an extension of policy gradient methods to a context involving a team of agents op- timizing aggregate performance through asynchronous distributed com- munication and computation. We establish that the dynamics of the pro- tocol approximate the solution to an ordinary differential equation that follows the gradient of the performance objective.

Examples include sensor networks, mobile-device networks, and communication switches. The practical challenge is to improve the network's overall performance using only local communication and modest computation at individual devices.

The approach extends policy-gradient methods for Markov decision processes to a team of agents. Devices communicate and compute asynchronously while contributing to an aggregate performance objective. A motivating sensor-network problem involves power consumption, delay, and buffer overflow, illustrating why local choices must be coordinated around consequences for the network as a whole.

The authors establish that the protocol's dynamics approximate an ordinary differential equation that follows the gradient of the performance objective. This provides a mathematical connection between the distributed updates and the desired optimization direction. Together with the protocol's stated scalability, the result explains how simple local operations can support optimization in large networks without requiring every device to perform a centralized computation.
summary.tldr: A scalable protocol uses local, asynchronous device updates to approximate policy-gradient optimization of overall network performance.

title: Distributed Optimization in Adaptive Networks

abstract: In typical classiﬁcation tasks, we seek a function which assigns a label to a sin- gle object. Kernel-based approaches, such as support vector machines (SVMs), which maximize the margin of conﬁdence of the classiﬁer, are the method of choice for many such tasks. Their popularity stems both from the ability to use high-dimensional feature spaces, and from their strong theoretical guaran- tees. However, many real-world tasks involve sequential, spatial, or structured data, where multiple labels must be assigned. Existing kernel-based methods ig- nore structure in the problem, assigning labels independently to each object, los- ing much useful information. Conversely, probabilistic graphical models, such as Markov networks, can represent correlations between labels, by exploiting problem structure, but cannot handle high-dimensional feature spaces, and lack strong theoretical generalization guarantees. In this paper, we present a new framework that combines the advantages of both approaches: Maximum mar- gin Markov (M3) networks incorporate both kernels, which efﬁciently deal with high-dimensional features, and the ability to capture correlations in structured data. We present an efﬁcient algorithm for learning M3 networks based on a compact quadratic program formulation. We provide a new theoretical bound for generalization in structured domains. Experiments on the task of handwrit- ten character recognition and collective hypertext classiﬁcation demonstrate very signiﬁcant gains over previous approaches.

paragraphs: Many classification problems require assigning several related labels, such as labels in a sequence or across spatially connected objects. Predicting each label independently can discard useful relationships. This paper introduces maximum-margin Markov networks to combine structured label modeling with the kernel-based, large-margin approach associated with support vector machines.

The framework uses kernels to work efficiently with high-dimensional features and Markov-network structure to capture correlations among labels. The authors provide an efficient learning algorithm based on a compact quadratic program. They also derive a theoretical generalization bound for structured domains, connecting the proposed framework to formal analysis of prediction beyond the training examples.

Experiments cover handwritten character recognition and collective hypertext classification. The authors report very significant gains over previous approaches on those tasks. The contribution brings together structured prediction, rich feature representations, a learning formulation, and a generalization result. The experimental evidence supports the value of this combination in the two stated application settings.
summary.tldr: Maximum-margin Markov networks combine kernel features and dependent labels, with an efficient learning formulation, a generalization bound, and strong reported experimental gains.

title: Max-Margin Markov Networks

abstract: Repeated spike patterns have often been taken as evidence for the synfire chain, a phenomenon that a stable spike synchrony propagates through a feedforward network. Inter-spike intervals which represent a repeated spike pattern are influenced by the propagation speed of a spike packet. However, the relation between the propagation speed and network struc- ture is not well understood. While it is apparent that the propagation speed depends on the excitatory synapse strength, it might also be related to spike patterns. We analyze a feedforward network with Mexican-Hat- type connectivity (FMH) using the Fokker-Planck equation. We show that both a uniform and a localized spike packet are stable in the FMH in a certain parameter region. We also demonstrate that the propagation speed depends on the distinct firing patterns in the same network.

paragraphs: A synfire chain involves a synchronized packet of neural spikes propagating through a feedforward network. The speed of propagation affects the intervals between spikes in repeated patterns. This paper investigates how that speed relates to network structure and to the particular firing pattern traveling through the network.

The authors analyze a feedforward network with Mexican-hat-type connectivity using the Fokker-Planck equation. Their analysis shows that both spatially uniform and localized spike packets can remain stable within a certain parameter region. Stability is therefore established for these two distinct activity patterns under the specified conditions, rather than asserted for every possible network configuration.

They also demonstrate that distinct firing patterns can propagate at different speeds in the same network. This means that propagation speed can reflect the form of the activity as well as the network's excitatory synaptic strength. The finding matters for interpreting repeated spike timing: a fixed network can support stable patterns whose timing differs because the propagating activity itself differs.
summary.tldr: A feedforward network can support stable uniform and localized spike packets whose propagation speeds depend on their firing patterns.

title: Theory of localized synfire chain: characteristic propagation speed of stable spike pattern

abstract: We describe semi-Markov conditional random ﬁelds (semi-CRFs), a con- ditionally trained version of semi-Markov chains. Intuitively, a semi- CRF on an input sequence x outputs a “segmentation” of x, in which labels are assigned to segments (i.e., subsequences) of x rather than to individual elements xi of x. Importantly, features for semi-CRFs can measure properties of segments, and transitions within a segment can be non-Markovian. In spite of this additional power, exact learning and inference algorithms for semi-CRFs are polynomial-time—often only a small constant factor slower than conventional CRFs. In experiments on ﬁve named entity recognition problems, semi-CRFs generally outper- form conventional CRFs.

paragraphs: Information extraction often needs to identify labeled spans within a sequence. This paper introduces semi-Markov conditional random fields, which predict a segmentation and assign labels to whole subsequences. That makes the segment itself a modeling unit, allowing the representation to address properties of a span directly rather than only labeling its individual elements.

Semi-CRFs are conditionally trained versions of semi-Markov chains. Their features can measure properties of complete segments, and transitions inside a segment can be non-Markovian. This gives the model additional expressive power for describing what happens within a labeled span while retaining an organized sequence of segments at the output level.

Despite that flexibility, exact learning and inference run in polynomial time and are often only a small constant factor slower than conventional CRFs. Across experiments on five named-entity recognition problems, semi-CRFs generally perform better than conventional CRFs. The result supports segment-level modeling for those tasks, with the computational claim showing that the extra expressiveness can remain compatible with exact, practical inference.
summary.tldr: Semi-CRFs label whole segments, enabling richer span features while retaining polynomial-time exact learning and inference.

title: Semi-Markov Conditional Random Fields for Information Extraction

abstract: Most existing tracking algorithms construct a representation of a target object prior to the tracking task starts, and utilize invariant features to handle appearance variation of the target caused by lighting, pose, and view angle change. In this paper, we present an efficient and effective online algorithm that incrementally learns and adapts a low dimensional eigenspace representation to reflect appearance changes of the target, thereby facilitating the tracking task. Furthermore, our incremental method correctly updates the sample mean and the eigenbasis, whereas existing incremental subspace update methods ignore the fact the sample mean varies over time. The tracking problem is formulated as a state inference problem within a Markov Chain Monte Carlo framework and a particle filter is incorporated for propagating sample distributions over time. Numerous experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed tracking algorithm in indoor and outdoor environments where the target objects undergo large pose and lighting changes.

paragraphs: This paper develops a visual tracker that learns its representation of the target while tracking it. The motivation is that lighting, pose, and viewing angle can change the object’s appearance after tracking begins. A compact representation that adapts to those changes can remain useful as new observations arrive.

The method incrementally updates a low-dimensional eigenspace representation. A specific contribution is that it updates both the sample mean and the eigenbasis, accounting for the fact that the average observed appearance changes over time. The authors contrast this with incremental subspace methods that neglect the changing mean.

Tracking is formulated as state inference within a Markov Chain Monte Carlo framework, with a particle filter carrying sample distributions forward over time. Experiments in indoor and outdoor environments demonstrate effectiveness when targets undergo large pose and lighting changes. The paper brings together evolving appearance learning and temporal state inference, making adaptation of the target model an ongoing part of the tracking procedure.
summary.tldr: An online visual tracker adapts a compact appearance model by updating both its mean and eigenbasis as the target changes.

title: Incremental Learning for Visual Tracking

abstract: It is well-known that everything that is learnable in the difﬁcult online setting, where an arbitrary sequences of examples must be labeled one at a time, is also learnable in the batch setting, where examples are drawn independently from a distribution. We show a result in the opposite di- rection. We give an efﬁcient conversion algorithm from batch to online that is transductive: it uses future unlabeled data. This demonstrates the equivalence between what is properly and efﬁciently learnable in a batch model and a transductive online model.
originalAbstract: It is well-known that everything that is learnable in the difﬁcult online setting, where an arbitrary sequences of examples must be labeled one at a time, is also learnable in the batch setting, where examples are drawn independently from a distribution. We show a result in the opposite di- rection. We give an efﬁcient conversion algorithm from batch to online that is transductive: it uses future unlabeled data. This demonstrates the equivalence between what is properly and efﬁciently learnable in a batch model and a transductive online model.

paragraphs: Batch learning and online learning place different demands on a learner. In the batch setting described here, examples are drawn independently from a distribution. In the online setting, an arbitrary sequence must be labeled one example at a time. The paper starts from the known direction that online learnability implies batch learnability and investigates a converse.

The authors provide an efficient procedure for converting a batch learning algorithm into an online one. The conversion is transductive: it has access to future examples without their labels. That access is a central condition of the result, because it gives the learner information about inputs it will later need to label while keeping their answers unknown.

The result establishes an equivalence between proper, efficient learnability in the batch model and in this transductive online model. Here, proper learning concerns predictions represented within the designated hypothesis class. The contribution clarifies how future unlabeled data can connect the two learning settings; it does not remove the transductive condition to establish the same equivalence for unrestricted online learning.
summary.tldr: An efficient conversion establishes equivalence between proper, efficient batch learning and online learning with access to future unlabeled inputs.

title: From Batch to Transductive Online Learning

abstract: In this paper we are presenting a novel multivariate analysis method. Our scheme is based on a novel kernel orthonormalized partial least squares (PLS) variant for feature extraction, imposing sparsity constrains in the solution to improve scalability. The algorithm is tested on a benchmark of UCI data sets, and on the analysis of integrated short-time music features for genre prediction. The upshot is that the method has strong expressive power even with rather few features, is clearly outperforming the ordinary kernel PLS, and therefore is an appealing method for feature extraction of labelled data.
originalAbstract: In this paper we are presenting a novel multivariate analysis method. Our scheme is based on a novel kernel orthonormalized partial least squares (PLS) variant for feature extraction, imposing sparsity constrains in the solution to improve scalability. The algorithm is tested on a benchmark of UCI data sets, and on the analysis of integrated short-time music features for genre prediction. The upshot is that the method has strong expressive power even with rather few features, is clearly outperforming the ordinary kernel PLS, and therefore is an appealing method for feature extraction of labelled data.

paragraphs: This paper develops a feature extraction method for labeled data using a new kernel orthonormalized partial least squares variant. Feature extraction seeks a representation that retains useful information in fewer variables. The authors focus on obtaining expressive features while making the method suitable for larger datasets.

Their approach imposes sparsity constraints on the solution to improve scalability. This brings the complexity of the learned representation into the design of the method itself. The intended combination is a kernel-based model with strong expressive capacity and a sparse solution that makes feature extraction more manageable as the amount of data grows.

The algorithm is evaluated on a benchmark of UCI datasets and on music genre prediction using integrated short-time music features. The authors report strong expressive power with relatively few extracted features and clear improvements over ordinary kernel PLS in their evaluations. These results support the method as an option for supervised feature extraction, particularly when a compact representation must still preserve information useful for the prediction task.
summary.tldr: A sparse kernel orthonormalized PLS method produces expressive compact features and outperforms ordinary kernel PLS in the reported evaluations.

title: Sparse Kernel Orthonormalized PLS for feature extraction in large data sets

abstract: Binocular fusion takes place over a limited region smaller than one degree of visual angle (Panum's fusional area), which is on the order of the range of preferred disparities measured in populations of disparity-tuned neurons in the visual cortex. However, the actual range of binocular disparities encountered in natural scenes ranges over tens of degrees. This discrepancy suggests that there must be a mechanism for detecting whether the stimulus disparity is either inside or outside of the range of the preferred disparities in the population. Here, we present a statistical framework to derive feature in a population of V1 disparity neuron to determine the stimulus disparity within the preferred disparity range of the neural population. When optimized for natural images, it yields a feature that can be explained by the normalization which is a common model in V1 neurons. We further makes use of the feature to estimate the disparity in natural images. Our proposed model generates more correct estimates than coarse-to-fine multiple scales approaches and it can also identify regions with occlusion. The approach suggests another critical role for normalization in robust disparity estimation.

paragraphs: The two eyes see slightly different images, and their displacement provides information about depth. Yet natural scenes contain a much wider range of binocular disparities than the preferred disparities of a population of cortical neurons. This paper addresses the resulting need to recognize when a stimulus falls within the population's useful disparity range.

The authors derive a statistical feature from the responses of V1 disparity neurons to help determine whether the disparity lies within that range. When optimized using natural images, the feature has an interpretation in terms of normalization, a common model of V1 processing. The same feature is then used to support disparity estimation in natural images.

The proposed model produces more correct estimates than the compared coarse-to-fine, multiple-scale approaches and can identify occluded regions. These findings connect confidence about the neural population's operating range with more robust estimation. They also suggest an additional role for normalization: helping a disparity system judge which image regions support a reliable estimate.
summary.tldr: A statistically derived feature interpretable as neural normalization helps assess disparity range, improve disparity estimates, and identify occlusions.

title: Estimating disparity with confidence from energy neurons

abstract: Support vector machines (SVM) are increasingly used in brain image analyses since they allow capturing complex multivariate relationships in the data. Moreover, when the kernel is linear, SVMs can be used to localize spatial patterns of discrimination between two groups of subjects. However, the features' spatial distribution is not taken into account. As a consequence, the optimal margin hyperplane is often scattered and lacks spatial coherence, making its anatomical interpretation difficult. This paper introduces a framework to spatially regularize SVM for brain image analysis. We show that Laplacian regularization provides a flexible framework to integrate various types of constraints and can be applied to both cortical surfaces and 3D brain images. The proposed framework is applied to the classification of MR images based on gray matter concentration maps and cortical thickness measures from 30 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 30 elderly controls. The results demonstrate that the proposed method enables natural spatial and anatomical regularization of the classifier.

paragraphs: Support vector machines can capture relationships across many brain-image measurements. With a linear kernel, their learned patterns can also help locate differences between groups. Standard fitting, however, does not account for where features lie in the brain. The resulting pattern can be spatially scattered, making its anatomical meaning difficult to interpret.

This paper introduces spatial regularization based on a Laplacian framework. The framework can incorporate different constraints and works with both cortical surfaces and three-dimensional brain images. Its purpose is to make spatial and anatomical relationships part of classifier fitting, so that the model's discriminating pattern is shaped by more than the measurements considered without spatial structure.

The authors apply the method to magnetic resonance images from 30 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 30 elderly controls, using gray matter concentration maps and cortical thickness measures. The results demonstrate natural spatial and anatomical regularization of the classifier. The stated contribution centers on incorporating meaningful structure into the learned pattern and supporting its anatomical interpretation.
summary.tldr: Laplacian regularization incorporates spatial and anatomical structure into SVMs for more coherent brain-image discrimination patterns.

title: Spatial and anatomical regularization of SVM for brain image analysis

abstract: In many clustering problems, we have access to multiple views of the data each of which could be individually used for clustering. Exploiting information from multiple views, one can hope to find a clustering that is more accurate than the ones obtained using the individual views. Since the true clustering would assign a point to the same cluster irrespective of the view, we can approach this problem by looking for clusterings that are consistent across the views, i.e., corresponding data points in each view should have same cluster membership. We propose a spectral clustering framework that achieves this goal by co-regularizing the clustering hypotheses, and propose two co-regularization schemes to accomplish this. Experimental comparisons with a number of baselines on two synthetic and three real-world datasets establish the efficacy of our proposed approaches.

paragraphs: A collection of items can have several views, each supplying information that could support clustering on its own. The paper asks how to use those views together. Its starting premise is that the intended cluster assignment for an item should remain the same regardless of which view is used to describe it.

The authors build a spectral clustering framework that encourages agreement between the clustering hypotheses associated with different views. They propose two co-regularization schemes for expressing this consistency requirement. The central idea is to make the views influence one another during clustering, so that the resulting assignments reflect both the available descriptions and their agreement about corresponding items.

Comparisons against several baselines on two synthetic and three real-world datasets support the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. The motivation is that multiple views may yield a more accurate clustering than individual views, and the experiments provide evidence for that hope in the tested settings. The shared-membership premise gives a concrete way to turn multiple descriptions into a coordinated clustering objective.
summary.tldr: Two co-regularization schemes improve multi-view spectral clustering by encouraging corresponding items to receive consistent cluster assignments.

title: Co-regularized Multi-view Spectral Clustering

abstract: In conventional causal discovery, structural equation models (SEM) are directly applied to the observed variables, meaning that the causal effect can be represented as a function of the direct causes themselves. However, in many real world problems, there are significant dependencies in the variances or energies, which indicates that causality may possibly take place at the level of variances or energies. In this paper, we propose a probabilistic causal scale-mixture model with spatiotemporal variance dependencies to represent a specific type of generating mechanism of the observations. In particular, the causal mechanism including contemporaneous and temporal causal relations in variances or energies is represented by a Structural Vector AutoRegressive model (SVAR). We prove the identifiability of this model under the non-Gaussian assumption on the innovation processes. We also propose algorithms to estimate the involved parameters and discover the contemporaneous causal structure. Experiments on synthesis and real world data are conducted to show the applicability of the proposed model and algorithms.

paragraphs: Conventional causal models describe how observed values depend on their direct causes. This paper considers a different possibility: causal relationships may operate through changes in variance or energy. Dependence in the strength of fluctuations can therefore be relevant even when a model focused on the observed values does not represent the intended mechanism.

The authors propose a probabilistic scale-mixture model for a specific observation-generating mechanism with variance dependencies across variables and time. A Structural Vector AutoRegressive model represents both contemporaneous relationships, occurring at the same time, and temporal relationships in variances or energies. This makes the level at which causality is modeled explicit.

The paper proves identifiability under a non-Gaussian assumption on the innovation processes. That assumption is part of the theoretical result, rather than a guarantee for arbitrary variance-dependent data. The authors also develop algorithms to estimate parameters and discover the contemporaneous causal structure. Experiments with synthetic and real data demonstrate the applicability of the model and algorithms to the proposed setting.
summary.tldr: A scale-mixture model represents causal relationships in variances or energies and is identifiable under non-Gaussian innovations.

title: Causal discovery with scale-mixture model for spatiotemporal variance dependencies

abstract: We present a novel approach to low-level vision problems that combines sparse coding and deep networks pre-trained with denoising auto-encoder (DA). We propose an alternative training scheme that successfully adapts DA, originally designed for unsupervised feature learning, to the tasks of image denoising and blind inpainting. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in the image denoising task. More importantly, in blind image inpainting task, the proposed method provides solutions to some complex problems that have not been tackled before. Specifically, we can automatically remove complex patterns like superimposed text from an image, rather than simple patterns like pixels missing at random. Moreover, the proposed method does not need the information regarding the region that requires inpainting to be given a priori. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in the tasks of image denoising and blind inpainting. We also show that our new training scheme for DA is more effective and can improve the performance of unsupervised feature learning.

paragraphs: Image denoising removes unwanted corruption, while inpainting reconstructs image regions that need repair. This paper combines sparse coding with deep networks pretrained using denoising autoencoders. Its main methodological change is an alternative training scheme that adapts denoising autoencoders from unsupervised feature learning to these image restoration tasks.

A central application is blind inpainting, where the region requiring repair is not supplied beforehand. The authors demonstrate removal of complex superimposed patterns, including text, extending beyond the simpler case of pixels missing at random. The approach therefore handles a setting in which the restoration system must operate without an externally provided map of the damaged region.

Experiments support the method's effectiveness for both denoising and blind inpainting, with state-of-the-art performance reported for denoising. The authors also find that their revised autoencoder training scheme is more effective for unsupervised feature learning. The contribution thus connects a change in representation training to practical restoration capabilities, including the stated ability to remove structured corruption without advance knowledge of its location.
summary.tldr: A revised denoising-autoencoder training scheme supports strong image denoising and removal of structured corruption without a supplied repair mask.

title: Image Denoising and Inpainting with Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Users want natural language processing (NLP) systems to be both fast and accurate, but quality often comes at the cost of speed. The field has been manually exploring various speed-accuracy tradeoffs (for particular problems and datasets). We aim to explore this space automatically, focusing here on the case of agenda-based syntactic parsing \cite{kay-1986}. Unfortunately, off-the-shelf reinforcement learning techniques fail to learn good policies: the state space is simply too large to explore naively. An attempt to counteract this by applying imitation learning algorithms also fails: the ``teacher'' is far too good to successfully imitate with our inexpensive features. Moreover, it is not specifically tuned for the known reward function. We propose a hybrid reinforcement/apprenticeship learning algorithm that, even with only a few inexpensive features, can automatically learn weights that achieve competitive accuracies at significant improvements in speed over state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: This paper seeks to learn the balance between speed and accuracy in natural language processing automatically. It focuses on agenda-based syntactic parsing, where prioritizing pending work affects both computation and the quality of the resulting analysis. The goal is to learn priorities using only a few inexpensive features.

The authors report that standard reinforcement learning performs poorly because the state space is too large for naive exploration. Imitation learning also fails in their setting: the teacher's behavior is too demanding to reproduce with the cheap features available to the learner. In addition, the teacher is not specifically optimized for the known reward function that expresses the desired tradeoff.

Their solution combines reinforcement learning with apprenticeship learning. This hybrid learns feature weights that achieve competitive parsing accuracy while substantially improving speed relative to the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. The finding supports learning a prioritization policy that fits both the available information and the computational objective, rather than assuming that direct exploration or teacher imitation alone will suffice.
summary.tldr: A hybrid reinforcement and apprenticeship learning method learns parsing priorities that substantially improve speed while retaining competitive accuracy.

title: Learned Prioritization for Trading Off Accuracy and Speed

abstract: Many applications in machine learning require optimizing unknown functions defined over a high-dimensional space from noisy samples that are expensive to obtain. We address this notoriously hard challenge, under the assumptions that the function varies only along some low-dimensional subspace and is smooth (i.e., it has a low norm in a Reproducible Kernel Hilbert Space). In particular, we present the SI-BO algorithm, which leverages recent low-rank matrix recovery techniques to learn the underlying subspace of the unknown function and applies Gaussian Process Upper Confidence sampling for optimization of the function. We carefully calibrate the exploration–exploitation tradeoff by allocating sampling budget to subspace estimation and function optimization, and obtain the first subexponential cumulative regret bounds and convergence rates for Bayesian optimization in high-dimensions under noisy observations. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in difficult scenarios.

paragraphs: Optimizing an unknown function is difficult when it has many inputs and each noisy evaluation is expensive. This paper assumes that the function actually changes only along a low-dimensional subspace. It also assumes smoothness, expressed through a low norm in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. These conditions provide structure that the optimization algorithm can exploit.

The proposed SI-BO algorithm first uses ideas from low-rank matrix recovery to learn the relevant subspace. It then uses Gaussian Process Upper Confidence sampling to optimize the function. The sampling budget must serve both purposes: discovering which directions matter and finding good function values within those directions.

The authors analyze this allocation to balance exploration and exploitation. Under the stated setting, they obtain subexponential cumulative regret bounds and convergence rates for high-dimensional Bayesian optimization with noisy observations. Numerical results demonstrate effectiveness in difficult scenarios. The result shows how learning a smaller underlying search space can make a structured high-dimensional optimization problem more manageable.
summary.tldr: SI-BO learns a low-dimensional active subspace and optimizes within it, with guarantees under stated subspace and smoothness assumptions.

title: High-Dimensional Gaussian Process Bandits

abstract: Many machine learning problems can be reduced to the maximization of submodular functions. Although well understood in the serial setting, the parallel maximization of submodular functions remains an open area of research with recent results only addressing monotone functions. The optimal algorithm for maximizing the more general class of non-monotone submodular functions was introduced by Buchbinder et al. and follows a strongly serial double-greedy logic and program analysis. In this work, we propose two methods to parallelize the double-greedy algorithm. The first, coordination-free approach emphasizes speed at the cost of a weaker approximation guarantee. The second, concurrency control approach guarantees a tight 1/2-approximation, at the quantifiable cost of additional coordination and reduced parallelism. As a consequence we explore the trade off space between guaranteed performance and objective optimality. We implement and evaluate both algorithms on multi-core hardware and billion edge graphs, demonstrating both the scalability and tradeoffs of each approach.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization appears in many machine learning problems, but moving effective serial algorithms into parallel execution can be difficult. This paper focuses on non-monotone objectives, the more general setting in which adding an item need not improve the objective. It develops two ways to parallelize the strongly sequential double-greedy algorithm.

The first method removes coordination to emphasize speed, accepting a weaker approximation guarantee. The second uses concurrency control and preserves a tight one-half approximation guarantee, at a quantifiable cost in coordination and available parallelism. These alternatives make explicit the relationship between execution speed and the strength of guaranteed solution quality.

The authors implement both methods on multicore hardware and evaluate them using graphs with a billion edges. The results demonstrate scalability and the practical tradeoffs of the two designs. The central contribution is therefore both algorithmic and comparative: it provides parallel methods while showing why maintaining a stronger optimization guarantee can require more coordination among concurrent operations.
summary.tldr: Two parallel double-greedy methods expose the tradeoff between faster coordination-free execution and preserving a tight one-half approximation guarantee.

title: Parallel Double Greedy Submodular Maximization

abstract: This paper identifies a severe problem of the counterfactual risk estimator typically used in batch learning from logged bandit feedback (BLBF), and proposes the use of an alternative estimator that avoids this problem.In the BLBF setting, the learner does not receive full-information feedback like in supervised learning, but observes feedback only for the actions taken by a historical policy.This makes BLBF algorithms particularly attractive for training online systems (e.g., ad placement, web search, recommendation) using their historical logs.The Counterfactual Risk Minimization (CRM) principle offers a general recipe for designing BLBF algorithms. It requires a counterfactual risk estimator, and virtually all existing works on BLBF have focused on a particular unbiased estimator.We show that this conventional estimator suffers from apropensity overfitting problem when used for learning over complex hypothesis spaces.We propose to replace the risk estimator with a self-normalized estimator, showing that it neatly avoids this problem.This naturally gives rise to a new learning algorithm -- Normalized Policy Optimizer for Exponential Models (Norm-POEM) --for structured output prediction using linear rules.We evaluate the empirical effectiveness of Norm-POEM on severalmulti-label classification problems, finding that it consistently outperforms the conventional estimator.

It requires a counterfactual risk estimator, and virtually all existing works on BLBF have focused on a particular unbiased estimator.We show that this conventional estimator suffers from apropensity overfitting problem when used for learning over complex hypothesis spaces.We propose to replace the risk estimator with a self-normalized estimator, showing that it neatly avoids this problem.This naturally gives rise to a new learning algorithm -- Normalized Policy Optimizer for Exponential Models (Norm-POEM) --for structured output prediction using linear rules.We evaluate the empirical effectiveness of Norm-POEM on severalmulti-label classification problems, finding that it consistently outperforms the conventional estimator.

paragraphs: Learning from logged bandit feedback means observing outcomes only for actions chosen by a historical policy. This differs from having full feedback for every possible action, but makes existing logs useful for training systems such as search, advertising, and recommendation. Counterfactual Risk Minimization provides a framework for learning in this setting using an estimated risk.

The paper identifies a problem with the conventional unbiased risk estimator when it is used to learn over complex hypothesis spaces: propensity overfitting. The finding highlights that an estimator's unbiasedness does not by itself establish that it behaves well as an optimization objective. The authors propose a self-normalized estimator and show that it avoids this identified problem.

The replacement leads to Norm-POEM, a learning algorithm for structured output prediction with linear rules. Evaluations on several multi-label classification problems find that it consistently outperforms the conventional estimator. The contribution therefore connects a diagnosis of an estimator's learning behavior to a concrete alternative and an implemented learning method with supporting empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: A self-normalized risk estimator avoids propensity overfitting in counterfactual learning and yields the empirically effective Norm-POEM algorithm.

title: The Self-Normalized Estimator for Counterfactual Learning

abstract: To infer a multilayer representation of high-dimensional count vectors, we propose the Poisson gamma belief network (PGBN) that factorizes each of its layers into the product of a connection weight matrix and the nonnegative real hidden units of the next layer. The PGBN's hidden layers are jointly trained with an upward-downward Gibbs sampler, each iteration of which upward samples Dirichlet distributed connection weight vectors starting from the first layer (bottom data layer), and then downward samples gamma distributed hidden units starting from the top hidden layer. The gamma-negative binomial process combined with a layer-wise training strategy allows the PGBN to infer the width of each layer given a fixed budget on the width of the first layer. The PGBN with a single hidden layer reduces to Poisson factor analysis. Example results on text analysis illustrate interesting relationships between the width of the first layer and the inferred network structure, and demonstrate that the PGBN, whose hidden units are imposed with correlated gamma priors, can add more layers to increase its performance gains over Poisson factor analysis, given the same limit on the width of the first layer.

paragraphs: The Poisson gamma belief network learns multilayer representations of high-dimensional count vectors. Each layer is factorized using a connection-weight matrix and the nonnegative hidden units of the next layer. With only one hidden layer, the model reduces to Poisson factor analysis, giving a direct connection between the proposed hierarchy and a simpler count-data model.

The hidden layers are trained jointly using an upward-downward Gibbs sampler. Each iteration samples Dirichlet-distributed connection weights moving upward from the data layer, then gamma-distributed hidden units moving downward from the top. A gamma-negative binomial process, combined with layer-wise training, allows the model to infer layer widths under a fixed budget for the first layer's width.

Text-analysis examples illustrate relationships between that first-layer budget and the inferred network structure. They also show that adding layers can increase performance gains over Poisson factor analysis under the same first-layer width limit. These findings support the usefulness of hierarchical representations with correlated gamma priors in the reported examples, rather than asserting that greater depth always helps.
summary.tldr: The Poisson gamma belief network learns hierarchical count-data representations and infers layer widths under a fixed first-layer budget.

title: The Poisson Gamma Belief Network

abstract: During the past few years, the machine learning community has paid attention to developping new methods for learning from weakly labeled data. This field covers different settings like semi-supervised learning, learning with label proportions, multi-instance learning, noise-tolerant learning, etc. This paper presents a generic framework to deal with these weakly labeled scenarios. We introduce the beta-risk as a generalized formulation of the standard empirical risk based on surrogate margin-based loss functions. This risk allows us to express the reliability on the labels and to derive different kinds of learning algorithms. We specifically focus on SVMs and propose a soft margin beta-svm algorithm which behaves better that the state of the art.
originalAbstract: During the past few years, the machine learning community has paid attention to developping new methods for learning from weakly labeled data. This field covers different settings like semi-supervised learning, learning with label proportions, multi-instance learning, noise-tolerant learning, etc. This paper presents a generic framework to deal with these weakly labeled scenarios. We introduce the beta-risk as a generalized formulation of the standard empirical risk based on surrogate margin-based loss functions. This risk allows us to express the reliability on the labels and to derive different kinds of learning algorithms. We specifically focus on SVMs and propose a soft margin beta-svm algorithm which behaves better that the state of the art.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning when labels provide incomplete or unreliable supervision. Its scope includes semi-supervised learning, learning from label proportions, multi-instance learning, and learning with noisy labels. These settings differ in what is known about the desired outputs, motivating a shared way to express the information available for training.

The proposed beta-risk generalizes standard empirical risk built from surrogate margin-based losses. Its key feature is the ability to represent label reliability within the training objective. This makes the treatment of uncertain supervision part of the risk formulation itself and provides a basis for deriving different learning algorithms within one framework.

The authors develop this idea specifically for support vector machines, introducing a soft-margin beta-SVM. They report that this algorithm performs better than the state of the art in the work presented. The contribution therefore combines a general formulation for weak supervision with a concrete classifier, connecting a flexible account of label reliability to an operational learning method.
summary.tldr: Beta-risk incorporates label reliability into a general learning objective and yields a soft-margin SVM for weak supervision.

title: beta-risk: a New Surrogate Risk for Learning from Weakly Labeled Data

abstract: Statistical methods for network data often parameterize the edge-probability by attributing latent traits such as block structure to the vertices and assume exchangeability in the sense of the Aldous-Hoover representation theorem. These assumptions are however incompatible with traits found in real-world networks such as a power-law degree-distribution. Recently, Caron & Fox (2014) proposed the use of a different notion of exchangeability after Kallenberg (2005) and obtained a network model which permits edge-inhomogeneity, such as a power-law degree-distribution whilst retaining desirable statistical properties. However, this model does not capture latent vertex traits such as block-structure. In this work we re-introduce the use of block-structure for network models obeying Kallenberg’s notion of exchangeability and thereby obtain a collapsed model which both admits the inference of block-structure and edge inhomogeneity. We derive a simple expression for the likelihood and an efficient sampling method. The obtained model is not significantly more difficult to implement than existing approaches to block-modelling and performs well on real network datasets.

paragraphs: Network models often describe connections through hidden properties of vertices, such as membership in groups. However, the abstract identifies a conflict between a commonly used exchangeability framework and network properties such as power-law degree distributions. An alternative exchangeability framework already allowed heterogeneous connectivity, but its existing model did not capture hidden group structure.

This paper brings block structure into that alternative framework using completely random measures. The resulting model supports inference about both vertex groups and uneven connectivity. These are distinct aspects of a network: identifying groups describes its organization, while accounting for edge inhomogeneity allows vertices to differ in how extensively they connect.

The authors derive a simple likelihood expression and an efficient sampling method for the collapsed model. They report that implementation is not significantly harder than existing block-modeling approaches and that the method performs well on real network datasets. Its main value is combining group discovery with a framework that permits heterogeneous sparse-network behavior, while retaining a practical route to statistical inference.
summary.tldr: The paper combines hidden network groups and heterogeneous connectivity within a statistical framework suitable for sparse networks.

title: Completely random measures for modelling block-structured sparse networks

abstract: We propose and analyze a new estimator of the covariance matrix that admits strong theoretical guarantees under weak assumptions on the underlying distribution, such as existence of moments of only low order. While estimation of covariance matrices corresponding to sub-Gaussian distributions is well-understood, much less in known in the case of heavy-tailed data. As K. Balasubramanian and M. Yuan write, data from real-world experiments oftentimes tend to be corrupted with outliers and/or exhibit heavy tails. In such cases, it is not clear that those covariance matrix estimators .. remain optimal'' and ..what are the other possible strategies to deal with heavy tailed distributions warrant further studies.'' We make a step towards answering this question and prove tight deviation inequalities for the proposed estimator that depend only on the parameters controlling the ``intrinsic dimension'' associated to the covariance matrix (as opposed to the dimension of the ambient space); in particular, our results are applicable in the case of high-dimensional observations.

paragraphs: A covariance matrix describes how variables fluctuate together. Estimating it becomes more challenging when the data have heavy tails, so unusually large observations occur more readily than in well-behaved sub-Gaussian settings. The paper addresses this gap by proposing a covariance estimator with theoretical guarantees that require only weak distributional assumptions, including the existence of low-order moments.

The main analysis establishes tight deviation inequalities for the estimator. These inequalities control how far its estimate can depart from the population covariance. Their dependence is expressed through parameters describing the covariance matrix’s intrinsic dimension, rather than the full number of coordinates in each observation.

That distinction matters for high-dimensional data: the number of recorded variables need not be the only measure governing the guarantee. The covariance structure itself determines the relevant intrinsic-dimension parameters. The result provides a theoretically supported strategy for heavy-tailed covariance estimation and applies to high-dimensional observations, extending the available analysis beyond the better-understood sub-Gaussian case.
summary.tldr: A covariance estimator obtains tight error guarantees for heavy-tailed data using intrinsic-dimension parameters and weak moment assumptions.

title: Estimation of the covariance structure of heavy-tailed distributions

abstract: Kernel machines as well as neural networks possess universal function approximation properties. Nevertheless in practice their ways of choosing the appropriate function class differ. Specifically neural networks learn a representation by adapting their basis functions to the data and the task at hand, while kernel methods typically use a basis that is not adapted during training. In this work, we contrast random features of approximated kernel machines with learned features of neural networks. Our analysis reveals how these random and adaptive basis functions affect the quality of learning. Furthermore, we present basis adaptation schemes that allow for a more compact representation, while retaining the generalization properties of kernel machines.

paragraphs: Kernel methods and neural networks both have broad abilities to approximate functions, yet they build useful representations differently. Neural networks adapt their internal features to the training data and task. Kernel methods typically work with a basis that stays fixed during training. This paper investigates how that distinction affects the quality of learning in practice.

The study compares random features used to approximate kernel machines with features learned by neural networks. The central question concerns the ingredients used to represent a function: how much does it matter whether those ingredients are chosen randomly or adjusted through learning? The empirical analysis examines the consequences of these choices beyond their shared approximation capabilities.

The authors also introduce ways to adapt the basis of a kernel representation. These schemes produce more compact representations while retaining the generalization properties of kernel machines. The contribution therefore connects the comparison to a practical design direction: feature adaptation can reduce representation size while preserving the useful learning behavior associated with the kernel approach.
summary.tldr: The paper studies random versus learned features and introduces basis adaptation schemes for more compact kernel representations.

title: An Empirical Study on The Properties of Random Bases for Kernel Methods

abstract: This paper introduces and addresses a wide class of stochastic bandit problems where the function mapping the arm to the corresponding reward exhibits some known structural properties. Most existing structures (e.g. linear, lipschitz, unimodal, combinatorial, dueling,...) are covered by our framework. We derive an asymptotic instance-specific regret lower bound for these problems, and develop OSSB, an algorithm whose regret matches this fundamental limit. OSSB is not based on the classical principle of ``optimism in the face of uncertainty'' or on Thompson sampling, and rather aims at matching the minimal exploration rates of sub-optimal arms as characterized in the derivation of the regret lower bound. We illustrate the efficiency of OSSB using numerical experiments in the case of the linear bandit problem and show that OSSB outperforms existing algorithms, including Thompson sampling
