paragraphs: In a stochastic bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses an arm and observes a random reward. This paper considers problems where the relationship between arms and rewards has known structure. Its framework encompasses many established forms, including linear, Lipschitz, unimodal, combinatorial, and dueling structures.

The authors derive an asymptotic regret lower bound specific to each problem instance. Regret measures the loss associated with choosing less rewarding arms, and the bound describes an unavoidable exploration cost. Their OSSB algorithm matches this limit by targeting the minimum exploration rates for suboptimal arms identified in the lower-bound analysis.

This design differs from optimism-based algorithms and Thompson sampling: exploration is explicitly organized around the rates needed to reach the theoretical limit. Numerical experiments on linear bandits show OSSB outperforming existing algorithms, including Thompson sampling. The theoretical result is asymptotic, while the experimental advantage is demonstrated in the linear setting. Together, these contributions connect a broad structural framework with an exploration strategy derived from its fundamental limits.
summary.tldr: OSSB targets theoretically minimal exploration rates and matches an instance-specific asymptotic regret bound for structured stochastic bandits.

title: Minimal Exploration in Structured Stochastic Bandits

abstract: We derive uniformly most powerful (UMP) tests for simple and one-sided hypotheses for a population proportion within the framework of Differential Privacy (DP), optimizing finite sample performance. We show that in general, DP hypothesis tests can be written in terms of linear constraints, and for exchangeable data can always be expressed as a function of the empirical distribution. Using this structure, we prove a ‘Neyman-Pearson lemma’ for binomial data under DP, where the DP-UMP only depends on the sample sum. Our tests can also be stated as a post-processing of a random variable, whose distribution we coin “Truncated-Uniform-Laplace” (Tulap), a generalization of the Staircase and discrete Laplace distributions. Furthermore, we obtain exact p-values, which are easily computed in terms of the Tulap random variable. We show that our results also apply to distribution-free hypothesis tests for continuous data. Our simulation results demonstrate that our tests have exact type I error, and are more powerful than current techniques.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to test claims about a population proportion while satisfying differential privacy. It derives uniformly most powerful tests for simple and one-sided hypotheses, focusing on performance at finite sample sizes. Within the relevant privacy and testing constraints, the goal is to maximize the ability to detect alternatives.

The authors express privacy requirements for hypothesis tests as linear constraints. For exchangeable data, they show that tests can be expressed using the empirical distribution. They use this structure to establish a private counterpart of the Neyman-Pearson lemma for binomial observations, where the resulting optimal test depends only on the sample sum.

The tests can also be implemented by processing a random variable from a newly introduced distribution called Tulap. This representation provides easily computed exact p-values. The authors extend their results to distribution-free tests for continuous data, and simulations show exact type I error and higher power than existing techniques. These findings connect privacy constraints to concrete optimal testing procedures.
summary.tldr: The paper derives optimal differentially private tests for specified binomial hypotheses, with exact p-values and finite-sample error control.

title: Differentially Private Uniformly Most Powerful Tests for Binomial Data

abstract: We introduce two novel tree search algorithms that use a policy to guide search. The first algorithm is a best-first enumeration that uses a cost function that allows us to provide an upper bound on the number of nodes to be expanded before reaching a goal state. We show that this best-first algorithm is particularly well suited for ``needle-in-a-haystack'' problems. The second algorithm, which is based on sampling, provides an upper bound on the expected number of nodes to be expanded before reaching a set of goal states. We show that this algorithm is better suited for problems where many paths lead to a goal. We validate these tree search algorithms on 1,000 computer-generated levels of Sokoban, where the policy used to guide search comes from a neural network trained using A3C. Our results show that the policy tree search algorithms we introduce are competitive with a state-of-the-art domain-independent planner that uses heuristic search.

paragraphs: A policy can guide a search procedure toward promising actions, but the search algorithm determines how that guidance is used. This paper introduces two policy-guided tree search methods and gives guarantees on how many nodes they expand before finding goals. The methods target different patterns in the paths that lead to successful outcomes.

The first uses best-first enumeration with a cost function that supports an upper bound on node expansions before reaching a goal. It is particularly suited to needle-in-a-haystack problems. The second uses sampling and bounds the expected number of expansions before reaching a set of goals. It is better suited to cases where many paths can lead to success.

The authors evaluate both algorithms on 1,000 computer-generated Sokoban levels. A neural policy trained using A3C guides the search. The results are competitive with a state-of-the-art domain-independent heuristic planner. The contribution therefore combines practical policy-guided search with distinct guarantees that clarify how the two algorithms fit different goal-path structures.
summary.tldr: Two policy-guided tree search algorithms bound search effort and suit different settings with rare or numerous paths to goals.

title: Single-Agent Policy Tree Search With Guarantees

abstract: The recent advances in Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have shown extremely good results for video human action classification, however, action detection is still a challenging problem. The current action detection approaches follow a complex pipeline which involves multiple tasks such as tube proposals, optical flow, and tube classification. In this work, we present a more elegant solution for action detection based on the recently developed capsule network. We propose a 3D capsule network for videos, called VideoCapsuleNet: a unified network for action detection which can jointly perform pixel-wise action segmentation along with action classification. The proposed network is a generalization of capsule network from 2D to 3D, which takes a sequence of video frames as input. The 3D generalization drastically increases the number of capsules in the network, making capsule routing computationally expensive. We introduce capsule-pooling in the convolutional capsule layer to address this issue and make the voting algorithm tractable. The routing-by-agreement in the network inherently models the action representations and various action characteristics are captured by the predicted capsules. This inspired us to utilize the capsules for action localization and the class-specific capsules predicted by the network are used to determine a pixel-wise localization of actions. The localization is further improved by parameterized skip connections with the convolutional capsule layers and the network is trained end-to-end with a classification as well as localization loss. The proposed network achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple action detection datasets including UCF-Sports, J-HMDB, and UCF-101 (24 classes) with an impressive ~20% improvement on UCF-101 and ~15% improvement on J-HMDB in terms of v-mAP scores.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in a video does not by itself identify the pixels where that action occurs. VideoCapsuleNet addresses classification and pixel-wise action segmentation together in a unified network. It extends capsule networks from images to sequences of video frames, representing action information through a three-dimensional capsule architecture.

That extension greatly increases the number of capsules and makes routing expensive. The authors introduce capsule pooling to make the voting procedure tractable. Class-specific capsules support action localization, and parameterized skip connections from convolutional capsule layers further improve it. The whole network is trained end to end using both classification and localization losses.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on UCF-Sports, J-HMDB, and the 24-class UCF-101 action-detection dataset. Reported v-mAP improvements are approximately 20% on UCF-101 and 15% on J-HMDB. These findings support a unified capsule-based approach that combines recognition with localization, while the pooling mechanism addresses the computational cost of bringing capsule routing into video.
summary.tldr: VideoCapsuleNet jointly classifies and localizes actions using a 3D capsule network with pooling that makes video routing tractable.

title: VideoCapsuleNet: A Simplified Network for Action Detection

abstract: The goal of confidence-set learning in the binary classification setting is to construct two sets, each with a specific probability guarantee to cover a class. An observation outside the overlap of the two sets is deemed to be from one of the two classes, while the overlap is an ambiguity region which could belong to either class. Instead of plug-in approaches, we propose a support vector classifier to construct confidence sets in a flexible manner. Theoretically, we show that the proposed learner can control the non-coverage rates and minimize the ambiguity with high probability. Efficient algorithms are developed and numerical studies illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Instead of plug-in approaches, we propose a support vector classifier to construct confidence sets in a flexible manner. Efficient algorithms are developed and numerical studies illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Binary classification does not always need to force an unambiguous label for every observation. Confidence-set learning instead constructs one set for each class, with a specified probability guarantee that the set covers that class. Where the two sets overlap, the procedure explicitly allows either label, representing ambiguity in the classification.

This paper proposes a support vector classifier for constructing those sets flexibly. The learning task must balance two goals: keeping each class’s non-coverage rate under control and making the ambiguous overlap small. Treating these goals together connects the reliability of the sets with how often the resulting classification can give a definite answer.

The authors prove that their learner can control non-coverage and minimize ambiguity with high probability. They also develop efficient algorithms and provide numerical evidence of effectiveness. The contribution is a direct support-vector approach to learning class-covering sets, with theoretical guarantees addressing both coverage and uncertainty. Its output makes ambiguity part of the prediction rule rather than requiring every observation to receive a single class.
summary.tldr: A support-vector method learns class confidence sets while controlling non-coverage and reducing ambiguous overlap with high probability.

title: Learning Confidence Sets using Support Vector Machines

abstract: Prior work has investigated variations of prediction markets that preserve participants' (differential) privacy, which formed the basis of useful mechanisms for purchasing data for machine learning objectives. Such markets required potentially unlimited financial subsidy, however, making them impractical. In this work, we design an adaptively-growing prediction market with a bounded financial subsidy, while achieving privacy, incentives to produce accurate predictions, and precision in the sense that market prices are not heavily impacted by the added privacy-preserving noise. We briefly discuss how our mechanism can extend to the data-purchasing setting, and its relationship to traditional learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: Prior work has investigated variations of prediction markets that preserve participants' (differential) privacy, which formed the basis of useful mechanisms for purchasing data for machine learning objectives. Such markets required potentially unlimited financial subsidy, however, making them impractical. In this work, we design an adaptively-growing prediction market with a bounded financial subsidy, while achieving privacy, incentives to produce accurate predictions, and precision in the sense that market prices are not heavily impacted by the added privacy-preserving noise. We briefly discuss how our mechanism can extend to the data-purchasing setting, and its relationship to traditional learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Prediction markets combine participants’ forecasts into market prices. Making these markets differentially private requires protecting information about individual participants, but earlier private designs could require an unlimited financial subsidy. That creates a practical obstacle: an operator might be unable to place a firm bound on the money needed to sustain the market.

The paper designs a prediction market that grows adaptively while keeping its required subsidy bounded. Its contribution is to achieve this financial constraint together with three other properties: participant privacy, incentives for accurate predictions, and prices that are not heavily distorted by the noise added for privacy. These properties matter jointly because a financially manageable market would have limited value if its privacy mechanism undermined its forecasts.

The result establishes that bounded subsidy can coexist with the paper’s privacy, incentive, and precision requirements. The authors also briefly discuss extending the mechanism to purchasing data for machine learning and its relationship to traditional learning algorithms. Those connections broaden the motivation beyond forecasting, while remaining extensions discussed by the paper.
summary.tldr: An adaptively growing prediction market combines differential privacy, useful prices, and prediction incentives with a bounded financial subsidy.

title: Bounded-Loss Private Prediction Markets

abstract: While deep reinforcement learning has successfully solved many challenging control tasks, its real-world applicability has been limited by the inability to ensure the safety of learned policies. We propose an approach to verifiable reinforcement learning by training decision tree policies, which can represent complex policies (since they are nonparametric), yet can be efficiently verified using existing techniques (since they are highly structured). The challenge is that decision tree policies are difficult to train. We propose VIPER, an algorithm that combines ideas from model compression and imitation learning to learn decision tree policies guided by a DNN policy (called the oracle) and its Q-function, and show that it substantially outperforms two baselines. We use VIPER to (i) learn a provably robust decision tree policy for a variant of Atari Pong with a symbolic state space, (ii) learn a decision tree policy for a toy game based on Pong that provably never loses, and (iii) learn a provably stable decision tree policy for cart-pole. In each case, the decision tree policy achieves performance equal to that of the original DNN policy.

In each case, the decision tree policy achieves performance equal to that of the original DNN policy.

paragraphs: Strong control performance does not automatically provide a guarantee about a learned policy's behavior. This paper pursues verifiable reinforcement learning by extracting decision tree policies from a trained deep network. Decision trees can represent complex behavior while offering a structure that existing verification techniques can analyze efficiently.

The proposed algorithm, VIPER, combines model compression and imitation learning. It learns a decision tree under guidance from a neural network policy and that policy's Q-function. This addresses the difficulty of training effective tree policies directly. The authors report that VIPER substantially outperforms two baselines, supporting the usefulness of this guided extraction process.

The demonstrations establish different properties in three settings: robustness for a symbolic-state variant of Atari Pong, never losing in a toy Pong-based game, and stability for cart-pole. In every case, the extracted tree matches the original network's performance. These are task-specific verified properties, showing that policy extraction can preserve performance while enabling formal analysis of the resulting controller in the demonstrated environments.
summary.tldr: VIPER extracts decision tree policies that match neural policy performance while enabling verified robustness, game outcomes, or stability in three demonstrated settings.

title: Verifiable Reinforcement Learning via Policy Extraction

abstract: We investigate multiarmed bandits with delayed feedback, where the delays need neither be identical nor bounded. We first prove that "delayed" Exp3 achieves the $O(\sqrt{(KT + D)\ln K})$ regret bound conjectured by Cesa-Bianchi et al. [2016] in the case of variable, but bounded delays. Here, $K$ is the number of actions and $D$ is the total delay over $T$ rounds. We then introduce a new algorithm that lifts the requirement of bounded delays by using a wrapper that skips rounds with excessively large delays. The new algorithm maintains the same regret bound, but similar to its predecessor requires prior knowledge of $D$ and $T$. For this algorithm we then construct a novel doubling scheme that forgoes the prior knowledge requirement under the assumption that the delays are available at action time (rather than at loss observation time). This assumption is satisfied in a broad range of applications, including interaction with servers and service providers. The resulting oracle regret bound is of order $\min_\beta (|S_\beta|+\beta \ln K + (KT + D_\beta)/\beta)$, where $|S_\beta|$ is the number of observations with delay exceeding $\beta$, and $D_\beta$ is the total delay of observations with delay below $\beta$. The bound relaxes to $O(\sqrt{(KT + D)\ln K})$, but we also provide examples where $D_\beta \ll D$ and the oracle bound has a polynomially better dependence on the problem parameters.

paragraphs: In bandit learning, the outcome of an action may arrive only after later decisions have already been made. This paper studies delays that can vary and need not have a fixed upper bound. It first establishes a regret guarantee for delayed Exp3 with variable bounded delays, depending on the number of actions, rounds, and total delay.

The authors then remove the bounded-delay requirement through a wrapper that skips rounds whose feedback is excessively delayed. This preserves the same regret bound but initially requires advance knowledge of the horizon and total delay. A new doubling scheme removes that prior-knowledge requirement when the delay is known at action time, an assumption the paper identifies as applicable to various service interactions.

The resulting oracle bound balances the cost of skipping long-delayed observations against the accumulated delay of the observations retained. It implies the original square-root regret bound, while the authors also give examples where it has polynomially better dependence on problem parameters. The analysis therefore distinguishes a few extreme delays from the more informative delay profile of the remaining observations.
summary.tldr: Skipping excessively delayed feedback enables bandit regret guarantees without bounded delays, with stronger adaptation when delays are known at action time.

title: Nonstochastic Multiarmed Bandits with Unrestricted Delays

abstract: Reasoning is an important ability that we learn from a very early age. Yet, reasoning is extremely hard for algorithms. Despite impressive recent progress that has been reported on tasks that necessitate reasoning, such as visual question answering and visual dialog, models often exploit biases in datasets. To develop models with better reasoning abilities, recently, the new visual commonsense reasoning(VCR) task has been introduced. Not only do models have to answer questions, but also do they have to provide a reason for the given answer. The proposed baseline achieved compelling results, leveraging a meticulously designed model composed of LSTM modules and attention nets. Here we show that a much simpler model obtained by ablating and pruning the existing intricate baseline can perform better with half the number of trainable parameters. By associating visual features with attribute information and better text to image grounding, we obtain further improvements for our simpler & effective baseline, TAB-VCR. We show that this approach results in a 5.3%, 4.4% and 6.5% absolute improvement over the previous state-of-the-art on question answering, answer justification and holistic VCR. Webpage: https://deanplayerljx.github.io/tabvcr/

paragraphs: Visual commonsense reasoning asks a model both to answer a question about an image and to justify the answer. This paper examines whether a complicated baseline is necessary for strong performance on that task. The motivation includes concern that apparent reasoning success can reflect dataset biases rather than the intended ability.

The authors simplify the existing baseline through ablation and pruning, obtaining better performance with half as many trainable parameters. They then improve this simpler model by associating visual features with attributes and strengthening text-to-image grounding. These additions emphasize the information available about visual content and how language is connected to it.

The resulting TAB-VCR model improves over the previous state of the art by 5.3 percentage points on question answering, 4.4 on answer justification, and 6.5 on holistic VCR. These benchmark gains show that architectural simplification can coexist with improved performance. They also highlight the value of richer visual attributes and better grounding within the proposed simpler baseline.
summary.tldr: TAB-VCR improves visual commonsense reasoning with a simpler baseline, visual attributes, and better text-to-image grounding.

title: TAB-VCR: Tags and Attributes based VCR Baselines

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering several sparse signal vectors from linear measurements when the identity of the measured signal is unknown. Each measurement uses a signal drawn uniformly from the collection and may contain noise. The problem extends compressed sensing by requiring recovery of a collection of signals from measurements whose source labels are hidden.

In the noisy setting, the authors give a method that handles more than two signal vectors, resolving an open question from earlier work. They also provide robust reconstruction: when the underlying signals are not exactly sparse, the algorithm still learns good sparse approximations. This broadens the recovery goal from ideal sparse signals to signals that only approximately have that structure.

For both noisy and noiseless measurements, the methods avoid a restrictive assumption required by previous work. The techniques differ between the settings: noiseless recovery uses a property of sparse polynomials, while noisy recovery develops connections to learning Gaussian mixtures. Together, the results extend the range of sparse-mixture recovery problems covered by algorithmic guarantees.
summary.tldr: New recovery methods handle noisy mixtures of more than two sparse signals and remain robust when the signals are only approximately sparse.

title: Sample Complexity of Learning Mixture of Sparse Linear Regressions

abstract: Novelty detection, a fundamental task in machine learning, has drawn a lot of recent attention due to its wide-ranging applications and the rise of neural approaches. In this work, we present a general framework for neural novelty detection that centers around a multivariate extension of the univariate quantile function. Our framework unifies and extends many classical and recent novelty detection algorithms, and opens the way to exploit recent advances in flow-based neural density estimation. We adapt the multiple gradient descent algorithm to obtain the first efficient end-to-end implementation of our framework that is free of tuning hyperparameters. Extensive experiments over a number of real datasets confirm the efficacy of our proposed method against state-of-the-art alternatives.

In this work, we present a general framework for neural novelty detection that centers around a multivariate extension of the univariate quantile function. Our framework unifies and extends many classical and recent novelty detection algorithms, and opens the way to exploit recent advances in flow-based neural density estimation. We adapt the multiple gradient descent algorithm to obtain the first efficient end-to-end implementation of our framework that is free of tuning hyperparameters. Extensive experiments over a number of real datasets confirm the efficacy of our proposed method against state-of-the-art alternatives.

paragraphs: Novelty detection concerns identifying observations that depart from familiar data. This paper develops a general neural framework for the task around a multivariate extension of the quantile function. Quantiles provide a way to describe positions within a distribution; extending that idea to multiple variables supplies the organizing principle for the proposed approach.

The framework brings together and extends a range of classical and recent novelty-detection algorithms. It also creates a route for using progress in flow-based neural density estimation. These connections matter because the contribution is broader than a single isolated detector: it provides a common formulation through which existing methods and newer density models can be related.

To make the framework practical, the authors adapt the multiple gradient descent algorithm and obtain an efficient end-to-end implementation described as free of tuning hyperparameters. Extensive experiments on several real datasets support its effectiveness against state-of-the-art alternatives. The stated findings combine a unifying mathematical framework with an implemented training procedure and empirical evidence that the resulting detector is useful.
summary.tldr: A multivariate quantile framework unifies novelty detectors and enables an efficient neural implementation without tuning hyperparameters.

title: Multivariate Triangular Quantile Maps for Novelty Detection

abstract: Humans reason with concepts and metaconcepts: we recognize red and blue from visual input; we also understand that they are colors, i.e., red is an instance of color. In this paper, we propose the visual concept-metaconcept learner (VCML) for joint learning of concepts and metaconcepts from images and associated question-answer pairs. The key is to exploit the bidirectional connection between visual concepts and metaconcepts. Visual representations provide grounding cues for predicting relations between unseen pairs of concepts. Knowing that red and blue are instances of color, we generalize to the fact that green is also an instance of color since they all categorize the hue of objects. Meanwhile, knowledge about metaconcepts empowers visual concept learning from limited, noisy, and even biased data. From just a few examples of purple cubes we can understand a new color purple, which resembles the hue of the cubes instead of the shape of them. Evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets validates our claims.

paragraphs: The paper distinguishes visual concepts, such as red and blue, from metaconcepts, such as color. Recognizing a visual property and understanding what kind of property it is are related abilities. The visual concept-metaconcept learner jointly learns both from images and associated question-answer pairs, using information that flows in both directions.

Visual representations help predict relationships between concept pairs that have not been observed together. For example, shared sensitivity to hue can support recognizing another concept as a color. Conversely, knowing the metaconcept can guide learning from limited, noisy, or biased examples, helping distinguish which visual attribute defines a new concept.

The abstract illustrates this with purple cubes: knowledge about color can help associate purple with hue rather than cube shape, even from only a few examples. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets support the claimed benefits of this bidirectional connection. The contribution is a joint learning approach in which visual grounding and knowledge about categories of concepts reinforce one another.
summary.tldr: VCML jointly learns visual concepts and metaconcepts so visual evidence and conceptual relationships can improve each other.

title: Visual Concept-Metaconcept Learning

abstract: We present ViLBERT (short for Vision-and-Language BERT), a model for learning task-agnostic joint representations of image content and natural language. We extend the popular BERT architecture to a multi-modal two-stream model, processing both visual and textual inputs in separate streams that interact through co-attentional transformer layers. We pretrain our model through two proxy tasks on the large, automatically collected Conceptual Captions dataset and then transfer it to multiple established vision-and-language tasks -- visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, referring expressions, and caption-based image retrieval -- by making only minor additions to the base architecture. We observe significant improvements across tasks compared to existing task-specific models -- achieving state-of-the-art on all four tasks. Our work represents a shift away from learning groundings between vision and language only as part of task training and towards treating visual grounding as a pretrainable and transferable capability.

paragraphs: ViLBERT learns representations that connect images and language before specializing in a particular downstream task. It extends BERT into a two-stream architecture: visual inputs and text are processed separately, while co-attentional transformer layers let the streams interact. This provides a shared model for learning relationships between the two input types.

The authors pretrain the model using two proxy tasks on the automatically collected Conceptual Captions dataset. They then transfer it to visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, referring expressions, and caption-based image retrieval. Only minor additions to the base architecture are needed for these different tasks.

The evaluations report significant improvements over existing task-specific models and state-of-the-art results on all four tasks. These findings support treating visual grounding—the connection between language and image content—as a capability that can be pretrained and transferred. The contribution is both architectural and methodological: interacting visual and textual streams are used to learn representations that serve several downstream purposes.
summary.tldr: ViLBERT pretrains interacting visual and language streams that transfer successfully to four vision-and-language tasks.

title: ViLBERT: Pretraining Task-Agnostic Visiolinguistic Representations for Vision-and-Language Tasks

abstract: We create a computationally tractable learning algorithm for contextual bandits with continuous actions having unknown structure. The new reduction-style algorithm composes with most supervised learning representations. We prove that this algorithm works in a general sense and verify the new functionality with large-scale experiments.
originalAbstract: We create a computationally tractable learning algorithm for contextual bandits with continuous actions having unknown structure. The new reduction-style algorithm composes with most supervised learning representations. We prove that this algorithm works in a general sense and verify the new functionality with large-scale experiments.

paragraphs: This paper addresses contextual bandit learning when actions range over a continuous space and the structure of that space is unknown. The central objective is computational tractability: the authors seek a learning procedure that can work in this setting while remaining feasible to compute. Continuous actions are a defining part of the problem being addressed.

The proposed algorithm uses a reduction-based design and can be combined with most supervised learning representations. This compatibility matters because the bandit method can work with a broad range of representations used for supervised learning. The contribution therefore includes both an algorithm for the continuous-action setting and a way to connect it to existing representation choices.

The authors provide a general theoretical result supporting the algorithm and verify its new functionality through large-scale experiments. The theory and experiments supply complementary evidence: one supports the method analytically, while the other demonstrates it in empirical use. Together, the stated results establish a computationally tractable approach with broad representational compatibility.
summary.tldr: A tractable reduction-based algorithm handles contextual bandits with continuous actions and works with most supervised learning representations.

title: Efficient Contextual Bandits with Continuous Actions

abstract: In this paper, we consider domain-invariant deep learning by explicitly modeling domain shifts with only a small amount of domain-specific parameters in a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). By exploiting the observation that a convolutional filter can be well approximated as a linear combination of a small set of dictionary atoms, we show for the first time, both empirically and theoretically, that domain shifts can be effectively handled by decomposing a convolutional layer into a domain-specific atom layer and a domain-shared coefficient layer, while both remain convolutional. An input channel will now first convolve spatially only with each respective domain-specific dictionary atom to ``absorb" domain variations, and then output channels are linearly combined using common decomposition coefficients trained to promote shared semantics across domains. We use toy examples, rigorous analysis, and real-world examples with diverse datasets and architectures, to show the proposed plug-in framework's effectiveness in cross and joint domain performance and domain adaptation. With the proposed architecture, we need only a small set of dictionary atoms to model each additional domain, which brings a negligible amount of additional parameters, typically a few hundred.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a convolutional neural network can work across domains while adding very few parameters for each domain. Its starting observation is that a convolutional filter can be approximated by combining a small collection of building blocks, called dictionary atoms. The authors use this decomposition to separate domain-specific variation from information shared across domains.

Each convolutional layer becomes two convolutional layers with different responsibilities. The first applies spatial filters using atoms specific to the input's domain, aiming to absorb domain variations. The second combines channels using coefficients shared across domains. Training these shared coefficients promotes common semantic information, while the atoms provide a compact place to represent differences.

The authors support this design with theoretical analysis, toy examples, and experiments across datasets and architectures. They report effectiveness for cross-domain performance, joint-domain performance, and domain adaptation. Adding another domain requires only a small dictionary, typically a few hundred extra parameters. The contribution is therefore a concrete way to accommodate domain differences without duplicating an entire network.
summary.tldr: Splitting convolutional filters into domain-specific atoms and shared coefficients supports learning across domains with very few additional parameters.

title: A Dictionary Approach to Domain-Invariant Learning in Deep Networks

abstract: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) approaches promise to provide more efficient solutions to sequential decision making problems, both in terms of statistical as well as computational efficiency. While this has been demonstrated empirically over time in a variety of tasks, theoretical results quantifying the benefits of such methods are still few and far between. In this paper, we discuss the kind of structure in a Markov decision process which gives rise to efficient HRL methods. Specifically, we formalize the intuition that HRL can exploit well repeating "subMDPs", with similar reward and transition structure. We show that, under reasonable assumptions, a model-based Thompson sampling-style HRL algorithm that exploits this structure is statistically efficient, as established through a finite-time regret bound. We also establish conditions under which planning with structure-induced options is near-optimal and computationally efficient.

While this has been demonstrated empirically over time in a variety of tasks, theoretical results quantifying the benefits of such methods are still few and far between. In this paper, we discuss the kind of structure in a Markov decision process which gives rise to efficient HRL methods. Specifically, we formalize the intuition that HRL can exploit well repeating "subMDPs", with similar reward and transition structure. We show that, under reasonable assumptions, a model-based Thompson sampling-style HRL algorithm that exploits this structure is statistically efficient, as established through a finite-time regret bound. We also establish conditions under which planning with structure-induced options is near-optimal and computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning promises to make sequential decisions more efficiently, both in the experience needed for learning and in the computation needed for planning. The paper investigates what structure in a decision problem can support these benefits. It focuses on recurring subproblems with similar rewards and transition behavior, described as repeating subMDPs.

The authors formalize how a hierarchy can exploit this repetition and analyze a model-based algorithm using a Thompson sampling-style approach. Under the paper's assumptions, they establish statistical efficiency through a finite-time regret bound. This connects reuse of recurring structure to a quantitative guarantee about the algorithm's learning performance.

The paper separately identifies conditions under which planning with options induced by that structure is computationally efficient and near-optimal. These are distinct benefits: learning efficiently concerns acquiring useful information, while planning efficiently concerns computing decisions. The results explain how repeated subproblem structure can support both, with the guarantees depending on the stated assumptions and planning conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper gives conditional learning and planning efficiency guarantees for hierarchical reinforcement learning that exploits recurring decision subproblems.

title: On Efficiency in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural datasets often contain measurements of neural activity across multiple trials of a repeated stimulus or behavior. An important problem in the analysis of such datasets is to characterize systematic aspects of neural activity that carry information about the repeated stimulus or behavior of interest, which can be considered ``signal'', and to separate them from the trial-to-trial fluctuations in activity that are not time-locked to the stimulus, which for purposes of such analyses can be considered ``noise''. Gaussian Process factor models provide a powerful tool for identifying shared structure in high-dimensional neural data. However, they have not yet been adapted to the problem of characterizing signal and noise in multi-trial datasets. Here we address this shortcoming by proposing ``signal-noise'' Poisson-spiking Gaussian Process Factor Analysis (SNP-GPFA), a flexible latent variable model that resolves signal and noise latent structure in neural population spiking activity. To learn the parameters of our model, we introduce a Fourier-domain black box variational inference method that quickly identifies smooth latent structure. The resulting model reliably uncovers latent signal and trial-to-trial noise-related fluctuations in large-scale recordings. We use this model to show that in monkey V1, noise fluctuations perturb neural activity within a subspace orthogonal to signal activity, suggesting that trial-by-trial noise does not interfere with signal representations. Finally, we extend the model to capture statistical dependencies across brain regions in multi-region data. We show that in mouse visual cortex, models with shared noise across brain regions out-perform models with independent per-region noise.

title: Identifying signal and noise structure in neural population activity with Gaussian process factor models

abstract: Zap Q-learning is a recent class of reinforcement learning algorithms, motivated primarily as a means to accelerate convergence. Stability theory has been absent outside of two restrictive classes: the tabular setting, and optimal stopping. This paper introduces a new framework for analysis of a more general class of recursive algorithms known as stochastic approximation. Based on this general theory, it is shown that Zap Q-learning is consistent under a non-degeneracy assumption, even when the function approximation architecture is nonlinear. Zap Q-learning with neural network function approximation emerges as a special case, and is tested on examples from OpenAI Gym. Based on multiple experiments with a range of neural network sizes, it is found that the new algorithms converge quickly and are robust to choice of function approximation architecture.

This paper extends the analytical treatment to nonlinear function approximation, addressing a setting that includes neural-network representations of action values.

The authors first develop a framework for analyzing stochastic approximation, a broader class of recursive algorithms. They use that theory to prove consistency of Zap Q-learning under a non-degeneracy assumption, even with nonlinear approximators. The assumption is part of the guarantee, so the result does not establish unconditional consistency for every nonlinear architecture or problem.

Across experiments with different network sizes, the algorithms converge quickly and show robustness to the choice of approximation architecture. The paper thus pairs a conditional theoretical extension with empirical evidence across several network configurations, broadening the support for Zap Q-learning beyond its previously analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: Zap Q-learning gains a consistency guarantee for nonlinear approximation under a non-degeneracy assumption, alongside promising neural-network experiments.

title: Zap Q-Learning With Nonlinear Function Approximation

abstract: Random Reshuffling (RR) is an algorithm for minimizing finite-sum functions that utilizes iterative gradient descent steps in conjunction with data reshuffling. Often contrasted with its sibling Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), RR is usually faster in practice and enjoys significant popularity in convex and non-convex optimization. The convergence rate of RR has attracted substantial attention recently and, for strongly convex and smooth functions, it was shown to converge faster than SGD if 1) the stepsize is small, 2) the gradients are bounded, and 3) the number of epochs is large. We remove these 3 assumptions, improve the dependence on the condition number from $\kappa^2$ to $\kappa$ (resp.\ from $\kappa$ to $\sqrt{\kappa}$) and, in addition, show that RR has a different type of variance. We argue through theory and experiments that the new variance type gives an additional justification of the superior performance of RR. To go beyond strong convexity, we present several results for non-strongly convex and non-convex objectives. We show that in all cases, our theory improves upon existing literature. Finally, we prove fast convergence of the Shuffle-Once (SO) algorithm, which shuffles the data only once, at the beginning of the optimization process. Our theory for strongly convex objectives tightly matches the known lower bounds for both RR and SO and substantiates the common practical heuristic of shuffling once or only a few times. As a byproduct of our analysis, we also get new results for the Incremental Gradient algorithm (IG), which does not shuffle the data at all.

This paper develops a simpler analysis that strengthens the explanation for reshuffling's observed performance.

These results support the practical habit of shuffling once or a few times, while the analysis additionally yields results for unshuffled incremental gradient updates.
summary.tldr: A stronger convergence analysis removes restrictive reshuffling assumptions and provides tight guarantees for both repeated and single shuffling.

title: Random Reshuffling: Simple Analysis with Vast Improvements

abstract: Inspired by BatchNorm, there has been an explosion of normalization layers in deep learning. Recent works have identified a multitude of beneficial properties in BatchNorm to explain its success. However, given the pursuit of alternative normalization layers, these properties need to be generalized so that any given layer's success/failure can be accurately predicted. In this work, we take a first step towards this goal by extending known properties of BatchNorm in randomly initialized deep neural networks (DNNs) to several recently proposed normalization layers. Our primary findings follow: (i) similar to BatchNorm, activations-based normalization layers can prevent exponential growth of activations in ResNets, but parametric techniques require explicit remedies; (ii) use of GroupNorm can ensure an informative forward propagation, with different samples being assigned dissimilar activations, but increasing group size results in increasingly indistinguishable activations for different samples, explaining slow convergence speed in models with LayerNorm; and (iii) small group sizes result in large gradient norm in earlier layers, hence explaining training instability issues in Instance Normalization and illustrating a speed-stability tradeoff in GroupNorm. Overall, our analysis reveals a unified set of mechanisms that underpin the success of normalization methods in deep learning, providing us with a compass to systematically explore the vast design space of DNN normalization layers.

paragraphs: Normalization layers can affect both the information traveling forward through a network and the gradients traveling backward. This paper extends explanations previously developed for BatchNorm to several other normalization methods. Its analysis focuses on randomly initialized deep networks, seeking shared mechanisms that help explain why different normalization choices succeed or fail.

The authors find that normalization based on activations can prevent exponential activation growth in residual networks, while parametric techniques need explicit remedies. They also examine whether different inputs remain distinguishable. GroupNorm can preserve informative differences between samples, but larger groups make their activations increasingly similar. The paper connects this effect to the slow convergence observed with LayerNorm.

Smaller groups introduce a different problem: large gradient norms in early layers. The analysis connects this behavior to instability in Instance Normalization and describes a tradeoff between speed and stability in GroupNorm. Together, these results offer a framework for reasoning about normalization design through activation growth, sample distinguishability, and gradient behavior.
summary.tldr: An analysis of normalization layers links activation growth, sample distinguishability, and gradient size to a speed–stability tradeoff.

title: Beyond BatchNorm: Towards a Unified Understanding of Normalization in Deep Learning

abstract: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) applications are used in manufacturing to model everything from coffee mugs to sports cars. These programs are complex and require years of training and experience to master. A component of all CAD models particularly difficult to make are the highly structured 2D sketches that lie at the heart of every 3D construction. In this work, we propose a machine learning model capable of automatically generating such sketches. Through this, we pave the way for developing intelligent tools that would help engineers create better designs with less effort. The core of our method is a combination of a general-purpose language modeling technique alongside an off-the-shelf data serialization protocol. Additionally, we explore several extensions allowing us to gain finer control over the generation process. We show that our approach has enough flexibility to accommodate the complexity of the domain and performs well for both unconditional synthesis and image-to-sketch translation.

Creating these sketches is a demanding part of using CAD software. This paper develops a machine learning model that generates them automatically, with the longer-term aim of supporting tools that reduce the effort engineers spend creating designs.

The method combines a general-purpose language modeling technique with an existing data serialization protocol. Serialization provides a way to express structured sketch data in a form the model can process and generate. This connects the task of producing a CAD sketch with the task of modeling a structured sequence. The authors also explore extensions that give finer control over generation.

The reported results cover both unconditional synthesis and translating images into sketches. The authors find that the approach can accommodate the domain's structural complexity and performs well in both settings. The contribution is a sketch-generation method and a route toward design assistance; the abstract presents broader intelligent engineering tools as a future possibility enabled by this work.
summary.tldr: The paper combines language modeling and data serialization to generate structured CAD sketches, including sketches derived from images.

title: Computer-Aided Design as Language

abstract: Training automated agents to complete complex tasks in interactive environments is challenging: reinforcement learning requires careful hand-engineering of reward functions, imitation learning requires specialized infrastructure and access to a human expert, and learning from intermediate forms of supervision (like binary preferences) is time-consuming and extracts little information from each human intervention. Can we overcome these challenges by building agents that learn from rich, interactive feedback instead? We propose a new supervision paradigm for interactive learning based on "teachable" decision-making systems that learn from structured advice provided by an external teacher. We begin by formalizing a class of human-in-the-loop decision making problems in which multiple forms of teacher-provided advice are available to a learner. We then describe a simple learning algorithm for these problems that first learns to interpret advice, then learns from advice to complete tasks even in the absence of human supervision. In puzzle-solving, navigation, and locomotion domains, we show that agents that learn from advice can acquire new skills with significantly less human supervision than standard reinforcement learning algorithms and often less than imitation learning.

paragraphs: Teaching an agent can require carefully designed rewards, expert demonstrations, or many small pieces of feedback. This paper explores richer, structured advice as another form of supervision. Its goal is to let an external teacher communicate useful guidance interactively and enable the learner to turn that guidance into skills.

The authors formalize decision-making problems in which several forms of teacher advice are available. Their learning algorithm has two stages: it first learns how to interpret advice, then learns from that advice to perform tasks. The resulting agent can complete tasks without continued human supervision, making advice a training resource rather than a permanent requirement during use.

Experiments cover puzzle solving, navigation, and locomotion. Agents trained with advice acquire new skills using significantly less human supervision than standard reinforcement-learning algorithms and often less than imitation learning. The comparison with imitation learning is therefore qualified rather than universal. The findings support structured advice as an information-rich teaching channel that can reduce the amount of human involvement needed in the evaluated interactive environments.
summary.tldr: Agents that learn to interpret and use structured advice acquire skills with less human supervision in the evaluated interactive tasks.

title: Teachable Reinforcement Learning via Advice Distillation

abstract: How can we make use of information parallelism in online decision-making problems while efficiently balancing the exploration-exploitation trade-off? In this paper, we introduce a batch Thompson Sampling framework for two canonical online decision-making problems with partial feedback, namely, stochastic multi-arm bandit and linear contextual bandit. Over a time horizon $T$, our batch Thompson Sampling policy achieves the same (asymptotic) regret bound of a fully sequential one while carrying out only $O(\log T)$ batch queries. To achieve this exponential reduction, i.e., reducing the number of interactions from $T$ to $O(\log T)$, our batch policy dynamically determines the duration of each batch in order to balance the exploration-exploitation trade-off. We also demonstrate experimentally that dynamic batch allocation outperforms natural baselines.

paragraphs: Online decision makers must balance trying uncertain options with exploiting options that already look promising. Sequential feedback helps manage that balance, but requiring a new interaction after every decision limits parallel execution. This paper develops a batched Thompson Sampling framework for stochastic multi-arm bandits and linear contextual bandits, two settings with partial feedback.

The policy dynamically chooses how long each batch should last. Batch duration becomes a decision variable used to balance exploration and exploitation, rather than being fixed throughout learning. This adaptation lets the method reduce the number of batch queries over a horizon of T decisions from T sequential interactions to O(log T).

Despite the much smaller number of feedback interactions, the method achieves the same asymptotic regret bound as a fully sequential policy. This concerns the growth rate of regret rather than identical performance at every finite horizon. Experiments additionally show that dynamic batch allocation outperforms natural baselines. Together, the results demonstrate that substantially less frequent feedback can preserve the stated long-run learning guarantee.
summary.tldr: Dynamically sized Thompson Sampling batches reduce feedback queries to O(log T) while preserving the sequential policy's asymptotic regret bound.

title: Parallelizing Thompson Sampling

abstract: In real word applications, data generating process for training a machine learning model often differs from what the model encounters in the test stage. Understanding how and whether machine learning models generalize under such distributional shifts have been a theoretical challenge. Here, we study generalization in kernel regression when the training and test distributions are different using methods from statistical physics. Using the replica method, we derive an analytical formula for the out-of-distribution generalization error applicable to any kernel and real datasets. We identify an overlap matrix that quantifies the mismatch between distributions for a given kernel as a key determinant of generalization performance under distribution shift. Using our analytical expressions we elucidate various generalization phenomena including possible improvement in generalization when there is a mismatch. We develop procedures for optimizing training and test distributions for a given data budget to find best and worst case generalizations under the shift. We present applications of our theory to real and synthetic datasets and for many kernels. We compare results of our theory applied to Neural Tangent Kernel with simulations of wide networks and show agreement. We analyze linear regression in further depth.

paragraphs: Kernel regression may be trained on one distribution and evaluated on another, making prediction performance difficult to anticipate. This paper uses tools from statistical physics to study that mismatch. Through the replica method, the authors derive an analytical expression for out-of-distribution generalization error that applies to arbitrary kernels and real datasets.

A key object is an overlap matrix that measures distribution mismatch in a way specific to the chosen kernel. This makes the relationship between the kernel and the shift central to the analysis. The expressions explain several phenomena, including the possibility that a training–test mismatch can improve generalization rather than necessarily making it worse.

The authors also develop procedures to optimize training and test distributions under a fixed data budget, identifying favorable and unfavorable shifts. Applications cover synthetic and real datasets with multiple kernels, alongside a deeper analysis of linear regression. For the Neural Tangent Kernel, theoretical predictions agree with simulations of wide networks, connecting the kernel analysis to that neural-network setting.
summary.tldr: A statistical-physics analysis characterizes kernel regression under distribution shift and explains why some mismatches can improve generalization.

title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Kernel Regression

abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning (RL) – in which agents learn about all the possible long-term consequences of their actions, and not just the expected value – is of great recent interest. One of the most important affordances of a distributional view is facilitating a modern, measured, approach to risk when outcomes are not completely certain. By contrast, psychological and neuroscientific investigations into decision making under risk have utilized a variety of more venerable theoretical models such as prospect theory that lack axiomatically desirable properties such as coherence. Here, we consider a particularly relevant risk measure for modeling human and animal planning, called conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), which quantifies worst-case outcomes (e.g., vehicle accidents or predation). We first adopt a conventional distributional approach to CVaR in a sequential setting and reanalyze the choices of human decision-makers in the well-known two-step task, revealing substantial risk aversion that had been lurking under stickiness and perseveration. We then consider a further critical property of risk sensitivity, namely time consistency, showing alternatives to this form of CVaR that enjoy this desirable characteristic. We use simulations to examine settings in which the various forms differ in ways that have implications for human and animal planning and behavior.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning represents the range of possible long-term outcomes, making it possible to reason about risk beyond an average reward. This paper examines conditional value-at-risk, or CVaR, as a model of human and animal planning. CVaR focuses on unfavorable outcomes, making it relevant to decisions involving severe adverse consequences.

The authors first apply a conventional distributional treatment of CVaR to sequential decisions. Reanalyzing human choices in the two-step task reveals substantial risk aversion that had been obscured by apparent stickiness and perseveration. This changes how repeated choices can be interpreted: some behavior attributed to repetition may reflect sensitivity to unfavorable outcomes.

The paper then studies time consistency, which concerns whether risk-sensitive plans remain consistent as decisions unfold. It presents alternatives to the initial CVaR formulation that possess this property. Simulations identify settings in which the different forms lead to different behavior. These results connect the mathematical choice of risk measure to interpretations of planning, showing that both risk aversion and its treatment across time can matter.
summary.tldr: CVaR-based analysis reveals risk aversion in human sequential choices and explores how time-consistent risk measures change planning.

title: Two steps to risk sensitivity

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering an unknown latent code vector under a known generative model. For a $d$-layer deep generative network $\mathcal{G}:\mathbb{R}^{n_0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n_d}$ with ReLU activation functions, let the observation be $\mathcal{G}(x)+\epsilon$ where $\epsilon$ is noise. We introduce a simple novel algorithm, Partially Linearized Update for Generative Inversion (PLUGIn), to estimate $x$ (and thus $\mathcal{G}(x)$). We prove that, when weights are Gaussian and layer widths $n_i \gtrsim 5^i n_0$ (up to log factors), the algorithm converges geometrically to a neighbourhood of $x$ with high probability. Note the inequality on layer widths allows $n_i>n_{i+1}$ when $i\geq 1$. To our knowledge, this is the first such result for networks with some contractive layers. After a sufficient number of iterations, the estimation errors for both $x$ and $\mathcal{G}(x)$ are at most in the order of $\sqrt{4^dn_0/n_d} \|\epsilon\|$. Thus, the algorithm can denoise when the expansion ratio $n_d/n_0$ is large. Numerical experiments on synthetic data and real data are provided to validate our theoretical results and to illustrate that the algorithm can effectively remove artifacts in an image.

paragraphs: PLUGIn addresses generative inversion: recovering the hidden code that produced an observation through a known neural generator. The observation may contain added noise, so recovering the code can also help reconstruct a cleaner generated output. The proposed algorithm uses partially linearized updates to estimate that code.

For a d-layer ReLU generator with Gaussian weights, the authors prove geometric convergence to a neighborhood of the true code with high probability, provided layer widths satisfy bounds growing roughly as 5 to the layer index times the input width, up to logarithmic factors. These conditions allow some layers to be narrower than their predecessors, extending the guarantee to networks with certain contractive layers.

After sufficiently many iterations, errors in both the latent code and generated output are bounded in order by the noise magnitude times the square root of 4^d n0/nd. Thus, a sufficiently large output-to-input expansion ratio can enable denoising. Synthetic and real-data experiments support the theory and illustrate removal of image artifacts.
summary.tldr: PLUGIn recovers latent codes from noisy generator outputs with conditional convergence guarantees that allow some contractive layers.

title: PLUGIn: A simple algorithm for inverting generative models with recovery guarantees

abstract: Estimating out-of-distribution (OOD) uncertainty is a major challenge for safely deploying machine learning models in the open-world environment. Improved methods for OOD detection in multi-class classification have emerged, while OOD detection methods for multi-label classification remain underexplored and use rudimentary techniques. We propose JointEnergy, a simple and effective method, which estimates the OOD indicator scores by aggregating label-wise energy scores from multiple labels. We show that JointEnergy can be mathematically interpreted from a joint likelihood perspective. Our results show consistent improvement over previous methods that are based on the maximum-valued scores, which fail to capture joint information from multiple labels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three common multi-label classification benchmarks, including MS-COCO, PASCAL-VOC, and NUS-WIDE. We show that JointEnergy can reduce the FPR95 by up to 10.05% compared to the previous best baseline, establishing state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: A multi-label classifier can assign several labels to one input, but it also needs a way to recognize inputs outside its familiar distribution. The paper addresses this less-explored uncertainty problem. Methods that rely on the largest label score discard information from the other labels, even though their combined behavior may help distinguish familiar inputs from unfamiliar ones.

The proposed method, JointEnergy, combines energy scores computed for individual labels into an overall indicator of whether an input is out of distribution. The authors also give this aggregation a mathematical interpretation through joint likelihood. This connects the combined score to information across labels rather than treating the most extreme individual score as sufficient.

Experiments on MS-COCO, PASCAL-VOC, and NUS-WIDE show consistent improvements over previous maximum-score approaches. The reported reduction in FPR95 reaches up to 10.05% relative to the previous best baseline. These findings support using information from multiple labels together for detection, with the largest reported improvement describing a best observed result rather than a uniform gain.
summary.tldr: JointEnergy improves out-of-distribution detection for multi-label classifiers by combining energy scores across labels.

title: Can multi-label classification networks know what they don’t know?

abstract: We present an extensive study of $H$-consistency bounds for multi-class classification. These are upper bounds on the target loss estimation error of a predictor in a hypothesis set $H$, expressed in terms of the surrogate loss estimation error of that predictor. They are stronger and more significant guarantees than Bayes-consistency, $H$-calibration or $H$-consistency, and more informative than excess error bounds derived for $H$ being the family of all measurable functions. We give a series of new $H$-consistency bounds for surrogate multi-class losses, including max losses, sum losses, and constrained losses, both in the non-adversarial and adversarial cases, and for different differentiable or convex auxiliary functions used. We also prove that no non-trivial $H$-consistency bound can be given in some cases. To our knowledge, these are the first $H$-consistency bounds proven for the multi-class setting. Our proof techniques are also novel and likely to be useful in the analysis of other such guarantees.

paragraphs: Classification systems often optimize a surrogate loss instead of the target loss used to judge predictions. This paper studies how errors measured by the surrogate control errors measured by the target in multiclass classification. Crucially, its guarantees account for the predictor's actual hypothesis set H, rather than assuming access to every measurable function.

An H-consistency bound gives an upper bound on target-loss estimation error in terms of surrogate-loss estimation error. This quantitative relationship provides more information than a consistency statement alone. It also makes the chosen family of predictors part of the analysis, which matters when translating a training objective into a guarantee about the desired prediction behavior.

The authors derive new bounds for max, sum, and constrained multiclass surrogate losses, examining different differentiable or convex auxiliary functions in both adversarial and non-adversarial settings. They also establish cases where no nontrivial bound is possible. The study therefore identifies both useful surrogate-to-target guarantees and circumstances where that form of guarantee cannot be obtained.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes multiclass surrogate-to-target error bounds for restricted hypothesis sets and identifies cases where useful bounds are impossible.

title: Multi-Class $H$-Consistency Bounds

abstract: Finance is a particularly challenging playground for deep reinforcement learning. However, establishing high-quality market environments and benchmarks for financial reinforcement learning is challenging due to three major factors, namely, low signal-to-noise ratio of financial data, survivorship bias of historical data, and backtesting overfitting. In this paper, we present an openly accessible FinRL-Meta library that has been actively maintained by the AI4Finance community. First, following a DataOps paradigm, we will provide hundreds of market environments through an automatic data curation pipeline that processes dynamic datasets from real-world markets into gym-style market environments. Second, we reproduce popular papers as stepping stones for users to design new trading strategies. We also deploy the library on cloud platforms so that users can visualize their own results and assess the relative performance via community-wise competitions. Third, FinRL-Meta provides tens of Jupyter/Python demos organized into a curriculum and a documentation website to serve the rapidly growing community. FinRL-Meta is available at: \url{https://github.com/AI4Finance-Foundation/FinRL-Meta}

paragraphs: FinRL-Meta addresses the infrastructure needed to study reinforcement learning in financial markets. The paper identifies three obstacles to reliable environments and benchmarks: weak signals amid noisy financial data, survivorship bias in historical records, and overfitting to backtests. These problems make preparing and evaluating learning systems a substantial part of the research challenge.

The library follows a DataOps approach, using an automated curation pipeline to turn changing real-market datasets into gym-style environments. The authors describe plans to provide hundreds of these environments. They also reproduce popular research papers, giving users starting points for developing trading strategies rather than requiring every experiment to begin with a new implementation.

Cloud deployment supports visualization and relative performance assessment through community competitions. A curriculum containing tens of Jupyter and Python demonstrations, together with documentation, helps users work with the library. The contribution is an openly accessible research platform combining data preparation, environments, reproduced methods, and teaching material. Its stated purpose is to support financial reinforcement learning research; the abstract does not present a claim of profitable trading.
summary.tldr: FinRL-Meta combines automated market-data curation, reinforcement learning environments, reproduced research, and educational resources in an open financial research platform.

title: FinRL-Meta: Market Environments and Benchmarks for Data-Driven Financial Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Sparsely gated Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) has demonstrated its effectiveness in scaling up deep neural networks to an extreme scale. Despite that numerous efforts have been made to improve the performance of MoE from the model design or system optimization perspective, existing MoE dispatch patterns are still not able to fully exploit the underlying heterogeneous network environments. In this paper, we propose TA-MoE, a topology-aware routing strategy for large-scale MoE trainging, from a model-system co-design perspective, which can dynamically adjust the MoE dispatch pattern according to the network topology. Based on communication modeling, we abstract the dispatch problem into an optimization objective and obtain the approximate dispatch pattern under different topologies. On top of that, we design a topology-aware auxiliary loss, which can adaptively route the data to fit in the underlying topology without sacrificing the model accuracy. Experiments show that TA-MoE can substantially outperform its counterparts on various hardware and model configurations, with roughly 1.01x-1.61x, 1.01x-4.77x, 1.25x-1.54x improvements over the popular DeepSpeed-MoE, FastMoE and FasterMoE systems.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models scale neural networks by routing data to selected experts. In distributed training, those routing decisions also determine communication across the hardware network. The paper argues that existing dispatch patterns do not fully exploit heterogeneous network environments, leaving useful system performance untapped.

TA-MoE makes routing sensitive to the network topology. The authors model communication, express dispatch as an optimization objective, and obtain approximate dispatch patterns for different topologies. They then introduce an auxiliary loss that encourages data routing to fit the underlying network. This links model training decisions with the communication costs imposed by the hardware.

Reported speed improvements are roughly 1.01–1.61 times over DeepSpeed-MoE, 1.01–4.77 times over FastMoE, and 1.25–1.54 times over FasterMoE. The ranges show that the benefit varies by configuration, while supporting topology-aware routing as a useful component of large-scale mixture-of-experts training.
summary.tldr: TA-MoE adapts expert routing to network topology, improving distributed training speed across tested configurations without sacrificing accuracy.

title: TA-MoE: Topology-Aware Large Scale Mixture-of-Expert Training

abstract: Surrogate models are necessary to optimize meaningful quantities in physical dynamics as their recursive numerical resolutions are often prohibitively expensive. It is mainly the case for fluid dynamics and the resolution of Navier–Stokes equations. However, despite the fast-growing field of data-driven models for physical systems, reference datasets representing real-world phenomena are lacking. In this work, we develop \textsc{AirfRANS}, a dataset for studying the two-dimensional incompressible steady-state Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes equations over airfoils at a subsonic regime and for different angles of attacks. We also introduce metrics on the stress forces at the surface of geometries and visualization of boundary layers to assess the capabilities of models to accurately predict the meaningful information of the problem. Finally, we propose deep learning baselines on four machine learning tasks to study \textsc{AirfRANS} under different constraints for generalization considerations: big and scarce data regime, Reynolds number, and angle of attack extrapolation.

paragraphs: AirfRANS is a dataset for studying learned approximations to fluid simulations around airfoils. Repeated numerical simulation can be expensive, creating a need for surrogate models when optimising physically meaningful quantities. The paper addresses a shortage of reference datasets for evaluating these data-driven models on problems connected to real physical phenomena.

The dataset covers two-dimensional, incompressible, steady-state Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes solutions in subsonic flow, with different angles of attack. These conditions define the physical setting represented by the data. Alongside the dataset, the authors introduce evaluation metrics concerning stress forces on geometry surfaces and visualisations of boundary layers. These tools focus assessment on physically relevant aspects of a prediction.

The paper also supplies deep learning baselines for four tasks: learning with abundant data, learning with scarce data, extrapolating across Reynolds numbers, and extrapolating across angles of attack. These tasks separate different generalisation demands rather than treating all prediction settings as equivalent. The contribution is a dataset and evaluation framework for examining how well learned fluid models preserve useful physical information under those demands.
summary.tldr: AirfRANS provides airfoil flow simulations, physically relevant evaluation tools, and four tasks for studying learned fluid simulation surrogates.

title: AirfRANS: High Fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics Dataset for Approximating Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes Solutions

abstract: Stochastic optimization of the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) is a crucial problem for machine learning. Although various algorithms have been extensively studied for AUPRC optimization, the generalization is only guaranteed in the multi-query case. In this work, we present the first trial in the single-query generalization of stochastic AUPRC optimization. For sharper generalization bounds, we focus on algorithm-dependent generalization. There are both algorithmic and theoretical obstacles to our destination. From an algorithmic perspective, we notice that the majority of existing stochastic estimators are biased when the sampling strategy is biased, and is leave-one-out unstable due to the non-decomposability. To address these issues, we propose a sampling-rate-invariant unbiased stochastic estimator with superior stability. On top of this, the AUPRC optimization is formulated as a composition optimization problem, and a stochastic algorithm is proposed to solve this problem. From a theoretical perspective, standard techniques of the algorithm-dependent generalization analysis cannot be directly applied to such a listwise compositional optimization problem. To fill this gap, we extend the model stability from instancewise losses to listwise losses and bridge the corresponding generalization and stability. Additionally, we construct state transition matrices to describe the recurrence of the stability, and simplify calculations by matrix spectrum. Practically, experimental results on three image retrieval datasets on speak to the effectiveness and soundness of our framework.
