paragraphs: Neighbor embedding helps visualize high-dimensional data by constructing a lower-dimensional representation of relationships between samples. Doing this collaboratively is difficult when data remain with separate participants: the objective depends on pairs of points, including relationships that cross participant boundaries. FedNE addresses this problem without requiring a pool of shareable data.

The method combines federated averaging with contrastive neighbor embedding. To compensate for missing repulsion between clients’ data, each client learns and shares a surrogate loss function. This supports alignment within a common embedding space. A separate data-mixing strategy augments local data to reduce problems caused by neighbors that local graphs cannot see and neighbors that those graphs identify incorrectly.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that FedNE preserves neighborhood structure and improves alignment in the global embedding space relative to several baselines. These are complementary goals: local relationships should remain meaningful, and the participants’ representations should fit together. The results support using surrogate objectives and local augmentation to address both challenges in federated visualization.
summary.tldr: FedNE uses shared surrogate losses and local data mixing to improve joint neighbor embeddings without exchanging local datasets.

title: FedNE: Surrogate-Assisted Federated Neighbor Embedding for Dimensionality Reduction

abstract: Foundation models are applied in a broad spectrum of settings with different inference constraints, from massive multi-accelerator clusters to resource-constrained standalone mobile devices. However, the substantial costs associated with training these models often limit the number of unique model sizes that can be offered. Consequently, practitioners are compelled to select a model that may not be optimally aligned with their specific latency and cost requirements. We present MatFormer, a novel Transformer architecture designed to provide elastic inference across diverse deployment constraints. MatFormer achieves this by incorporating a nested Feed Forward Network (FFN) block structure within a standard Transformer model. During training, we optimize the parameters of multiple nested FFN blocks with varying sizes, enabling the extraction of hundreds of accurate smaller models without incurring additional computational costs. We empirically validate the efficacy of MatFormer across different model classes (decoders and encoders) and modalities (language and vision), demonstrating its potential for real-world deployment. We show that a 850M decoder-only MatFormer language model (MatLM) allows us to extract multiple smaller models spanning from 582M to 850M parameters, each exhibiting better validation loss and one-shot downstream evaluations than independently trained counterparts. Furthermore, we observe that smaller encoders extracted from a universal MatFormer-based ViT (MatViT) encoder preserve the metric-space structure for adaptive large-scale retrieval. Finally, we showcase that speculative decoding with the accurate and consistent submodels extracted from MatFormer can lead to significant reduction in inference latency.

paragraphs: A model that fits a large accelerator cluster may be unsuitable for a mobile device, yet separately training many sizes is expensive. MatFormer addresses this mismatch by placing feed-forward networks of different sizes inside one transformer as nested blocks. The authors also show that accurate, consistent submodels can significantly reduce inference latency through speculative decoding. Together, the findings support a single trained model family that offers multiple deployment choices while retaining useful relationships among its smaller and larger members.
summary.tldr: MatFormer trains nested transformer components together so one model can supply accurate submodels for different inference budgets.

title: MatFormer: Nested Transformer for Elastic Inference

abstract: Animist worldviews treat beings, plants, landscapes, and even tools as persons endowed with spirit, an orientation that has long shaped human–nonhuman relations through ritual and moral practice. While modern industrial societies have often imagined technology as mute and mechanical, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), especially large language models (LLMs), invite people to anthropomorphize and attribute inner life to devices. This paper introduces A(I)nimism, an interactive installation exploring how large language objects (LLOs) can mediate animistic relationships with everyday things. Housed within a physical “portal,” the system uses GPT-4 Vision, voice input, and memory-based agents to create evolving object-personas. Encounters unfold through light, sound, and touch in a ritual-like process of request, conversation, and transformation that is designed to evoke empathy, wonder, and reflection. We situate the project within anthropological perspectives, speculative design, and spiritual HCI. AI’s opacity, we argue, invites animistic interpretation, allowing LLOs to re-enchant the mundane and spark new questions of agency, responsibility, and design.

paragraphs: A(I)nimism explores how AI might change people’s relationships with everyday objects by giving those objects conversational personas. Its starting point is animism, in which humans relate to nonhuman beings and things as persons with spirit. The project brings that orientation into an interactive installation concerned with empathy, wonder, and responsibility.

The installation places a system inside a physical portal and combines GPT-4 Vision, voice input, and agents with memory. Together, these components create object personas that can evolve through interaction. Light, sound, and touch organize encounters into a ritual-like sequence of making a request, conversing, and experiencing a transformation.

The paper situates this experience within anthropology, speculative design, and spiritual approaches to human–computer interaction. Its argument is that the difficulty of understanding AI’s internal operation can invite animistic interpretations. The installation makes that possibility tangible, asking how apparently responsive objects might reshape ideas of agency and care. Empathy and reflection are design intentions here, rather than reported measurements of participants’ responses.
summary.tldr: A(I)nimism gives everyday objects evolving AI personas within a ritual-like installation exploring empathy, agency, and animistic relationships.

title: A(I)nimism: Re-enchanting the World Through AI-Mediated Object Interaction

abstract: Many domain experts do not have the time or expertise to write formal Bayesian models. This paper takes an informal problem description as input, and combines a large language model and a probabilistic programming language to define a joint distribution over formal models, latent variables, and data. A posterior over latent variables follows by conditioning on observed data and integrating over formal models. This presents a challenging inference problem. We suggest an inference recipe that amounts to generating many formal models from the large language model, performing approximate inference on each, and then doing a weighted aver- age. This is justified and analyzed as a combination of self-normalized importance sampling, MCMC, and importance-weighted variational inference. Experimentally, this produces sensible predictions from only data and an informal problem description, without the need to specify a formal model.

paragraphs: Formal Bayesian modeling can require expertise and time that domain specialists do not have. It combines a language model with a probabilistic programming language to represent uncertainty jointly over formal models, latent variables, and data.

title: Large Language Bayes

abstract: With the rapid growth of video generative models (VGMs), it is essential to develop reliable and comprehensive automatic metrics for AI-generated videos (AIGVs). Existing methods either use off-the-shelf models optimized for other tasks or rely on human assessment data to train specialized evaluators. These approaches are constrained to specific evaluation aspects and are difficult to scale with the increasing demands for finer-grained and more comprehensive evaluations. To address this issue, this work investigates the feasibility of using multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as a unified evaluator for AIGVs, leveraging their strong visual perception and language understanding capabilities. To evaluate the performance of automatic metrics in unified AIGV evaluation, we introduce a benchmark called UVE-Bench. UVE-Bench collects videos generated by state-of-the-art VGMs and provides pairwise human preference annotations across 15 evaluation aspects. Using UVE-Bench, we extensively evaluate 18 MLLMs. Our empirical results suggest that while advanced MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2VL-72B and InternVL2.5-78B) still lag behind human evaluators, they demonstrate promising ability in unified AIGV evaluation, significantly surpassing existing specialized evaluation methods. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of key design choices that impact the performance of MLLM-driven evaluators, offering valuable insights for future research on AIGV evaluation.

This paper asks whether multimodal language models can provide a broader, unified evaluation approach using their visual and language capabilities.

The authors introduce UVE-Bench, which contains videos from advanced video generators and pairwise human preferences across 15 evaluation aspects. Pairwise judgments record which of two videos people prefer for a given aspect. The benchmark provides a shared basis for testing how well automatic evaluators reproduce these assessments across a broad set of criteria.

An evaluation of 18 multimodal language models finds that advanced models, including Qwen2VL-72B and InternVL2.5-78B, significantly outperform existing specialized evaluation methods. They still fall behind human evaluators, so the results support promise rather than equivalence to human judgment. The paper also analyzes evaluator design choices, connecting the benchmark comparison to decisions that affect how multimodal models perform this evaluation role.
summary.tldr: UVE-Bench shows that advanced multimodal models can outperform specialized video evaluators across many aspects while still trailing human evaluators.

title: UVE: Are MLLMs Unified Evaluators for AI-Generated Videos?

abstract: Today, people can easily record memorable moments, ranging from concerts, sports events, lectures, family gatherings, and birthday parties with multiple consumer cameras. However, synchronizing these cross‑camera streams remains challenging. Existing methods assume controlled settings, specific targets, manual correction, or costly hardware. We present VisualSync, an optimization framework based on multi‑view dynamics that aligns unposed, unsynchronized videos at millisecond accuracy. Our key insight is that any moving 3D point, when co‑visible in two cameras, obeys epipolar constraints once properly synchronized. To exploit this, VisualSync leverages off‑the‑shelf 3D reconstruction, feature matching, and dense tracking to extract tracklets, relative poses, and cross‑view correspondences. It then jointly minimizes the epipolar error to estimate each camera’s time offset. Experiments on four diverse, challenging datasets show that VisualSync outperforms baseline methods, achieving an average synchronization error below 130 ms.

paragraphs: Videos of the same event recorded by different cameras can start at different times, making synchronization difficult. VisualSync estimates these time offsets from object motion across views. It targets videos that are both unsynchronized and unposed, using visual evidence to align streams whose camera relationships are not supplied in advance.

The key geometric observation concerns a moving 3D point visible in two cameras: at the correct synchronization, its projections satisfy epipolar constraints. VisualSync uses existing 3D reconstruction, feature matching, and dense tracking methods to obtain short tracks, relative camera poses, and cross-view correspondences. It then jointly estimates camera time offsets by minimizing the associated epipolar error.

Experiments on four diverse, challenging datasets show better synchronization than baseline methods, with average error below 130 milliseconds. The reported evidence supports motion-based geometric alignment across the tested settings. Shared visibility of moving points is central to the method’s reasoning, because those cross-view observations provide the constraints that connect camera timing to geometric consistency.
summary.tldr: VisualSync synchronizes unposed camera videos through cross-view motion geometry, reporting average error below 130 milliseconds across four datasets.

title: Visual Sync: Multi‑Camera Synchronization via Cross‑View Object Motion

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-label probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, and vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and they display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks—removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training and fine-tuning strategies.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how different attention heads contribute to language-model reasoning. Rather than treating all heads as interchangeable, it asks whether particular heads specialize in functions such as retrieving information or performing logical reasoning. The authors introduce CogQA, a dataset that breaks complex questions into successive subquestions and associates those steps with specific cognitive functions.

A multi-label probing method connects attention-head behavior to these function labels. Across the model families examined, the analysis identifies specialized groups called cognitive heads. The authors characterize these groups as consistently sparse, with their numbers and locations differing across functions. They also find interactions and hierarchical organization, suggesting that the relevant heads have structured relationships rather than acting as isolated components.

The paper goes beyond identifying associations by modifying the cognitive heads. Removing them reduces reasoning performance, while augmenting them improves accuracy in the reported experiments. Together, these findings support their functional importance in the studied models. The framework offers a way to connect internal components with recognizable reasoning operations and suggests directions for model design, training, and fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: CogQA and attention-head analysis reveal sparse functional specializations whose removal or augmentation changes reasoning performance.

title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning

abstract: Preference learning has become a common approach in various recent methods for aligning large language models with human values. These methods optimize the preference margin between chosen and rejected responses, subject to certain constraints for avoiding over-optimization. In this paper, we report surprising empirical findings that simple ReLU activation can learn meaningful alignments even using \emph{none} of the following: (i) sigmoid-based gradient constraints, (ii) explicit regularization terms. Our experiments show that over-optimization does exist, but a threshold parameter $\gamma$ plays an essential role in preventing it by dynamically filtering training examples. We further provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that ReLU-based Preference Optimization (RePO) corresponds to the convex envelope of the 0-1 loss, establishing its fundamental soundness. Our ``RePO'' method achieves competitive or superior results compared to established preference optimization approaches. We hope this simple baseline will motivate researchers to rethink the fundamental mechanisms behind preference optimization for language model alignment.

paragraphs: RePO investigates how simple the objective for language-model preference learning can be while still producing useful alignment. Preference methods encourage a model to favor chosen responses over rejected ones, usually with mechanisms intended to prevent excessive optimization. This paper studies a ReLU-based objective without sigmoid-based gradient constraints or explicit regularization terms.

The experiments show that these omissions do not prevent meaningful alignment, but over-optimization remains a real concern. A threshold parameter, gamma, plays an essential role by dynamically filtering training examples. The result therefore points to the importance of controlling which examples continue to influence learning, rather than demonstrating that unrestricted preference optimization is harmless.

The theoretical analysis connects RePO to the convex envelope of the zero-one loss, providing a formal foundation for the objective. Empirically, it achieves competitive or better results than established preference optimization approaches. The contribution is a simple baseline that helps isolate which mechanisms matter: successful learning can occur without the two omitted components, while threshold-based example filtering remains central to the reported behavior.
summary.tldr: RePO achieves competitive preference learning with a simple ReLU objective whose threshold filters examples to help prevent over-optimization.

title: RePO: Understanding Preference Learning Through ReLU-Based Optimization

abstract: AI agents today are mostly siloed — they either retrieve and reason over vast amount of digital information and knowledge obtained online; or interact with the physical world through embodied perception, planning and action — but rarely both. This separation limits their ability to solve tasks that require integrated physical and digital intelligence, such as cooking from online recipes, navigating with dynamic map data, or interpreting real-world landmarks using web knowledge. We introduce \textsc{Embodied Web Agents}, a novel paradigm for AI agents that fluidly bridge embodiment and web-scale reasoning. To operationalize this concept, we first develop the \textsc{Embodied Web Agents} task environments, a unified simulation platform that integrates realistic 3D indoor and outdoor environments with functional web interfaces. Building upon this platform, we construct and release the \textsc{Embodied Web Agents} Benchmark, which encompasses a diverse suite of tasks including cooking, navigation, shopping, tourism, and geolocation — all requiring coordinated reasoning across physical and digital realms for systematic assessment of cross-domain intelligence. Experimental results reveal significant performance gaps between state-of-the-art AI systems and human capabilities, establishing both challenges and opportunities at the intersection of embodied cognition and web-scale knowledge access.

paragraphs: An agent following an online recipe must connect digital instructions with actions in a physical environment. This paper studies that combination, arguing that agents focused separately on web information or embodied action leave an important capability gap. Similar coordination is needed when navigating with changing maps or interpreting landmarks using online knowledge.

The authors introduce Embodied Web Agents as a paradigm and build a simulation platform to evaluate it. The platform combines realistic indoor and outdoor 3D environments with working web interfaces. Its benchmark covers cooking, navigation, shopping, tourism, and geolocation. Each task requires coordinated reasoning across the simulated physical environment and digital information, making that connection an explicit target of evaluation.

Experiments reveal substantial gaps between state-of-the-art AI systems and human capabilities on these tasks. The contribution is therefore both an environment for studying integrated behavior and evidence that current systems struggle with it. The benchmark gives researchers a common setting for testing whether an agent can turn information obtained online into appropriate situated decisions and actions.
summary.tldr: Embodied Web Agents provides simulations and a benchmark for tasks combining web information with physical action, revealing substantial AI–human performance gaps.

title: Embodied Web Agents: Bridging Physical-Digital Realms for Integrated Agent Intelligence

abstract: Learning robot control policies from human videos is a promising direction for scaling up robot learning. However, how to extract action knowledge (or action representations) from videos for policy learning remains a key challenge. Existing action representations such as video frames, pixelflow, and pointcloud flow have inherent limitations such as modeling complexity or loss of information. In this paper, we propose to use object-centric 3D motion field to represent actions for robot learning from human videos, and present a novel framework for extracting this representation from videos for zero-shot control. We introduce two novel components. First, a novel training pipeline for training a ``denoising'' 3D motion field estimator to extract fine object 3D motions from human videos with noisy depth robustly. Second, a dense object-centric 3D motion field prediction architecture that favors both cross-embodiment transfer and policy generalization to background. We evaluate the system in real world setups. Experiments show that our method reduces 3D motion estimation error by over 50% compared to the latest method, achieve 55% average success rate in diverse tasks where prior approaches fail ($\lesssim 10$\%), and can even acquire fine-grained manipulation skills like insertion.

paragraphs: Human videos could provide a large source of robot-learning experience, but extracting usable action information from them is difficult. This paper represents actions through object-centered three-dimensional motion fields. The representation focuses on how objects move, providing action information for a framework that extracts knowledge from video for zero-shot robot control.

One contribution is a training pipeline for a denoising motion estimator that recovers fine object movements despite noisy depth information. Another is a dense motion-field prediction architecture designed to support transfer between human and robot embodiments and generalization across backgrounds. Together, these components address both the quality of the extracted motion and its usefulness for robot policies.

In real-world experiments, the method reduces 3D motion estimation error by more than 50% relative to the latest method used for comparison. It achieves 55% average task success where prior approaches achieve approximately 10% or less, and demonstrates fine manipulation such as insertion. These results support object-centered motion as a useful representation for transferring action knowledge from human videos.
summary.tldr: Object-centered 3D motion fields transfer manipulation knowledge from human videos, achieving 55% average success in the reported real-world tasks.

title: Object-centric 3D Motion Field for Robot Learning from Human Videos

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly saturating existing benchmarks, necessitating new open-ended evaluations. We introduce the Factorio Learning Environment (FLE), based on the game of Factorio, that tests agents in long-term planning, spatial reasoning, program synthesis, and resource optimization. FLE provides exponentially scaling challenges -- from basic automation to complex factories processing millions of resource units per second. We provide two settings: (1) open-play with the open-ended task of building the largest factory on an procedurally generated map and (2) lab-play consisting of 33 bounded tasks accross three settings with fixed resources. We demonstrate across both settings that models still lack strong spatial reasoning. In lab-play, we find that LLMs exhibit promising short-horizon skills, yet are unable to operate effectively in constrained environments, reflecting limitations in error analysis. In open-play, while LLMs discover automation strategies that improve growth (e.g electric-powered drilling), they fail to achieve complex automation (e.g electronic-circuit manufacturing)

paragraphs: The Factorio Learning Environment evaluates language-model agents through factory building in the game Factorio. It combines long-term planning, spatial reasoning, program synthesis, and resource management within one environment. Challenges grow from basic automation toward factories processing millions of resource units per second, creating room for evaluation beyond tasks that current models are already saturating.

The environment offers two complementary settings. Open-play asks agents to build the largest factory they can on a procedurally generated map. Lab-play provides 33 bounded tasks across three settings with fixed resources. The first setting examines sustained expansion, while the second makes agents work within explicit resource constraints and a more tightly specified task.

The evaluations expose weak spatial reasoning in both settings. In lab-play, models show promising short-term skills but struggle to operate effectively under constraints, which the authors connect to limited error analysis. In open-play, they discover useful automation such as electric drilling but fail at more complex processes such as electronic-circuit manufacturing. Successful local actions therefore do not consistently develop into effective factory-scale behavior.
summary.tldr: Factorio Learning Environment tests sustained factory-building skills and reveals gaps between language models’ short-term actions and complex automation.

title: Factorio Learning Environment

abstract: We present MGE-LDM, a unified latent diffusion framework for simultaneous music generation, source imputation, and query-driven source separation. Unlike prior approaches constrained to fixed instrument classes, MGE-LDM learns a joint distribution over full mixtures, submixtures, and individual stems within a single compact latent diffusion model. At inference, MGE-LDM enables (1) complete mixture generation, (2) partial generation (i.e., source imputation), and (3) text-conditioned extraction of arbitrary sources. By formulating both separation and imputation as conditional inpainting tasks in the latent space, our approach supports flexible, class-agnostic manipulation of arbitrary instrument sources. Notably, MGE-LDM can be trained jointly across heterogeneous multi-track datasets (e.g., Slakh2100, MUSDB18, MoisesDB) without relying on predefined instrument categories.

paragraphs: MGE-LDM brings music creation and source extraction into one latent diffusion framework. It learns a joint distribution over complete musical mixtures, mixtures containing only some sources, and individual source tracks, or stems. This shared representation supports working with music at several levels of composition within a single compact model.

At inference, the model can generate a complete mixture, generate missing sources, or extract a source described through text. Separation and source imputation are both formulated as conditional inpainting in latent space. In this formulation, the available information conditions the process of producing the requested source content.

The framework does not depend on a predefined list of instrument categories. That design supports class-agnostic manipulation and joint training across heterogeneous multitrack datasets, including Slakh2100, MUSDB18, and MoisesDB. The contribution described in the abstract is this unified capability: generation, completion, and extraction share one model and one conditional formulation. It provides a way to accommodate differently organized music datasets without requiring a common fixed instrument taxonomy.
summary.tldr: MGE-LDM unifies music generation, missing-source generation, and text-guided source extraction through conditional inpainting in a shared latent diffusion model.

title: MGE-LDM: Joint Latent Diffusion for Simultaneous Music Generation and Source Extraction

abstract: Speculative Decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by employing a small draft model to generate predictions, which are then verified by a larger target model. The effectiveness of SD hinges on the alignment between these models, which is typically enhanced by Knowledge Distillation (KD). However, conventional KD methods aim to minimize the KL divergence between the draft and target models across all tokens, a goal that is misaligned with the true objective of SD, which is to maximize token acceptance rate. Therefore, draft models often struggle to fully assimilate the target model's knowledge due to capacity constraints, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this challenge, we propose AdaSPEC, a novel method that incorporates selective token filtering into the KD process. AdaSPEC utilizes a reference model to identify and filter out difficult-to-fit tokens, enabling the distillation of a draft model that better aligns with the target model on simpler tokens. This approach improves the overall token acceptance rate without compromising generation quality. We evaluate AdaSPEC across diverse tasks, including arithmetic reasoning, instruction-following, coding, and summarization, using model configurations of 31M/1.4B and 350M/2.7B parameters. Our results demonstrate that AdaSPEC consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art DistillSpec method, achieving higher acceptance rates across all tasks (up to 15\%). The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/yuezhouhu/adaspec}.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language generation by having a small model propose tokens for a larger model to verify. Its effectiveness depends on how often those proposals are accepted. AdaSPEC starts from a mismatch in conventional training: making the small model imitate the larger model across every token does not directly optimize acceptance.

Because the draft model has limited capacity, trying to fit difficult tokens can interfere with learning the tokens it can model well. AdaSPEC uses a reference model to identify difficult-to-fit tokens and filters them out during knowledge distillation. This concentrates the draft model's training on simpler tokens where stronger alignment with the target is achievable.

The authors evaluate the method on arithmetic reasoning, instruction following, coding, and summarization, using two draft-and-target size combinations. AdaSPEC achieves higher acceptance rates than DistillSpec across all evaluated tasks, with reported improvements of up to 15%, without compromising generation quality. The practical contribution is a training objective better matched to the draft model's role: producing proposals that survive verification, rather than reproducing every aspect of the target's predictions.
summary.tldr: AdaSPEC improves speculative decoding by filtering difficult tokens during draft-model distillation, increasing acceptance rates without compromising generation quality.

title: AdaSPEC: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Speculative Decoders

abstract: **Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection** is essential for ensuring the reliability and safety of machine learning systems. In recent years, it has received increasing attention, particularly through post-hoc detection and training-based methods. In this paper, we focus on **post-hoc OOD detection**, which enables identifying OOD samples without altering the model's training procedure or objective. Our primary goal is to investigate the relationship between **model capacity** and its OOD detection performance. Specifically, we aim to answer the following question: *Does the Double Descent phenomenon manifest in post-hoc OOD detection?* This question is crucial, as it can reveal whether overparameterization, which is already known to benefit generalization, can also enhance OOD detection. Despite the growing interest in these topics by the classic supervised machine learning community, this intersection remains unexplored for OOD detection. We empirically demonstrate that the Double Descent effect does indeed appear in post-hoc OOD detection. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights to explain why this phenomenon emerges in such setting. Finally, we show that the overparameterized regime does not yield superior results consistently, and we propose a method to identify the optimal regime for OOD detection based on our observations.

Specifically, we aim to answer the following question: *Does the Double Descent phenomenon manifest in post-hoc OOD detection?* This question is crucial, as it can reveal whether overparameterization, which is already known to benefit generalization, can also enhance OOD detection. We empirically demonstrate that the Double Descent effect does indeed appear in post-hoc OOD detection. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights to explain why this phenomenon emerges in such setting. Finally, we show that the overparameterized regime does not yield superior results consistently, and we propose a method to identify the optimal regime for OOD detection based on our observations.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the kind of data a model is expected to handle. This paper studies post-hoc detection, which uses an already trained model without changing its training objective or procedure. The authors investigate whether increasing model capacity changes detection performance in the same nonmonotonic way observed in double descent.

Double descent describes a pattern in which increasing model complexity can improve performance, then worsen it, and then improve it again. The authors empirically observe this phenomenon in post-hoc out-of-distribution detection and provide theoretical insights into why it can arise. This connects a question about model size with a separate question about recognizing unfamiliar inputs.

The findings also qualify the appeal of simply using a larger model: the overparameterized regime does not consistently deliver the best detection results. Based on their observations, the authors propose a method for identifying the most suitable regime. The practical implication is that capacity should be assessed for detection itself, rather than assuming that benefits associated with overparameterization automatically carry over.
summary.tldr: Post-hoc out-of-distribution detection exhibits double descent, but overparameterized models do not consistently provide the best detection performance.

title: Double Descent Meets Out-of-Distribution Detection: Theoretical Insights and Empirical Analysis on the Role of Model Complexity

abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-quality synthesis of specific subjects, such as identities or objects. This capability, while unlocking new possibilities in content creation, also introduces significant privacy risks, as personalization techniques can be misused by malicious users to generate unauthorized images. Although several studies have attempted to counter this by generating adversarially perturbed samples designed to disrupt personalization, they rely on unrealistic assumptions and become ineffective in the presence of even a few clean images or under simple image transformations. To address these challenges, we shift the protection target from the images to the diffusion model itself to hinder the personalization of specific subjects, through our novel framework called $\textbf{A}$nti-$\textbf{P}$ersonalized $\textbf{D}$iffusion $\textbf{M}$odels ($\textbf{APDM}$). We first provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that a naive approach of existing loss functions to diffusion models is inherently incapable of ensuring convergence for robust anti-personalization. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Direct Protective Optimization (DPO), a novel loss function that effectively disrupts subject personalization in the target model without compromising generative quality. Moreover, we propose a new dual-path optimization strategy, coined Learning to Protect (L2P). By alternating between personalization and protection paths, L2P simulates future personalization trajectories and adaptively reinforces protection at each step. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance in preventing unauthorized personalization. The code is available at https://github.com/KU-VGI/APDM.

A second component, Learning to Protect, alternates between personalization and protection paths. title: Perturb a Model, Not an Image: Towards Robust Privacy Protection via Anti-Personalized Diffusion Models

abstract: By sharing information across multiple agents, collaborative perception helps autonomous vehicles mitigate occlusions and improve overall perception accuracy. While most previous work focus on vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-infrastructure collaboration, with limited attention to aerial perspectives provided by UAVs, which uniquely offer dynamic, top-down views to alleviate occlusions and monitor large-scale interactive environments. A major reason for this is the lack of high-quality datasets for aerial-ground collaborative scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present AGC-Drive, the first large-scale real-world dataset for Aerial-Ground Cooperative 3D perception. The data collection platform consists of two vehicles, each equipped with five cameras and one LiDAR sensor, and one UAV carrying a forward-facing camera and a LiDAR sensor, enabling comprehensive multi-view and multi-agent perception. Consisting of approximately 80K LiDAR frames and 360K images, the dataset covers 14 diverse real-world driving scenarios, including urban roundabouts, highway tunnels, and on/off ramps. Notably, 17\% of the data comprises dynamic interaction events, including vehicle cut-ins, cut-outs, and frequent lane changes. AGC-Drive contains 350 scenes, each with approximately 100 frames and fully annotated 3D bounding boxes covering 13 object categories. We provide benchmarks for two 3D perception tasks: vehicle-to-vehicle collaborative perception and vehicle-to-UAV collaborative perception. Additionally, we release an open-source toolkit, including spatiotemporal alignment verification tools, multi-agent visualization systems, and collaborative annotation utilities. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PercepX/AGC-Drive.

AGC-Drive supplies a dataset specifically for this setting.

summary.tldr: AGC-Drive provides real-world vehicle and drone sensor data, annotations, benchmarks, and tools for studying collaborative three-dimensional perception.

title: AGC-Drive: A Large-Scale Dataset for Real-World Aerial-Ground Collaboration in Driving Scenarios

abstract: Deep multi-modal clustering (DMC) aims to explore the correlated information from different modalities to improve the clustering performance. Most existing DMCs attempt to investigate the consistency or/and complementarity information by fusing all modalities, but this will lead to the following challenges: 1) Information conflicts between modalities emerge. 2) Information-rich modalities may be weakened. To address the above challenges, we propose a diversity-oriented deep multi-modal clustering (DDMC) method, where the core is dominant modality enhancement instead of multi-modal fusion. Specifically, we select the modality with the highest average silhouette coefficient as the dominant modality, then learn the diversity information between the dominant madality and the remaining ones with diversity learning, and finally enhance the dominant modality for clustering. Extensive experiments show the superiority of the proposed method over several compared DMC methods. To our knowledge, this is the first work to perform multi-modal clustering by enhancing the dominant modality instead of fusion.

paragraphs: Multi-modal clustering groups examples using information from several modalities. Combining every modality can introduce conflicts, and a modality that carries especially useful information may lose influence in the combined representation. This paper proposes building the clustering process around a selected dominant modality and using the others to enhance it.

The method, called diversity-oriented deep multi-modal clustering, selects the modality with the highest average silhouette coefficient. This score assesses how well separated its clusters are. It then learns diversity information between that selected modality and each remaining modality. That information strengthens the dominant representation used for clustering, giving the other modalities a supporting role without requiring all of them to be fused together.

Experiments show better performance than several compared deep multi-modal clustering methods. The stated finding supports dominant-modality enhancement as a useful alternative when combining modalities risks weakening informative structure. The contribution concerns both the selection of a clustering foundation and the way other modalities contribute: their differences become resources for improving that foundation.
summary.tldr: DDMC improves multi-modal clustering by selecting a dominant modality and enhancing it with diversity information from the others.

title: Diversity-oriented Deep Multi-modal Clustering

abstract: AI-based talking-head videoconferencing systems reduce bandwidth by transmitting a latent representation of a speaker’s pose and expression, which is used to synthesize frames on the receiver's end. However, these systems are vulnerable to “puppeteering” attacks, where an adversary controls the identity of another person in real-time. Traditional deepfake detectors fail here, as all video content is synthetic. We propose a novel biometric defense that detects identity leakage in the transmitted latent representation. Our metric-learning approach disentangles identity cues from pose and expression, enabling detection of unauthorized swaps. Experiments across multiple talking-head models show that our method consistently outperforms prior defenses, operates in real time on consumer GPUs, and generalizes well to out-of-distribution data. By targeting the latent features shared during normal operation, our method offers a practical and robust safeguard against puppeteering.

paragraphs: Some AI videoconferencing systems transmit compact representations of a speaker’s pose and expression, then synthesize video at the receiving end. This saves bandwidth but permits puppeteering attacks, where an adversary controls another person’s apparent identity in real time. Ordinary deepfake detection is poorly suited to this setting because legitimate video is also synthetic.

The proposed defense examines the transmitted latent representation for biometric information that remains alongside pose and expression. A metric-learning approach disentangles those identity cues from the intended motion information. The resulting identity evidence enables detection of unauthorized swaps using features already shared during the system’s normal operation.

Experiments across multiple talking-head models show consistent improvements over prior defenses. The authors also report real-time operation on consumer GPUs and good generalization to out-of-distribution data. These findings support the practicality of checking latent identity information within the tested systems. The key insight is that identity leakage in a representation intended to convey motion can become useful evidence for identifying impersonation.
summary.tldr: A biometric defense detects videoconferencing impersonation by extracting identity cues that leak into transmitted pose-and-expression representations.

title: Unmasking Puppeteers: Leveraging Biometric Leakage to Expose Impersonation in AI-Based Videoconferencing

abstract: Sparse variable selection improves interpretability and generalization in high-dimensional learning by selecting a small subset of informative features. Recent advances in Mixed Integer Programming (MIP) have enabled solving large-scale non-private sparse regression—known as Best Subset Selection (BSS)—with millions of variables in minutes. However, extending these algorithmic advances to the setting of Differential Privacy (DP) has remained largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce two new differentially private estimators for sparse variable selection, levering modern MIP techniques. Our framework is general and applies broadly to problems like sparse regression or classification, and we provide theoretical support recovery guarantees in the case of BSS. Inspired by the exponential mechanism, we develop structured sampling procedures that efficiently explore the non-convex objective landscape, avoiding the exhaustive combinatorial search in the exponential mechanism. We complement our theoretical findings with extensive numerical experiments, using both least squares and hinge loss for our objective function, and demonstrate that our methods achieve state-of-the-art empirical support recovery, outperforming competing algorithms in settings with up to $p=10^4$.

paragraphs: Selecting a small set of informative variables can make a model easier to interpret and help it generalize. Modern mixed integer programming has made this selection practical for large non-private regression problems. This paper investigates how to bring those optimization advances into variable selection with differential privacy, introducing two private estimators.

The approach uses structured sampling procedures inspired by the exponential mechanism. Rather than exhaustively examining every possible feature subset, these procedures explore the non-convex objective using modern integer programming techniques. The framework accommodates objectives for both regression and classification. For best subset selection, the authors also provide theoretical guarantees about recovering the relevant variables, a property called support recovery.

Numerical experiments use least squares and hinge loss, testing settings with up to 10,000 variables. The methods achieve state-of-the-art empirical support recovery and outperform competing algorithms in those experiments. The contribution is therefore both computational and statistical: it connects private selection to practical optimization tools while supporting feature recovery through theory in the best subset setting and experiments across two objectives.
summary.tldr: Two private variable-selection methods use integer programming and structured sampling to recover informative features without exhaustive subset search.

title: Differentially Private High-dimensional Variable Selection via Integer Programming

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable efficient scaling of large language models but face prohibitive memory demands due to massive parameterization. Existing pruning methods rely on heuristic metrics or impractical enumeration of expert subsets, leading to suboptimal performance or scalability. In this paper, we propose Shapley-MoE, an efficient pruning method for MoE models inspired by cooperative game theory. By quantifying each expert’s contribution via Shapley value, our method identifies important experts without exhaustive combination evaluations. To overcome the NP-hard complexity of exact Shapley computation, we introduce a Monte Carlo sampling strategy for efficient approximation that reduces complexity to quadratic time. However, vanilla Monte Carlo sampling still faces issues of insufficient estimation accuracy and low sampling efficiency. To address these issues, we further propose two novel methods to improve sampling accuracy and efficiency: (1) Early Truncation, which early terminates unstable sampling steps caused by overly small expert subsets, and (2) Router-Guided Importance Sampling, which prioritize sampling important expert subsets using gating activation probabilities. Both theoretical and experimental analyses show that both methods can accelerate Shapley value estimation and improve accuracy. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that our pruned MoE models outperform existing expert pruning methods. Notably, when applied to the Qwen2-57B-A14B model, our method reduces the number of experts by 25% with only a 0.92 increase in perplexity and over 96.4% of the average zero-shot accuracy is maintained.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models can scale efficiently in computation while still demanding substantial memory for their parameters. Shapley-MoE aims to reduce that burden by identifying which experts contribute most and pruning others. It bases importance on Shapley values from cooperative game theory, which assess contributions in the context of different expert combinations.

The resulting pruned models outperform existing expert-pruning methods in the reported evaluations. This example shows how a contribution-based pruning criterion can remove substantial expert capacity while retaining much of the measured predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Shapley-MoE efficiently estimates expert contributions to prune mixture-of-experts models while retaining much of their measured performance.

title: Discovering Important Experts for Mixture-of-Experts Models Pruning Through a Theoretical Perspective

abstract: What is a gait? Appearance-based gait networks consider a gait as the human shape and motion information from images. Model-based gait networks treat a gait as the human inherent structure from points. However, the considerations remain vague for humans to comprehend truly. In this work, we introduce a novel paradigm Vocabulary-Guided Gait Recognition, dubbed Gait-World, which attempts to explore gait concepts through human vocabularies with Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Despite VLMs have achieved the remarkable progress in various vision tasks, the cognitive capability regarding gait modalities remains limited. The success element in Gait-World is the proper vocabulary prompt where this paradigm carefully selects gait cycle actions as Vocabulary Base, bridging the gait and vocabulary feature spaces and further promoting human understanding for the gait. How to extract gait features? Although previous gait networks have made significant progress, learning solely from gait modalities on limited gait databases makes it difficult to learn robust gait features for practicality. Therefore, we propose the first Gait-World model, dubbed $\alpha$-Gait, which guides the gait network learning with universal vocabulary knowledge from VLMs. However, due to the heterogeneity of the modalities, directly integrating vocabulary and gait features is highly challenging as they reside in different embedding spaces. To address the issues, $\alpha$-Gait designs Vocabulary Relation Mapper and Gait Fine-grained Detector to map and establish vocabulary relations in the gait space for detecting corresponding gait features. Extensive experiments on CASIA-B, CCPG, SUSTech1K, Gait3D and GREW reveal the potential value and research directions of vocabulary information from VLMs in the gait field.

paragraphs: Gait-World explores how human vocabulary can help describe and recognize walking patterns. Existing gait networks use appearance, motion, or structural information, but those learned concepts can be difficult for people to interpret. The paper selects actions within a gait cycle as a vocabulary base, aiming to connect gait representations with understandable language.

Its first model, α-Gait, uses vocabulary knowledge from vision-language models to guide a gait network. Directly combining the two sources is difficult because vocabulary and gait features occupy different representation spaces. A Vocabulary Relation Mapper and Gait Fine-grained Detector establish vocabulary relations within the gait space and detect the corresponding gait features.

Experiments on CASIA-B, CCPG, SUSTech1K, Gait3D, and GREW reveal potential value in bringing vocabulary information into gait recognition. The stated conclusion emphasizes that potential and the research directions it opens. The approach matters because it offers both a source of guidance beyond limited gait datasets and a route toward connecting learned walking features with concepts people can name.
summary.tldr: Gait-World uses vocabulary about gait-cycle actions to guide gait feature learning and connect walking representations with human concepts.

title: Vocabulary-Guided Gait Recognition

abstract: Continuous time systems are often modeled using discrete time dynamics but this requires a small simulation step to maintain accuracy. In turn, this requires a large planning horizon which leads to computationally demanding planning problems and reduced performance. Previous work in model-free reinforcement learning has partially addressed this issue using action repeats where a policy is learned to determine a discrete action duration. Instead we propose to control the continuous decision timescale directly by using temporally-extended actions and letting the planner treat the duration of the action as an additional optimization variable along with the standard action variables. This additional structure has multiple advantages. It speeds up simulation time of trajectories and, importantly, it allows for deep horizon search in terms of primitive actions while using a shallow search depth in the planner. In addition, in the model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) setting, it reduces compounding errors from model learning and improves training time for models. We show that this idea is effective and that the range for action durations can be automatically selected using a multi-armed bandit formulation and integrated into the MBRL framework. An extensive experimental evaluation both in planning and in MBRL, shows that our approach yields faster planning, better solutions, and that it enables solutions to problems that are not solved in the standard formulation.

paragraphs: Planning for continuous-time systems often uses small discrete simulation steps to maintain accuracy. Looking far ahead then requires many planning steps, making the search expensive and potentially reducing solution quality. The paper addresses this mismatch between the short timescale needed for simulation and the longer timescale useful for decision-making.

Its approach makes action duration a continuous optimization variable alongside the action itself. The planner therefore chooses both what to do and how long to do it. These temporally extended actions allow a shallow planning search to cover many primitive action steps and speed up trajectory simulation. In model-based reinforcement learning, the approach also reduces accumulating model-learning errors and improves model training time.

The authors further use a multi-armed bandit formulation to select the range of action durations automatically within the learning framework. Experiments in planning and model-based reinforcement learning report faster planning and better solutions. They also show solutions to problems left unsolved by the standard formulation, supporting action duration as a useful part of the planning decision.
summary.tldr: Optimizing action duration alongside action choice enables faster, longer-reaching planning and improves model-based reinforcement learning in experiments.

title: Improving planning and MBRL with temporally-extended actions

abstract: Noisy labels often compel models to overfit, especially in multi-label classification tasks. Existing methods for noisy multi-label learning (NML) primarily follow a discriminative paradigm, which relies on noise transition matrix estimation or small-loss strategies to correct noisy labels. However, they remain substantial optimization difficulties compared to noisy single-label learning. In this paper, we propose a Co-Occurrence-Aware Diffusion (CAD) model, which reformulates NML from a generative perspective. We treat features as conditions and multi-labels as diffusion targets, optimizing the diffusion model for multi-label learning with theoretical guarantees. Benefiting from the diffusion model's strength in capturing multi-object semantics and structured label matrix representation, we can effectively learn the posterior mapping from features to true multi-labels. To mitigate the interference of noisy labels in the forward process, we guide generation using pseudo-clean labels reconstructed from the latent neighborhood space, replacing original point-wise estimates with neighborhood-based proxies. In the reverse process, we further incorporate label co-occurrence constraints to enhance the model's awareness of incorrect generation directions, thereby promoting robust optimization. Extensive experiments on both synthetic (Pascal-VOC, MS-COCO) and real-world (NUS-WIDE) noisy datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

The diffusion model uses features as conditions and multi-label outputs as generation targets. To reduce the influence of noisy labels in its forward process, it constructs pseudo-clean labels from neighborhoods in a learned latent space. These neighborhood-based proxies replace estimates made separately for each example, allowing nearby examples to inform the guidance used during learning.

During reverse generation, constraints on label co-occurrence help identify incorrect directions and encourage more robust optimization. The paper provides theoretical guarantees for its diffusion-based learning formulation and reports improvements over state-of-the-art methods on Pascal-VOC and MS-COCO with synthetic noise and NUS-WIDE with real-world noise. The findings support using both local neighborhood structure and relationships between labels to learn through corrupted supervision.
summary.tldr: CAD generates label combinations with diffusion, using neighborhood-derived guidance and label co-occurrence constraints to resist noisy supervision.

title: Noisy Multi-Label Learning through Co-Occurrence-Aware Diffusion

abstract: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) are the building block of graph foundation models, but fundamentally suffer from oversmoothing and oversquashing. There has recently been a surge of interest in fixing both issues. Existing efforts primarily adopt global approaches, which may be beneficial in some regions but detrimental in others, ultimately leading to the suboptimal expressiveness. In this paper, we begin by revisiting oversquashing through a global measure -- spectral gap $\lambda$ -- and prove that the increase of $\lambda$ leads to gradient vanishing with respect to the input features, thereby undermining the effectiveness of message passing. Motivated by such theoretical insights, we propose a local approach that adaptively adjusts message passing based on local structures. To achieve this, we connect local Riemannian geometry with MPNNs, and establish a novel nonhomogeneous boundary condition to address both oversquashing and oversmoothing. Building on the Robin condition, we design a GBN network with local bottleneck adjustment, coupled with theoretical guarantees. Extensive experiments on homophilic and heterophilic graphs show the expressiveness of GBN. Furthermore, GBN does not exhibit performance degradation even when the network depth exceeds $256$ layers.

paragraphs: Graph message-passing networks face two related difficulties: repeated updates can make node representations too similar, while communication bottlenecks can compress information excessively. These problems are known as oversmoothing and oversquashing. The paper argues that globally modifying message passing can help some parts of a graph while harming others, limiting the network’s expressive power.

The authors first analyze oversquashing through the spectral gap, a global graph measure. Their theoretical analysis shows that increasing this gap leads to vanishing gradients with respect to input features, weakening effective message passing. Motivated by this result, they connect local Riemannian geometry to message passing and introduce a nonhomogeneous boundary condition.

Their GBN network builds on the Robin boundary condition to adjust bottlenecks according to local structure, with accompanying theoretical guarantees. Experiments cover graphs where connected nodes tend to be similar and graphs where they tend to differ. The reported results show strong expressiveness and no performance degradation even beyond 256 layers in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: GBN uses local geometric adjustments to address graph message-passing bottlenecks and representation collapse, supporting very deep networks in experiments.

title: Deeper with Riemannian Geometry: Overcoming Oversmoothing and Oversquashing for Graph Foundation Models

abstract: Common Neighbors (CNs) and their higher-order variants are important pairwise features widely used in state-of-the-art link prediction methods. However, existing methods often struggle with the repetition across different orders of CNs and fail to fully leverage their potential. We identify that these limitations stem from two key issues: redundancy and over-smoothing in high-order common neighbors. To address these challenges, we design orthogonalization to eliminate redundancy between different-order CNs and normalization to mitigate over-smoothing. By combining these two techniques, we propose Orthogonal Common Neighbor (OCN), a novel approach that significantly outperforms the strongest baselines by an average of 7.7\% on popular link prediction benchmarks. A thorough theoretical analysis is provided to support our method. Ablation studies also verify the effectiveness of our orthogonalization and normalization techniques.

By combining these two techniques, we propose Orthogonal Common Neighbor (OCN), a novel approach that significantly outperforms the strongest baselines by an average of 7.7\% on popular link prediction benchmarks. paragraphs: Link prediction uses information about a pair of nodes to estimate whether they should be connected. Shared neighbors, including higher-order variants, are useful signals for this task. The paper examines why using information from more neighborhood orders does not automatically deliver its full potential: different orders can repeat information and become overly smoothed.

Orthogonal Common Neighbor addresses these problems with two operations. Orthogonalization removes redundancy between common-neighbor features from different orders. Normalization mitigates over-smoothing, helping retain distinctions that would otherwise become less useful. Together, the operations aim to make higher-order relational information contribute more effectively to the final link prediction.

On popular link-prediction benchmarks, OCN exceeds the strongest compared baselines by a reported average of 7.7%. The paper supplies theoretical analysis and ablation studies that support the method and verify the contributions of both operations. Its central insight is that the organization of neighborhood information matters alongside its availability. Separating repeated signals and controlling smoothing can improve the value of features that existing predictors already recognize as important.
summary.tldr: OCN removes redundancy and mitigates over-smoothing in higher-order common-neighbor features, improving reported link-prediction performance by an average of 7.7%.

title: OCN: Effectively Utilizing Higher-Order Common Neighbors for Better Link Prediction

abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have long depended on Gaussian priors, with little exploration of alternative distributions. We introduce a Proper Hölder-Kullback Dirichlet framework that uses time-varying multiplicative transformations to define both forward and reverse diffusion processes. Moving beyond conventional reweighted evidence lower bounds (ELBO) or Kullback–Leibler upper bounds (KLUB), we propose two novel divergence measures: the Proper Hölder Divergence (PHD) and the Proper Hölder–Kullback (PHK) divergence, the latter designed to restore symmetry missing in existing formulations. When optimizing our Dirichlet diffusion model with PHK, we achieve a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) of 2.78 on unconditional CIFAR-10. Comprehensive experiments on natural-image datasets validate the generative strengths of model and confirm PHK’s effectiveness in model training. These contributions expand the diffusion-model family with principled non-Gaussian processes and effective optimization tools, offering new avenues for versatile, high-fidelity generative modeling.

paragraphs: Diffusion generative models have largely relied on Gaussian priors. This paper explores a different distributional foundation through a Dirichlet diffusion framework. It defines both forward and reverse processes using multiplicative transformations that change over time, expanding the mathematical choices available for constructing diffusion models.

The authors also introduce two divergence measures for training: Proper Hölder Divergence and Proper Hölder–Kullback divergence. The latter is designed to restore symmetry missing from existing formulations. These objectives provide alternatives to the reweighted evidence lower bounds and Kullback–Leibler upper bounds discussed in the paper, pairing a different diffusion process with new optimization tools.

With the Proper Hölder–Kullback objective, the Dirichlet model obtains a Fréchet Inception Distance of 2.78 on unconditional CIFAR-10 generation. Experiments on natural-image datasets further support its generative performance and the training objective's effectiveness. The results establish a concrete non-Gaussian option for diffusion modeling and suggest that both the process distribution and the divergence used to train it can be productive design choices.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet diffusion framework and new divergence objectives provide a non-Gaussian route to high-quality image generation.

title: Proper Hölder-Kullback Dirichlet Diffusion: A Framework for High Dimensional Generative Modeling

abstract: We propose a Predictable Dual-View Hashing (PDH) algorithm which embeds proximity of data samples in the original spaces. We create a cross-view hamming space with the ability to compare information from previously incomparable domains with a notion of ‘predictability’. By performing comparative experimental analysis on two large datasets, PASCAL-Sentence and SUN-Attribute, we demonstrate the superiority of our method to the state-of-the-art dual-view binary code learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: We propose a Predictable Dual-View Hashing (PDH) algorithm which embeds proximity of data samples in the original spaces. We create a cross-view hamming space with the ability to compare information from previously incomparable domains with a notion of ‘predictability’. By performing comparative experimental analysis on two large datasets, PASCAL-Sentence and SUN-Attribute, we demonstrate the superiority of our method to the state-of-the-art dual-view binary code learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Data from different domains can be difficult to compare because each domain has its own representation and notion of proximity. The paper introduces Predictable Dual-View Hashing, or PDH, to construct a shared binary representation. Its objective includes retaining proximity relationships among samples from their original spaces.

PDH creates a cross-view Hamming space, where information from the two views can be compared through binary codes. The method uses a notion of predictability to support comparison across domains that were previously incomparable. The shared space therefore connects two requirements: representing relationships within the original views and making relationships across views accessible.

The authors evaluate PDH on the PASCAL-Sentence and SUN-Attribute datasets through comparisons with state-of-the-art dual-view binary-code learning methods. They report superior performance in those experiments. The significance is an empirical demonstration that the proposed shared representation can improve cross-view comparison on the evaluated datasets while incorporating proximity from the original data spaces.
summary.tldr: PDH maps two data views into a shared binary space and improves on compared dual-view hashing methods in two datasets.

title: Predictable Dual-View Hashing

abstract: We show how deep learning methods can be applied in the context of crowdsourcing and unsupervised ensemble learning. First, we prove that the popular model of Dawid and Skene, which assumes that all classifiers are conditionally independent, is \em equivalent to a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) with a single hidden node. Hence, under this model, the posterior probabilities of the true labels can be instead estimated via a trained RBM. Next, to address the more general case, where classifiers may strongly violate the conditional independence assumption, we propose to apply RBM-based Deep Neural Net (DNN). Experimental results on various simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed DNN approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, in particular when the data violates the conditional independence assumption.
