First, we prove that the popular model of Dawid and Skene, which assumes that all classifiers are conditionally independent, is \em equivalent to a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) with a single hidden node. Hence, under this model, the posterior probabilities of the true labels can be instead estimated via a trained RBM. Next, to address the more general case, where classifiers may strongly violate the conditional independence assumption, we propose to apply RBM-based Deep Neural Net (DNN). Experimental results on various simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed DNN approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, in particular when the data violates the conditional independence assumption.

paragraphs: Unsupervised ensemble learning combines predictions from several classifiers when the true labels are unavailable for ordinary supervised combination. A related problem arises in crowdsourcing, where several workers supply answers of uncertain reliability. This paper connects a classical probabilistic model for such answers with neural network models, then extends that connection to more dependent collections of predictors.

The authors prove that the Dawid–Skene model is equivalent to a restricted Boltzmann machine with one hidden node. Dawid–Skene assumes that classifier outputs are independent once the true label is known. Under that model, the equivalence means a trained restricted Boltzmann machine can estimate the posterior probabilities of the unknown true labels.

To address settings where conditional independence is strongly violated, the authors propose a deep neural network based on restricted Boltzmann machines. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show improvements over other leading methods, particularly when the independence assumption fails. The theoretical equivalence establishes the connection for the classical model; the experimental results support the deeper approach for the more general setting.
summary.tldr: The paper connects Dawid–Skene label aggregation to a restricted Boltzmann machine and uses a deeper network to handle dependent classifiers.

title: A Deep Learning Approach to Unsupervised Ensemble Learning

abstract: Clustering is a powerful tool in data analysis, but it is often difficult to find a grouping that aligns with a user’s needs. To address this, several methods incorporate constraints obtained from users into clustering algorithms, but unfortunately do not apply to hierarchical clustering. We design an interactive Bayesian algorithm that incorporates user interaction into hierarchical clustering while still utilizing the geometry of the data by sampling a constrained posterior distribution over hierarchies. We also suggest several ways to intelligently query a user. The algorithm, along with the querying schemes, shows promising results on real data.
originalAbstract: Clustering is a powerful tool in data analysis, but it is often difficult to find a grouping that aligns with a user’s needs. To address this, several methods incorporate constraints obtained from users into clustering algorithms, but unfortunately do not apply to hierarchical clustering. We design an interactive Bayesian algorithm that incorporates user interaction into hierarchical clustering while still utilizing the geometry of the data by sampling a constrained posterior distribution over hierarchies. We also suggest several ways to intelligently query a user. The algorithm, along with the querying schemes, shows promising results on real data.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a practical difficulty in clustering: a grouping suggested by the data may not match the user’s needs. It focuses on hierarchical clustering, where groups are organized at multiple levels. The authors seek a way for user feedback to shape this hierarchy while retaining information about the geometry of the data.

Their algorithm takes a Bayesian approach, sampling from a posterior distribution over hierarchies subject to constraints obtained through interaction. This combines user-provided requirements with the structure supported by the observations. Representing possible hierarchies through a constrained posterior gives the interaction a role within the clustering procedure itself.

The authors also propose several strategies for choosing questions to ask the user. This makes query selection a second part of the approach, alongside incorporating the answers into clustering. The algorithm and querying schemes show promising results on real data. Those findings support the feasibility of interactive hierarchical clustering that responds to user needs while continuing to use the data’s geometric organization.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian hierarchical clustering algorithm incorporates user constraints and proposes query strategies, with promising results on real data.

title: Interactive Bayesian Hierarchical Clustering

abstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the strongly convex sum of a finite number of convex functions. Standard algorithms for solving this problem in the class of incremental/stochastic methods have at most a linear convergence rate. We propose a new incremental method whose convergence rate is superlinear – the Newton-type incremental method (NIM). The idea of the method is to introduce a model of the objective with the same sum-of-functions structure and further update a single component of the model per iteration. We prove that NIM has a superlinear local convergence rate and linear global convergence rate. Experiments show that the method is very effective for problems with a large number of functions and a small number of variables.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of minimizing the strongly convex sum of a finite number of convex functions. Standard algorithms for solving this problem in the class of incremental/stochastic methods have at most a linear convergence rate. We propose a new incremental method whose convergence rate is superlinear – the Newton-type incremental method (NIM). The idea of the method is to introduce a model of the objective with the same sum-of-functions structure and further update a single component of the model per iteration. We prove that NIM has a superlinear local convergence rate and linear global convergence rate. Experiments show that the method is very effective for problems with a large number of functions and a small number of variables.

paragraphs: The paper studies objectives formed by adding finitely many convex functions, with the additional assumption that their sum is strongly convex. Standard incremental or stochastic methods for this setting have convergence rates that are at most linear. The authors seek faster convergence while retaining the incremental idea of updating only part of the optimization machinery at each iteration.

Their Newton-type incremental method, NIM, maintains a model of the objective that preserves its sum-of-functions structure. Each iteration updates a single component of that model. This construction brings Newton-type optimization into an incremental method, connecting information about individual component functions to progress on the overall objective.

The analysis establishes linear global convergence and superlinear local convergence. The distinction matters: the stronger rate applies near the solution, rather than throughout the entire optimization process. Experiments find the method particularly effective when there are many component functions but relatively few variables. That reported setting identifies where the proposed combination of incremental updates and faster local convergence is practically promising.
summary.tldr: NIM updates one objective-model component per iteration and achieves linear global convergence with superlinear convergence near the solution.

title: A Superlinearly-Convergent Proximal Newton-type Method for the Optimization of Finite Sums

abstract: There is a need for simple yet accurate white-box learning systems that train quickly and with little data. To this end, we showcase REBEL, a multi-class boosting method, and present a novel family of weak learners called localized similarities. Our framework provably minimizes the training error of any dataset at an exponential rate. We carry out experiments on a variety of synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating a consistent tendency to avoid overfitting. We evaluate our method on MNIST and standard UCI datasets against other state-of-the-art methods, showing the empirical proficiency of our method.
originalAbstract: There is a need for simple yet accurate white-box learning systems that train quickly and with little data. To this end, we showcase REBEL, a multi-class boosting method, and present a novel family of weak learners called localized similarities. Our framework provably minimizes the training error of any dataset at an exponential rate. We carry out experiments on a variety of synthetic and real datasets, demonstrating a consistent tendency to avoid overfitting. We evaluate our method on MNIST and standard UCI datasets against other state-of-the-art methods, showing the empirical proficiency of our method.

paragraphs: This paper presents REBEL, a boosting method for classification problems with multiple classes. The motivating goal is a simple, inspectable learning system that is accurate while requiring little data and training time. Alongside the boosting framework, the authors introduce a family of weak learners called localized similarities, which supply the components used by the method.

The theoretical result concerns fitting the training data: the framework is proved to minimize training error at an exponential rate for any dataset. That is a claim about how quickly training error is reduced. It is distinct from the question of whether the resulting classifier will perform well on examples outside the training set.

The authors investigate that second question empirically using synthetic and real datasets. They report a consistent tendency to avoid overfitting and evaluate REBEL against state-of-the-art methods on MNIST and standard UCI datasets. The stated findings support its practical effectiveness, while keeping the observed resistance to overfitting separate from the formal guarantee about training error.
summary.tldr: REBEL combines multiclass boosting with localized-similarity weak learners, offering an exponential training-error guarantee and encouraging empirical generalization.

title: A Simple Multi-Class Boosting Framework with Theoretical Guarantees and Empirical Proficiency

abstract: This paper investigates the problem of interactively learning behaviors communicated by a human teacher using positive and negative feedback. Much previous work on this problem has made the assumption that people provide feedback for decisions that is dependent on the behavior they are teaching and is independent from the learner’s current policy. We present empirical results that show this assumption to be false—whether human trainers give a positive or negative feedback for a decision is influenced by the learner’s current policy. Based on this insight, we introduce Convergent Actor-Critic by Humans (COACH), an algorithm for learning from policy-dependent feedback that converges to a local optimum. Finally, we demonstrate that COACH can successfully learn multiple behaviors on a physical robot.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates the problem of interactively learning behaviors communicated by a human teacher using positive and negative feedback. Much previous work on this problem has made the assumption that people provide feedback for decisions that is dependent on the behavior they are teaching and is independent from the learner’s current policy. We present empirical results that show this assumption to be false—whether human trainers give a positive or negative feedback for a decision is influenced by the learner’s current policy. Based on this insight, we introduce Convergent Actor-Critic by Humans (COACH), an algorithm for learning from policy-dependent feedback that converges to a local optimum. Finally, we demonstrate that COACH can successfully learn multiple behaviors on a physical robot.

paragraphs: When a person teaches an agent with positive and negative feedback, the meaning of that feedback may depend on how the agent currently behaves. Previous work often assumed that feedback depended on the intended behavior but was independent of the learner’s current policy. This paper tests that assumption directly.

The empirical results show that the learner’s policy influences whether trainers respond positively or negatively to a decision. Consequently, a feedback signal cannot always be interpreted independently of the learner’s current behavior. The paper uses this observation as the basis for Convergent Actor-Critic by Humans, or COACH, an algorithm designed for policy-dependent human feedback.

COACH converges to a local optimum, which is a more specific claim than finding the best possible behavior globally. The authors also demonstrate that it can learn multiple behaviors on a physical robot. Together, the evidence about human responses and the robot demonstrations support a learning formulation that accounts for feedback changing with the learner’s policy.
summary.tldr: COACH learns from human feedback whose meaning depends on the learner’s current policy and converges to a local optimum.

title: Interactive Learning from Policy-Dependent Human Feedback

abstract: The most prevalent notions of fairness in machine learning fix a small collection of pre-defined groups (such as race or gender), and then ask for approximate parity of some statistic of the classifier (such as false positive rate) across these groups. Constraints of this form are susceptible to fairness gerrymandering, in which a classifier is fair on each individual group, but badly violates the fairness constraint on structured subgroups, such as certain combinations of protected attribute values. We thus consider fairness across exponentially or infinitely many subgroups, defined by a structured class of functions over the protected attributes. We first prove that the problem of auditing subgroup fairness for both equality of false positive rates and statistical parity is computationally equivalent to the problem of weak agnostic learning — which means it is hard in the worst case, even for simple structured subclasses. However, it also suggests that common heuristics for learning can be applied to successfully solve the auditing problem in practice. We then derive an algorithm that provably converges in a polynomial number of steps to the best subgroup-fair distribution over classifiers, given access to an oracle which can solve the agnostic learning problem. The algorithm is based on a formulation of subgroup fairness as a zero-sum game between a Learner (the primal player) and an Auditor (the dual player). We implement a variant of this algorithm using heuristic oracles, and show that we can effectively both audit and learn fair classifiers on a real dataset.

paragraphs: A classifier can satisfy a fairness requirement for broad demographic groups while violating it for combinations of those groups. The paper calls this fairness gerrymandering. It considers fairness over exponentially or infinitely many subgroups specified by a structured family of functions of protected attributes.

The authors prove that auditing subgroup fairness for statistical parity and false-positive-rate equality is computationally equivalent to weak agnostic learning. This establishes worst-case difficulty even for simple subgroup families. The connection also suggests a practical route: learning heuristics can serve as tools for finding subgroup violations.

For training, the paper formulates a zero-sum game between a learner and an auditor. Given an oracle that solves agnostic learning, its algorithm provably converges in polynomially many steps to the best subgroup-fair distribution over classifiers. The oracle requirement is essential to that guarantee. A variant using heuristic oracles successfully audits and learns fair classifiers on a real dataset, providing empirical evidence alongside the conditional theory.
summary.tldr: A learner–auditor framework addresses hidden subgroup unfairness, with oracle-dependent convergence guarantees and a practical demonstration using heuristics.

title: Preventing Fairness Gerrymandering: Auditing and Learning for Subgroup Fairness

abstract: We introduce a new class of inter-domain variational Gaussian processes (GP) where data is mapped onto the unit hypersphere in order to use spherical harmonic representations. Our inference scheme is comparable to variational Fourier features, but it does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, and leads to diagonal covariance matrices between inducing variables. This enables a speed-up in inference, because it bypasses the need to invert large covariance matrices. Our experiments show that our model is able to fit a regression model for a dataset with 6 million entries two orders of magnitude faster compared to standard sparse GPs, while retaining state of the art accuracy. We also demonstrate competitive performance on classification with non-conjugate likelihoods.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new class of inter-domain variational Gaussian processes (GP) where data is mapped onto the unit hypersphere in order to use spherical harmonic representations. Our inference scheme is comparable to variational Fourier features, but it does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, and leads to diagonal covariance matrices between inducing variables. This enables a speed-up in inference, because it bypasses the need to invert large covariance matrices. Our experiments show that our model is able to fit a regression model for a dataset with 6 million entries two orders of magnitude faster compared to standard sparse GPs, while retaining state of the art accuracy. We also demonstrate competitive performance on classification with non-conjugate likelihoods.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process inference can become expensive when it requires operations on large covariance matrices. This paper proposes a class of inter-domain variational Gaussian processes that first maps data onto a unit hypersphere. The construction then uses spherical harmonics to represent features, changing the representation used to make approximate inference computationally manageable.

A central benefit is that the covariance matrix between inducing variables becomes diagonal. This avoids the need to invert a large covariance matrix and enables faster inference. The authors compare the scheme conceptually with variational Fourier features and state that their approach avoids the curse of dimensionality affecting that alternative.

In a regression experiment with six million entries, the method fits the model two orders of magnitude faster than standard sparse Gaussian processes while retaining state-of-the-art accuracy. The authors also report competitive classification performance with non-conjugate likelihoods. These findings connect the computational advantage of the inducing-variable structure to substantial measured speed gains and useful predictive performance in the studied tasks.
summary.tldr: Spherical harmonic features produce diagonal inducing-variable covariances, enabling substantially faster sparse Gaussian-process inference in the reported experiments.

title: Sparse Gaussian Processes with Spherical Harmonic Features

abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation models significantly speed up decoding by allowing for parallel prediction of the entire target sequence. However, modeling word order is more challenging due to the lack of autoregressive factors in the model. This difficultly is compounded during training with cross entropy loss, which can highly penalize small shifts in word order. In this paper, we propose aligned cross entropy (AXE) as an alternative loss function for training of non-autoregressive models. AXE uses a differentiable dynamic program to assign loss based on the best possible monotonic alignment between target tokens and model predictions. AXE-based training of conditional masked language models (CMLMs) substantially improves performance on major WMT benchmarks, while setting a new state of the art for non-autoregressive models.
originalAbstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation models significantly speed up decoding by allowing for parallel prediction of the entire target sequence. However, modeling word order is more challenging due to the lack of autoregressive factors in the model. This difficultly is compounded during training with cross entropy loss, which can highly penalize small shifts in word order. In this paper, we propose aligned cross entropy (AXE) as an alternative loss function for training of non-autoregressive models. AXE uses a differentiable dynamic program to assign loss based on the best possible monotonic alignment between target tokens and model predictions. AXE-based training of conditional masked language models (CMLMs) substantially improves performance on major WMT benchmarks, while setting a new state of the art for non-autoregressive models.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive translation predicts an entire target sequence in parallel, enabling faster decoding. Its challenge is organizing those predictions into the correct word order without the sequential dependencies used by autoregressive models. Ordinary cross entropy adds another difficulty: a small shift in token positions can receive a large penalty even when much of the predicted content is appropriate.

Aligned cross entropy, or AXE, changes how the training loss compares predictions with the target. A differentiable dynamic program finds the best monotonic alignment between them and assigns loss using that alignment. Monotonicity preserves sequence order while allowing the comparison to accommodate positional shifts. The training signal therefore depends on an aligned correspondence rather than rigid position-by-position matching.

The authors apply AXE to conditional masked language models and report substantial improvements on major WMT benchmarks, reaching a new state of the art for non-autoregressive models. The finding shows that the way a loss measures sequence disagreement can materially affect translation quality, alongside the model’s parallel prediction design.
summary.tldr: AXE trains parallel translation models using an alignment-aware loss, reducing sensitivity to token shifts and improving reported benchmark performance.

title: Aligned Cross Entropy for Non-Autoregressive Machine Translation

abstract: We consider a decentralized stochastic learning problem where data points are distributed among computing nodes communicating over a directed graph. As the model size gets large, decentralized learning faces a major bottleneck that is the heavy communication load due to each node transmitting large messages (model updates) to its neighbors. To tackle this bottleneck, we propose the quantized decentralized stochastic learning algorithm over directed graphs that is based on the push-sum algorithm in decentralized consensus optimization. We prove that our algorithm achieves the same convergence rates of the decentralized stochastic learning algorithm with exact-communication for both convex and non-convex losses. Numerical evaluations corroborate our main theoretical results and illustrate significant speed-up compared to the exact-communication methods.
originalAbstract: We consider a decentralized stochastic learning problem where data points are distributed among computing nodes communicating over a directed graph. As the model size gets large, decentralized learning faces a major bottleneck that is the heavy communication load due to each node transmitting large messages (model updates) to its neighbors. To tackle this bottleneck, we propose the quantized decentralized stochastic learning algorithm over directed graphs that is based on the push-sum algorithm in decentralized consensus optimization. We prove that our algorithm achieves the same convergence rates of the decentralized stochastic learning algorithm with exact-communication for both convex and non-convex losses. Numerical evaluations corroborate our main theoretical results and illustrate significant speed-up compared to the exact-communication methods.

paragraphs: In decentralized learning, computing nodes hold different data and exchange model updates with neighboring nodes. As models grow, sending these updates can become a major bottleneck. This paper studies how to reduce that communication burden when the connections between nodes form a directed graph.

The proposed algorithm quantizes communicated updates, using a more compact representation of the messages. It builds on push-sum, a method used for decentralized consensus optimization. The approach therefore combines reduced communication with a coordination mechanism suited to directed communication links.

The authors prove that the resulting method matches the convergence rates of decentralized stochastic learning with exact communication for both convex and non-convex losses. This is a statement about convergence rates, rather than identical behavior at every update. Numerical evaluations support the theory and show significant speed-ups over exact-communication methods. The combined result suggests that reducing message precision can ease a practical communication bottleneck while retaining the established rate of learning progress in the analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: A quantized push-sum learning algorithm reduces communication over directed graphs while matching exact-communication convergence rates in the analyzed settings.

title: Quantized Decentralized Stochastic Learning over Directed Graphs

abstract: A key challenge on the path to developing agents that learn complex human-like behavior is the need to quickly and accurately quantify human-likeness. While human assessments of such behavior can be highly accurate, speed and scalability are limited. We address these limitations through a novel automated Navigation Turing Test (ANTT) that learns to predict human judgments of human-likeness. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our automated NTT on a navigation task in a complex 3D environment. We investigate six classification models to shed light on the types of architectures best suited to this task, and validate them against data collected through a human NTT. Our best models achieve high accuracy when distinguishing true human and agent behavior. At the same time, we show that predicting finer-grained human assessment of agents’ progress towards human-like behavior remains unsolved. Our work takes an important step towards agents that more effectively learn complex human-like behavior.

summary.tldr: Learned navigation evaluators distinguish humans from agents well, but finer-grained prediction of perceived human-likeness remains unresolved.

title: Navigation Turing Test (NTT): Learning to Evaluate Human-Like Navigation

abstract: We study regularized deep neural networks (DNNs) and introduce a convex analytic framework to characterize the structure of the hidden layers. We show that a set of optimal hidden layer weights for a norm regularized DNN training problem can be explicitly found as the extreme points of a convex set. For the special case of deep linear networks, we prove that each optimal weight matrix aligns with the previous layers via duality. More importantly, we apply the same characterization to deep ReLU networks with whitened data and prove the same weight alignment holds. As a corollary, we also prove that norm regularized deep ReLU networks yield spline interpolation for one-dimensional datasets which was previously known only for two-layer networks. Furthermore, we provide closed-form solutions for the optimal layer weights when data is rank-one or whitened. The same analysis also applies to architectures with batch normalization even for arbitrary data. Therefore, we obtain a complete explanation for a recent empirical observation termed Neural Collapse where class means collapse to the vertices of a simplex equiangular tight frame.

Together, the findings connect regularization and architectural structure to precise geometric properties of optimal representations.

title: Revealing the Structure of Deep Neural Networks via Convex Duality

abstract: We give a simple proof for the global convergence of gradient descent in training deep ReLU networks with the standard square loss, and show some of its improvements over the state-of-the-art. In particular, while prior works require all the hidden layers to be wide with width at least $\Omega(N^8)$ ($N$ being the number of training samples), we require a single wide layer of linear, quadratic or cubic width depending on the type of initialization. Unlike many recent proofs based on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), our proof need not track the evolution of the entire NTK matrix, or more generally, any quantities related to the changes of activation patterns during training. Instead, we only need to track the evolution of the output at the last hidden layer, which can be done much more easily thanks to the Lipschitz property of ReLU. Some highlights of our setting: (i) all the layers are trained with standard gradient descent, (ii) the network has standard parameterization as opposed to the NTK one, and (iii) the network has a single wide layer as opposed to having all wide hidden layers as in most of NTK-related results.

Its main architectural improvement is that only one hidden layer needs to be wide. Depending on initialization, the required width grows linearly, quadratically, or cubically with the number of training examples.

The proof changes which quantities must be monitored during training. Many neural tangent kernel analyses track the entire kernel matrix or changes in activation patterns. Here, the authors need only track the output of the last hidden layer. ReLU's Lipschitz property makes controlling the evolution of that output easier.

The result applies in a setting where every layer is trained by standard gradient descent and the network uses standard parameterization. Compared with the cited earlier requirements for all hidden layers to have width at least on the order of the eighth power of sample count, these are substantially reduced sufficient width requirements. The exact requirement remains dependent on initialization.
summary.tldr: A simpler convergence proof requires only one wide ReLU layer, with sufficient width ranging from linear to cubic in sample count depending on initialization.

title: On the Proof of Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Deep ReLU Networks with Linear Widths

abstract: Latent variable models have been successfully applied in lossless compression with the bits-back coding algorithm. However, bits-back suffers from an increase in the bitrate equal to the KL divergence between the approximate posterior and the true posterior. In this paper, we show how to remove this gap asymptotically by deriving bits-back coding algorithms from tighter variational bounds. The key idea is to exploit extended space representations of Monte Carlo estimators of the marginal likelihood. Naively applied, our schemes would require more initial bits than the standard bits-back coder, but we show how to drastically reduce this additional cost with couplings in the latent space. When parallel architectures can be exploited, our coders can achieve better rates than bits-back with little additional cost. We demonstrate improved lossless compression rates in a variety of settings, especially in out-of-distribution or sequential data compression.

paragraphs: Bits-back coding uses latent-variable models for lossless compression, but an imperfect approximate posterior adds to the bitrate. The extra amount equals the KL divergence between the approximate and true posteriors. This paper develops coding schemes that can remove this gap asymptotically by drawing on tighter variational bounds.

The central construction represents Monte Carlo estimates of marginal likelihood in an expanded space. This connects improved probabilistic estimates to actual compression procedures. A direct implementation would need more starting bits than standard bits-back coding, so the authors introduce couplings in the latent space to substantially reduce that additional requirement. Starting-bit cost is therefore addressed as part of the coding design.

The authors demonstrate better lossless compression rates across multiple settings, particularly for out-of-distribution data and sequential compression. They also state that, when parallel architectures are available, the improved rates can come with little extra cost. The findings connect tighter inference bounds to practical compression improvements while keeping the asymptotic and parallel-computation qualifications explicit.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo bits-back coders improve lossless compression and asymptotically eliminate the bitrate gap caused by approximate posterior inference.

title: Improving Lossless Compression Rates via Monte Carlo Bits-Back Coding

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution examples is important for safety-critical machine learning applications such as detecting novel biological phenomena and self-driving cars. However, existing research mainly focuses on simple small-scale settings. To set the stage for more realistic out-of-distribution detection, we depart from small-scale settings and explore large-scale multiclass and multi-label settings with high-resolution images and thousands of classes. To make future work in real-world settings possible, we create new benchmarks for three large-scale settings. To test ImageNet multiclass anomaly detectors, we introduce the Species dataset containing over 700,000 images and over a thousand anomalous species. We leverage ImageNet-21K to evaluate PASCAL VOC and COCO multilabel anomaly detectors. Third, we introduce a new benchmark for anomaly segmentation by introducing a segmentation benchmark with road anomalies. We conduct extensive experiments in these more realistic settings for out-of-distribution detection and find that a surprisingly simple detector based on the maximum logit outperforms prior methods in all the large-scale multi-class, multi-label, and segmentation tasks, establishing a simple new baseline for future work.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to recognize examples outside the kinds of data a model is expected to handle. This paper moves evaluation beyond small, simple settings toward high-resolution images, thousands of classes, multiple labels, and spatial anomaly detection. Its central contribution includes benchmarks that make these larger and more varied settings accessible for further study.

For ImageNet multiclass detectors, the authors introduce Species, containing more than 700,000 images and over a thousand anomalous species. They use ImageNet-21K to evaluate multilabel detectors associated with PASCAL VOC and COCO. A third benchmark evaluates anomaly segmentation using road anomalies, extending the problem from recognizing unusual images to identifying anomalous regions.

A logit is a model score before conversion into a probability. The result establishes a straightforward baseline across the new evaluations and shows why methods should be tested under broader conditions before judging their relative effectiveness.
summary.tldr: New large-scale anomaly benchmarks reveal that a simple maximum-logit detector outperforms prior methods across the evaluated task types.

title: Scaling Out-of-Distribution Detection for Real-World Settings

abstract: With the development of deep learning (DL) technologies, the demand for DL-based services on personal devices, such as mobile phones, also increases rapidly. In this paper, we propose a novel personalization method, Variational On-the-Fly Personalization. Compared to the conventional personalization methods that require additional fine-tuning with personal data, the proposed method only requires forwarding a handful of personal data on-the-fly. Assuming even a single personal data can convey the characteristics of a target person, we develop the variational hyper-personalizer to capture the weight distribution of layers that fits the target person. In the testing phase, the hyper-personalizer estimates the model’s weights on-the-fly based on personality by forwarding only a small amount of (even a single) personal enrollment data. Hence, the proposed method can perform the personalization without any training software platform and additional cost in the edge device. In experiments, we show our approach can effectively generate reliable personalized models via forwarding (not back-propagating) a handful of samples.

paragraphs: Personalizing a deep-learning service usually requires additional training on a person's data. This paper proposes generating personalized model weights through forward computation instead. The aim is to make personalization possible on devices such as phones without installing a training platform or performing additional fine-tuning there.

The method uses a variational hyper-personalizer to capture a distribution over layer weights suited to the target person. It assumes that even one personal example can convey useful characteristics of that person. At test time, a small enrollment set passes through the hyper-personalizer, which estimates personalized weights on the fly. The personal examples therefore inform weight generation directly.

Experiments show that forwarding a handful of examples can produce reliable personalized models without back-propagating through those examples. The approach can also use a single enrollment example, under the motivating assumption that it carries relevant personal information. Its practical contribution is to move the personalization procedure from device-side fine-tuning to inference through an already learned weight-generating model.
summary.tldr: A variational hyper-personalizer generates personalized model weights from a few enrollment examples without device-side fine-tuning.

title: Variational On-the-Fly Personalization

abstract: Recent sharpness-aware minimisation (SAM) is known to find flat minima which is beneficial for better generalisation with improved robustness. SAM essentially modifies the loss function by the maximum loss value within the small neighborhood around the current iterate. However, it uses the Euclidean ball to define the neighborhood, which can be less accurate since loss functions for neural networks are typically defined over probability distributions (e.g., class predictive probabilities), rendering the parameter space no more Euclidean. In this paper we consider the information geometry of the model parameter space when defining the neighborhood, namely replacing SAM’s Euclidean balls with ellipsoids induced by the Fisher information. Our approach, dubbed Fisher SAM, defines more accurate neighborhood structures that conform to the intrinsic metric of the underlying statistical manifold. For instance, SAM may probe the worst-case loss value at either a too nearby or inappropriately distant point due to the ignorance of the parameter space geometry, which is avoided by our Fisher SAM. Another recent Adaptive SAM approach that stretches/shrinks the Euclidean ball in accordance with the scales of the parameter magnitudes, might be dangerous, potentially destroying the neighborhood structure even severely. We demonstrate the improved performance of the proposed Fisher SAM on several benchmark datasets/tasks.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization evaluates the worst loss in a small neighborhood around the current model parameters. This encourages solutions with flatter surrounding loss, associated with better generalization and robustness. The paper questions how that neighborhood is defined: ordinary SAM uses a Euclidean ball, although neural networks often represent probability distributions.

Fisher SAM replaces that ball with an ellipsoid determined by Fisher information. This makes the neighborhood reflect the statistical geometry of the model's parameter space. The motivation is that a seemingly small or large parameter displacement need not correspond to the same degree of change in the underlying distribution. Ignoring that geometry can make SAM probe points at inappropriate distances.

The authors also caution that adapting neighborhood shape using parameter magnitudes can potentially distort its structure severely. Their proposed alternative ties the shape to information geometry instead. Experiments on several benchmark datasets and tasks demonstrate improved performance for Fisher SAM, supporting the practical value of changing how the sharpness neighborhood is measured.
summary.tldr: Fisher SAM uses information-geometric neighborhoods to measure sharpness and improves performance on the evaluated benchmarks.

title: Fisher SAM: Information Geometry and Sharpness Aware Minimisation

abstract: How to properly model the inter-frame relation within the video sequence is an important but unsolved challenge for video restoration (VR). In this work, we propose an unsupervised flow-aligned sequence-to-sequence model (S2SVR) to address this problem. On the one hand, the sequence-to-sequence model, which has proven capable of sequence modeling in the field of natural language processing, is explored for the first time in VR. Optimized serialization modeling shows potential in capturing long-range dependencies among frames. On the other hand, we equip the sequence-to-sequence model with an unsupervised optical flow estimator to maximize its potential. The flow estimator is trained with our proposed unsupervised distillation loss, which can alleviate the data discrepancy and inaccurate degraded optical flow issues of previous flow-based methods. With reliable optical flow, we can establish accurate correspondence among multiple frames, narrowing the domain difference between 1D language and 2D misaligned frames and improving the potential of the sequence-to-sequence model. S2SVR shows superior performance in multiple VR tasks, including video deblurring, video super-resolution, and compressed video quality enhancement. https://github.com/linjing7/VR-Baseline

paragraphs: Video restoration requires understanding relationships between frames, including information separated by substantial time or displaced by motion. This paper explores sequence-to-sequence modeling for that purpose. Its premise is that sequence modeling can capture long-range dependencies, provided the method accounts for the spatial misalignment that makes video frames different from a one-dimensional language sequence.

S2SVR combines the sequence model with an unsupervised optical-flow estimator. A proposed unsupervised distillation loss trains the estimator and can alleviate data discrepancies and inaccurate flow from degraded images that affect earlier flow-based approaches. Reliable flow establishes correspondences across frames, helping the sequence model relate the same scene content at different positions.

The authors report superior performance on video deblurring, video super-resolution, and compressed-video quality enhancement. These results support combining temporal sequence modeling with motion-based alignment across several restoration tasks. The approach's significance is the connection between those components: alignment helps make the relationships the sequence model needs to learn more coherent, while sequence modeling offers a way to use information across longer frame sequences.
summary.tldr: S2SVR combines sequence-to-sequence modeling with unsupervised optical-flow alignment to improve several video-restoration tasks.

title: Unsupervised Flow-Aligned Sequence-to-Sequence Learning for Video Restoration

abstract: Dynamic mechanism design has garnered significant attention from both computer scientists and economists in recent years. By allowing agents to interact with the seller over multiple rounds, where agents’ reward functions may change with time and are state-dependent, the framework is able to model a rich class of real-world problems. In these works, the interaction between agents and sellers is often assumed to follow a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We focus on the setting where the reward and transition functions of such an MDP are not known a priori, and we are attempting to recover the optimal mechanism using an a priori collected data set. In the setting where the function approximation is employed to handle large state spaces, with only mild assumptions on the expressiveness of the function class, we are able to design a dynamic mechanism using offline reinforcement learning algorithms. Moreover, learned mechanisms approximately have three key desiderata: efficiency, individual rationality, and truthfulness. Our algorithm is based on the pessimism principle and only requires a mild assumption on the coverage of the offline data set. To the best of our knowledge, our work provides the first offline RL algorithm for dynamic mechanism design without assuming uniform coverage.

paragraphs: Dynamic mechanism design studies repeated interactions between a seller and agents whose rewards may depend on time and state. This paper considers interactions modeled as a Markov decision process when neither rewards nor transition rules are known beforehand. The aim is to learn a mechanism from an already collected dataset, making the problem an offline learning task.

The authors use offline reinforcement learning with function approximation to address large state spaces. Their algorithm follows a pessimism principle and assumes mild conditions on both the expressiveness of the function class and the coverage provided by the dataset. It does not require uniform data coverage, a distinction the authors identify as a first for offline reinforcement learning in dynamic mechanism design, to their knowledge.

The learned mechanisms approximately satisfy efficiency, individual rationality, and truthfulness. These concern desirable collective outcomes, agents’ willingness to participate, and incentives to report honestly. The qualification matters: the result provides approximate properties under the stated learning assumptions. It connects learning from incomplete prior experience to mechanism design while explicitly accounting for the uncertainty associated with offline data.
summary.tldr: A pessimistic offline RL method learns dynamic mechanisms with approximate efficiency, individual rationality, and truthfulness without requiring uniform data coverage.

title: Pessimism meets VCG: Learning Dynamic Mechanism Design via Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In the context of supervised learning, we introduce the concept of e-value. An e-value is a scalar quantity that represents the proximity of the sampling distribution of parameter estimates in a model trained on a subset of features to that of the model trained on all features (i.e. the full model). Under general conditions, a rank ordering of e-values separates models that contain all essential features from those that do not. For a p-dimensional feature space, this requires fitting only the full model and evaluating p+1 models, as opposed to the traditional requirement of fitting and evaluating 2^p models. The above e-values framework is applicable to a wide range of parametric models. We use data depths and a fast resampling-based algorithm to implement a feature selection procedure, providing consistency results. Through experiments across several model settings and synthetic and real datasets, we establish that the e-values can be a promising general alternative to existing model-specific methods of feature selection.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a feature-selection quantity called an e-value. Here, it measures how close the sampling distribution of parameter estimates for a model using fewer features is to the corresponding distribution for the full model. This makes the full model a reference for assessing which subsets retain the features needed to represent the relationship being learned.

Under general conditions, ordering models by their e-values separates those containing all essential features from those missing some. For p features, the proposed framework requires fitting only the full model and evaluating p+1 models. This substantially reduces the work relative to fitting and evaluating all 2^p possible subsets described in the paper’s comparison.

The implementation uses data depths and a fast resampling procedure, and the authors provide consistency results for feature selection. The framework applies to a broad range of parametric models. Experiments spanning several model settings and synthetic and real datasets suggest that it is a promising general alternative to methods designed for individual model classes, with its selection guarantees tied to the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: The proposed e-values compare parameter-estimate distributions to select essential features while requiring only one full-model fit and p+1 model evaluations.

title: Feature selection using e-values

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are found to be vulnerable to adversarial noise. They are typically misled by adversarial samples to make wrong predictions. To alleviate this negative effect, in this paper, we investigate the dependence between outputs of the target model and input adversarial samples from the perspective of information theory, and propose an adversarial defense method. Specifically, we first measure the dependence by estimating the mutual information (MI) between outputs and the natural patterns of inputs (called natural MI) and MI between outputs and the adversarial patterns of inputs (called adversarial MI), respectively. We find that adversarial samples usually have larger adversarial MI and smaller natural MI compared with those w.r.t. natural samples. Motivated by this observation, we propose to enhance the adversarial robustness by maximizing the natural MI and minimizing the adversarial MI during the training process. In this way, the target model is expected to pay more attention to the natural pattern that contains objective semantics. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method could effectively improve the adversarial accuracy against multiple attacks.

In this way, the target model is expected to pay more attention to the natural pattern that contains objective semantics. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method could effectively improve the adversarial accuracy against multiple attacks.

paragraphs: Adversarial inputs can cause neural networks to make incorrect predictions. This paper investigates that vulnerability by asking which parts of an input are statistically associated with the model's output. It separates dependence on natural patterns from dependence on adversarial patterns, using estimated mutual information to quantify each relationship.

The authors observe that adversarial examples usually have greater adversarial mutual information and lower natural mutual information than natural examples. They turn this observation into a training objective: increase dependence between predictions and natural patterns while reducing dependence between predictions and adversarial patterns. The intended effect is to direct the model toward patterns carrying the input's meaningful content.

Empirical evaluations show improved adversarial accuracy against multiple attacks. The finding supports mutual-information estimation as a useful training signal for the evaluated defenses. The distinction between observation and intention matters: the information pattern is reported as typical, and greater attention to natural semantics is the expected mechanism, rather than a universal guarantee about every trained model.
summary.tldr: Training to increase natural-pattern mutual information and reduce adversarial-pattern mutual information improves accuracy against multiple evaluated attacks.

title: Improving Adversarial Robustness via Mutual Information Estimation

abstract: Multimodal machine learning has achieved remarkable progress in a wide range of scenarios. However, the reliability of multimodal learning remains largely unexplored. In this paper, through extensive empirical studies, we identify current multimodal classification methods suffer from unreliable predictive confidence that tend to rely on partial modalities when estimating confidence. Specifically, we find that the confidence estimated by current models could even increase when some modalities are corrupted. To address the issue, we introduce an intuitive principle for multimodal learning, i.e., the confidence should not increase when one modality is removed. Accordingly, we propose a novel regularization technique, i.e., Calibrating Multimodal Learning (CML) regularization, to calibrate the predictive confidence of previous methods. This technique could be flexibly equipped by existing models and improve the performance in terms of confidence calibration, classification accuracy, and model robustness.

paragraphs: Multimodal classifiers combine several kinds of input, but their confidence does not always reflect the reliability of that combined evidence. Through extensive empirical studies, this paper finds that existing methods can base confidence on only some modalities. In some cases, corrupting a modality even makes the model more confident.

The authors propose a guiding principle: removing one modality should not increase predictive confidence. They translate that principle into Calibrating Multimodal Learning, or CML, a regularization technique that can be added to existing models. It targets how confidence responds to the available inputs, addressing a behavior that classification accuracy alone does not fully describe.

The reported findings indicate that CML can improve confidence calibration, classification accuracy, and robustness. These are distinct benefits: a model’s confidence can become more trustworthy while its predictions also improve. The contribution is an adaptable training technique built around an explicit confidence constraint. The principle is proposed as a way to improve multimodal learning, rather than established as a universal law about every possible combination of inputs.
summary.tldr: CML regularization can improve multimodal reliability by discouraging confidence from increasing when an input modality is removed.

title: Calibrating Multimodal Learning

abstract: We present the task of "Social Rearrangement", consisting of cooperative everyday tasks like setting up the dinner table, tidying a house or unpacking groceries in a simulated multi-agent environment. In Social Rearrangement, two robots coordinate to complete a long-horizon task, using onboard sensing and egocentric observations, and no privileged information about the environment. We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC) in this task, where an agent collaborates with a new partner, emulating a scenario where a robot collaborates with a new human partner. Prior ZSC approaches struggle to generalize in our complex and visually rich setting, and on further analysis, we find that they fail to generate diverse coordination behaviors at training time. To counter this, we propose Behavior Diversity Play (BDP), a novel ZSC approach that encourages diversity through a discriminability objective. Our results demonstrate that BDP learns adaptive agents that can tackle visual coordination, and zero-shot generalize to new partners in unseen environments, achieving 35% higher success and 32% higher efficiency compared to baselines.

Each robot relies on onboard sensing and its own viewpoint, without privileged environmental information. The central challenge is coordinating with a new partner without first training together.

The authors find that earlier zero-shot coordination approaches struggle in this visually rich setting. Their analysis identifies insufficient variety in training-time coordination behaviors as a cause. Behavior Diversity Play addresses this through a discriminability objective that encourages distinguishable behaviors, giving training a stronger emphasis on diversity in how agents cooperate.

The resulting agents adapt to new partners in previously unseen environments. In the reported comparisons, BDP achieves 35% higher success and 32% higher efficiency than baselines. The findings connect training-time behavioral diversity with better coordination under unfamiliar partnerships. Although the task is motivated by robots working with new human partners, the reported setting involves cooperation between two simulated robots.
summary.tldr: Encouraging diverse coordination behaviors helps simulated robots cooperate with unfamiliar partners in unseen environments.

title: Adaptive Coordination in Social Embodied Rearrangement

abstract: Recent multimodal models such as DALL-E and CM3 have achieved remarkable progress in text-to-image and image-to-text generation. However, these models store all their knowledge (e.g., the appearance of the Eiffel Tower) in the model parameters, requiring increasingly larger models and training data to capture more knowledge. To integrate knowledge in a more scalable and modular way, we propose a retrieval-augmented multimodal model, which enables a base multimodal model (generator) to refer to relevant text and images fetched by a retriever from external memory (e.g., documents on the web). Specifically, for the retriever, we use a pretrained CLIP, and for the generator, we train a CM3 Transformer on the LAION dataset. Our resulting model, named Retrieval-Augmented CM3 (RA-CM3), is the first multimodal model that can retrieve and generate both text and images. We show that RA-CM3 significantly outperforms baseline multimodal models such as DALL-E and CM3 on both image and caption generation tasks (12 FID and 17 CIDEr improvements on MS-COCO), while requiring much less compute for training ($<$30% of DALL-E). Moreover, we show that RA-CM3 exhibits novel capabilities such as faithful image generation and multimodal in-context learning (e.g., image generation from demonstrations).

title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Modeling

abstract: The ability to properly benchmark model performance in the face of spurious correlations is important to both build better predictors and increase confidence that models are operating as intended. We demonstrate that characterizing (as opposed to simply quantifying) model mistakes across subgroups is pivotal to properly reflect model biases, which are ignored by standard metrics such as worst-group accuracy or accuracy gap. Inspired by the hypothesis testing framework, we introduce SkewSize, a principled and flexible metric that captures bias from mistakes in a model’s predictions. It can be used in multi-class settings or generalised to the open vocabulary setting of generative models. SkewSize is an aggregation of the effect size of the interaction between two categorical variables: the spurious variable representing the bias attribute the model’s prediction. We demonstrate the utility of SkewSize in multiple settings including: standard vision models trained on synthetic data, vision models trained on ImageNet, and large scale vision-and-language models from the BLIP-2 family. In each case, the proposed SkewSize is able to highlight biases not captured by other metrics, while also providing insights on the impact of recently proposed techniques, such as instruction tuning.

paragraphs: A model’s accuracy across groups does not fully describe its biases. Two groups may have similar error rates while the model makes systematically different kinds of mistakes for each. This paper argues that evaluating spurious correlations requires examining the relationship between a bias attribute and the predictions involved in those errors.

The authors introduce SkewSize, a metric inspired by hypothesis testing. It aggregates effect sizes describing the interaction between a categorical bias variable and the model’s predicted category. This shifts attention from the number of mistakes to their structure. The metric supports multiclass prediction and can also be extended to generative models with open vocabularies.

The paper demonstrates SkewSize on vision models trained with synthetic data, ImageNet models, and vision-and-language models from the BLIP-2 family. Across these settings, it reveals biases missed by other metrics and offers insight into the effects of techniques such as instruction tuning. The contribution is a way to characterize error patterns that standard worst-group accuracy or accuracy-gap summaries can leave hidden.
summary.tldr: SkewSize detects model biases by measuring how prediction mistakes relate to bias attributes, revealing patterns that accuracy summaries can miss.

title: Evaluating Model Bias Requires Characterizing its Mistakes

abstract: Deep Multi-view Clustering (DMVC) stands out as a widely adopted technique aiming at enhanced clustering performance by leveraging diverse data sources. However, the critical issue of vulnerability to adversarial attacks is unexplored due to the lack of well-defined attack objectives. To fill this crucial gap, this paper is the first work to investigate the possibility of adversarial attacks on DMVC models. Specifically, we introduce an adversarial attack with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) with the aim to maximally change the complementarity and consistency of multiple views, thus leading to wrong clustering. Building upon this adversarial context, in the realm of defense, we propose a novel Adversarially Robust Deep Multi-View Clustering by leveraging adversarial training. Based on the analysis from an information-theoretic perspective, we design an Attack Mitigator that provides a foundation to guarantee the adversarial robustness of our DMVC models. Experiments conducted on multi-view datasets confirmed that our attack framework effectively reduces the clustering performance of the target model. Furthermore, our proposed adversarially robust method is also demonstrated to be an effective defense against such attacks. This work is a pioneer in exploring adversarial threats and advancing both theoretical understanding and practical strategies for robust multi-view clustering. Code is available at https://github.com/libertyhhn/AR-DMVC.

paragraphs: Deep multi-view clustering groups examples using several sources of information about them. Its usefulness depends on how those views agree and how they contribute complementary information. This paper investigates whether an attacker can exploit those relationships to make the resulting groups wrong, addressing a threat that the authors describe as previously unexplored.

The attack uses a generative adversarial network to alter consistency and complementarity across views as strongly as possible. That objective gives the attacker a concrete way to target clustering without relying on an ordinary supervised prediction objective. The defense then uses adversarial training and an Attack Mitigator developed through information-theoretic analysis to support robustness.

Experiments on multi-view datasets show that the attack reduces the target model's clustering performance and that the proposed defense effectively counters such attacks. The contribution connects a clearly defined attack objective with a corresponding defense: relationships that help combine multiple views can also become attack targets, so robustness must account for how those views interact.
summary.tldr: The paper attacks relationships among data views to disrupt clustering and develops an adversarially trained defense.

title: Adversarially Robust Deep Multi-View Clustering: A Novel Attack and Defense Framework

abstract: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable results for a wide range of tasks. However, deploying these models for inference has been a significant challenge due to their unprecedented resource requirements. This has forced existing deployment frameworks to use multi-GPU inference pipelines, which are often complex and costly, or to use smaller and less performant models. In this work, we demonstrate that the main bottleneck for generative inference with LLMs is memory bandwidth, rather than compute, specifically for single batch inference. While quantization has emerged as a promising solution by representing weights with reduced precision, previous efforts have often resulted in notable performance degradation. To address this, we introduce SqueezeLLM, a post-training quantization framework that not only enables lossless compression to ultra-low precisions of up to 3-bit, but also achieves higher quantization performance under the same memory constraint. Our framework incorporates two novel ideas: (i) sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization, which searches for the optimal bit precision assignment based on second-order information; and (ii) the Dense-and-Sparse decomposition that stores outliers and sensitive weight values in an efficient sparse format. When applied to the LLaMA models, our 3-bit quantization significantly reduces the perplexity gap from the FP16 baseline by up to 2.1x as compared to the state-of-the-art methods with the same memory requirement. Furthermore, when deployed on an A6000 GPU, our quantized models achieve up to 2.3x speedup compared to the baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/SqueezeAILab/SqueezeLLM.

paragraphs: Large language models are expensive to deploy, and this paper identifies memory bandwidth as the main bottleneck for single-batch generative inference. Reducing weight precision can ease that bottleneck, but quantization can degrade model quality. SqueezeLLM is a post-training framework designed to improve the tradeoff between memory use and performance.

The framework combines sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization with a dense-and-sparse decomposition. Second-order information guides precision assignment according to weight sensitivity. Outliers and sensitive values are stored separately in an efficient sparse format. Together, these choices allow the compressed representation to account for weights whose quantization requires particular care.

The authors describe lossless compression down to 3-bit precision and report improved quantization performance at the same memory budget. On LLaMA models, 3-bit SqueezeLLM reduces the perplexity gap from FP16 by up to a factor of 2.1 compared with competing methods using the same memory. Deployment on an A6000 GPU yields up to 2.3 times speedup over the baseline. These reported results connect compression quality with practical inference efficiency.
summary.tldr: SqueezeLLM combines sensitivity-aware quantization with sparse storage of exceptional weights to improve low-bit model quality and inference speed.

title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization

abstract: Continuously learning a variety of audio-video semantics over time is crucial for audio-related reasoning tasks in our ever-evolving world. However, this is a nontrivial problem and poses two critical challenges: sparse spatio-temporal correlation between audio-video pairs and multimodal correlation overwriting that forgets audio-video relations. To tackle this problem, we propose a new continual audio-video pre-training method with two novel ideas: (1) Localized Patch Importance Scoring: we introduce a multimodal encoder to determine the importance score for each patch, emphasizing semantically intertwined audio-video patches. (2) Replay-guided Correlation Assessment: to reduce the corruption of previously learned audiovisual knowledge due to drift, we propose to assess the correlation of the current patches on the past steps to identify the patches exhibiting high correlations with the past steps. Based on the results from the two ideas, we perform probabilistic patch selection for effective continual audio-video pre-training. Experimental validation on multiple benchmarks shows that our method achieves a $3.69%$p of relative performance gain in zero-shot retrieval tasks compared to strong continual learning baselines, while reducing memory consumption by $\sim 45 %$.

paragraphs: Continually learning from audio and video presents two connected difficulties. Meaningful relationships may occur only in limited spatial or temporal regions, and learning new material can overwrite previously acquired audiovisual relationships. STELLA addresses both by deciding which patches deserve attention during continual pretraining.

A multimodal encoder first scores patch importance, emphasizing audio and video patches that are semantically connected. A replay-guided correlation assessment then examines how current patches relate to earlier learning steps. It identifies patches with strong past correlations to help reduce corruption of previously learned knowledge as the model changes. These two assessments guide probabilistic patch selection.

Across multiple benchmarks, STELLA improves zero-shot retrieval compared with strong continual learning baselines while reducing memory consumption by approximately 45%. The results support selecting patches using both present cross-modal relevance and relationships to prior learning. This connects the method's two goals: concentrating training on useful audiovisual correspondences and protecting knowledge that could otherwise be overwritten during continued pretraining.
summary.tldr: STELLA selects informative audiovisual patches using current relevance and past correlations, improving continual retrieval performance while reducing memory use.

title: STELLA: Continual Audio-Video Pre-training with SpatioTemporal Localized Alignment

abstract: Recent research has made significant progress in designing fusion modules for audio-visual speech separation. However, they predominantly focus on multi-modal fusion at a single temporal scale of auditory and visual features without employing selective attention mechanisms, which is in sharp contrast with the brain. To address this, We propose a novel model called intra- and inter-attention network (IIANet), which leverages the attention mechanism for efficient audio-visual feature fusion. IIANet consists of two types of attention blocks: intra-attention (IntraA) and inter-attention (InterA) blocks, where the InterA blocks are distributed at the top, middle and bottom of IIANet. Heavily inspired by the way how human brain selectively focuses on relevant content at various temporal scales, these blocks maintain the ability to learn modality-specific features and enable the extraction of different semantics from audio-visual features. Comprehensive experiments on three standard audio-visual separation benchmarks (LRS2, LRS3, and VoxCeleb2) demonstrate the effectiveness of IIANet, outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable inference time. In particular, the fast version of IIANet (IIANet-fast) has only 7% of CTCNet’s MACs and is 40% faster than CTCNet on CPUs while achieving better separation quality, showing the great potential of attention mechanism for efficient and effective multimodal fusion.

paragraphs: Audio-visual speech separation combines auditory and visual information to separate speech. The paper argues that existing fusion modules often operate at a single temporal scale and lack selective attention. IIANet draws inspiration from how the brain focuses on relevant content across different timescales, using attention to make the interaction between audio and video more selective.

The architecture contains intra-attention and inter-attention blocks. These preserve the ability to learn features specific to each modality while enabling the extraction of different meanings from their combination. Inter-attention blocks appear at the top, middle, and bottom of the network, allowing audio-visual interaction at multiple levels rather than confining it to one fusion point.

Experiments on LRS2, LRS3, and VoxCeleb2 report better separation than previous state-of-the-art methods with comparable inference time. A faster variant, IIANet-fast, uses only 7% of CTCNet’s multiply-accumulate operations and runs 40% faster on CPUs while achieving better separation quality. These results show that the proposed attention design can improve both separation effectiveness and computational efficiency in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: IIANet uses attention within and between audio and visual features at multiple levels to improve speech separation and efficiency.

title: IIANet: An Intra- and Inter-Modality Attention Network for Audio-Visual Speech Separation

abstract: This work tackles the problem of geo-localization with a new paradigm using a large vision-language model (LVLM) augmented with human inference knowledge. A primary challenge here is the scarcity of data for training the LVLM - existing street-view datasets often contain numerous low-quality images lacking visual clues, and lack any reasoning inference. To address the data-quality issue, we devise a CLIP-based network to quantify the degree of street-view images being locatable, leading to the creation of a new dataset comprising highly locatable street views. To enhance reasoning inference, we integrate external knowledge obtained from real geo-localization games, tapping into valuable human inference capabilities. The data are utilized to train GeoReasoner, which undergoes fine-tuning through dedicated reasoning and location-tuning stages. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations illustrate that GeoReasoner outperforms counterpart LVLMs by more than 25% at country-level and 38% at city-level geo-localization tasks, and surpasses StreetCLIP performance while requiring fewer training resources. The data and code are available at https://github.com/lingli1996/GeoReasoner.

paragraphs: GeoReasoner tackles identifying locations from street-view images using a large vision-language model augmented with human inference knowledge. The paper identifies two weaknesses in existing training data: many images contain few useful location clues, and the datasets lack explanations of the reasoning needed to infer a location. Both affect what the model can learn from examples.

To improve image selection, the authors build a CLIP-based network that scores how locatable a street view is and use it to construct a dataset of highly locatable images. They also incorporate external knowledge from real geo-localization games, drawing on human inference. GeoReasoner then undergoes separate reasoning-tuning and location-tuning stages using these data.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations report improvements over counterpart vision-language models of more than 25% for country-level and 38% for city-level geo-localization. GeoReasoner also surpasses StreetCLIP while using fewer training resources. The findings connect stronger localization performance with training that combines informative visual examples and human reasoning knowledge, addressing data quality and inference guidance within the same approach.
summary.tldr: GeoReasoner combines informative street-view images with human geo-localization knowledge to improve country- and city-level location prediction.

title: GeoReasoner: Geo-localization with Reasoning in Street Views using a Large Vision-Language Model

abstract: The emergence of vision-language models, such as CLIP, has spurred a significant research effort towards their application for downstream supervised learning tasks. Although some previous studies have explored the unsupervised fine-tuning of CLIP, they often rely on prior knowledge in the form of class names associated with ground truth labels. This paper explores a realistic unsupervised fine-tuning scenario, considering the presence of out-of-distribution samples from unknown classes within the unlabeled data. In particular, we focus on simultaneously enhancing out-of-distribution detection and the recognition of instances associated with known classes. To tackle this problem, we present a simple, efficient, and effective approach called Universal Entropy Optimization (UEO). UEO leverages sample-level confidence to approximately minimize the conditional entropy of confident instances and maximize the marginal entropy of less confident instances. Apart from optimizing the textual prompt, UEO incorporates optimization of channel-wise affine transformations within the visual branch of CLIP. Extensive experiments across 15 domains and 4 different types of prior knowledge validate the effectiveness of UEO compared to baseline methods. The code is at https://github.com/tim-learn/UEO.
