In particular, we focus on simultaneously enhancing out-of-distribution detection and the recognition of instances associated with known classes. To tackle this problem, we present a simple, efficient, and effective approach called Universal Entropy Optimization (UEO). UEO leverages sample-level confidence to approximately minimize the conditional entropy of confident instances and maximize the marginal entropy of less confident instances. Apart from optimizing the textual prompt, UEO incorporates optimization of channel-wise affine transformations within the visual branch of CLIP. Extensive experiments across 15 domains and 4 different types of prior knowledge validate the effectiveness of UEO compared to baseline methods. The code is at https://github.com/tim-learn/UEO.

paragraphs: Unsupervised adaptation of CLIP becomes more complicated when unlabeled data include classes outside the known set. This paper studies that setting, aiming to improve both recognition of known classes and detection of out-of-distribution samples. The setup extends beyond approaches that rely on class-name knowledge associated with the data’s ground-truth labels.

Universal Entropy Optimization, or UEO, uses each sample’s confidence to guide its treatment. It approximately minimizes conditional entropy for confident instances and maximizes marginal entropy for less confident ones. The distinction matters: the second objective operates on marginal predictions, rather than simply imposing the same confidence objective on every image.

The method adapts both the textual prompt and channel-wise affine transformations in CLIP’s visual branch. Experiments span 15 domains and four types of prior knowledge, supporting its effectiveness relative to baseline methods. The findings show the value of confidence-dependent adaptation when unlabeled data mix known and unknown classes, with both recognition and out-of-distribution detection included in the learning objective.
summary.tldr: UEO adapts CLIP using confidence-dependent entropy objectives to improve known-class recognition and unknown-class detection in unlabeled data.

title: Realistic Unsupervised CLIP Fine-tuning with Universal Entropy Optimization

abstract: Catastrophic overfitting (CO) presents a significant challenge in single-step adversarial training (AT), manifesting as highly distorted deep neural networks (DNNs) that are vulnerable to multi-step adversarial attacks. However, the underlying factors that lead to the distortion of decision boundaries remain unclear. In this work, we delve into the specific changes within different DNN layers and discover that during CO, the former layers are more susceptible, experiencing earlier and greater distortion, while the latter layers show relative insensitivity. Our analysis further reveals that this increased sensitivity in former layers stems from the formation of $\textit{pseudo-robust shortcuts}$, which alone can impeccably defend against single-step adversarial attacks but bypass genuine-robust learning, resulting in distorted decision boundaries. Eliminating these shortcuts can partially restore robustness in DNNs from the CO state, thereby verifying that dependence on them triggers the occurrence of CO. This understanding motivates us to implement adaptive weight perturbations across different layers to hinder the generation of $\textit{pseudo-robust shortcuts}$, consequently mitigating CO. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method, $\textbf{L}$ayer-$\textbf{A}$ware Adversarial Weight $\textbf{P}$erturbation (LAP), can effectively prevent CO and further enhance robustness.

paragraphs: Single-step adversarial training can suffer catastrophic overfitting: a network becomes vulnerable to multi-step attacks despite its training procedure. This paper examines how that failure develops across network layers. The authors find that earlier layers experience distortion sooner and more strongly, while later layers are relatively less sensitive.

Their analysis attributes the earlier layers’ sensitivity to pseudo-robust shortcuts. These shortcuts can defend perfectly against single-step attacks on their own while bypassing genuinely robust learning, producing distorted decision boundaries. This intervention supports the authors’ conclusion that dependence on the shortcuts triggers the failure.

The resulting method, Layer-Aware Adversarial Weight Perturbation, or LAP, applies adaptive weight perturbations across layers to hinder shortcut formation. Extensive experiments show that it can prevent catastrophic overfitting and improve robustness. The contribution connects a layer-specific account of the failure mechanism with a training intervention designed around that account.
summary.tldr: The paper links catastrophic overfitting to early-layer pseudo-robust shortcuts and introduces layer-aware perturbations that mitigate their formation.

title: Layer-Aware Analysis of Catastrophic Overfitting: Revealing the Pseudo-Robust Shortcut Dependency

abstract: Despite the widespread adoption of prompting, prompt tuning and prefix-tuning of transformer models, our theoretical understanding of these fine-tuning methods remains limited. A key question is whether one can arbitrarily modify the behavior of a pretrained model by prompting or prefix-tuning it. Formally, whether prompting and prefix-tuning a pretrained model can universally approximate sequence-to-sequence functions. This paper answers in the affirmative and demonstrates that much smaller pretrained models than previously thought can be universal approximators when prefixed. In fact, prefix-tuning a single attention head is sufficient to approximate any continuous function making the attention mechanism uniquely suited for universal approximation. Moreover, any sequence-to-sequence function can be approximated by prefixing a transformer with depth linear in the sequence length. Beyond these density-type results, we also offer Jackson-type bounds on the length of the prefix needed to approximate a function to a desired precision.

paragraphs: Prompting and prefix tuning change how a pretrained transformer behaves through its supplied context. This paper asks a theoretical expressiveness question: can such changes make a pretrained model approximate arbitrary sequence-to-sequence functions? The authors establish affirmative universal-approximation results and show that smaller models than previously thought can have this capacity.

One result shows that prefix tuning a single attention head is sufficient to approximate any continuous function. Another shows that prefixing a transformer whose depth grows linearly with sequence length can approximate any sequence-to-sequence function. These are sufficiency results about model capacity under the paper's constructions, rather than claims that every pretrained transformer automatically has these properties.

The analysis also goes beyond establishing that an approximation exists. It gives Jackson-type bounds relating the necessary prefix length to a desired approximation precision. This adds a quantitative resource question to the expressiveness result: how long a prefix is needed to reach a given accuracy. Together, the results clarify the theoretical power of prefix-based adaptation.
summary.tldr: The paper proves universal-approximation results for prefix-tuned attention and transformers, including bounds on prefix length for a desired precision.

title: Prompting a Pretrained Transformer Can Be a Universal Approximator

abstract: This paper introduces a finite smoothing algorithm (FSA), a novel approach to tackle computational challenges in applying support vector machines (SVM) and quantile regression to high-dimensional data. The critical issue with these methods is the non-smooth nature of their loss functions, which traditionally limits the use of highly efficient coordinate descent techniques in high-dimensional settings. FSA innovatively addresses this issue by transforming these loss functions into their smooth counterparts, thereby facilitating more efficient computation. A distinctive feature of FSA is its theoretical foundation: FSA can yield exact solutions, not just approximations, despite the smoothing approach. Our simulation and benchmark tests demonstrate that FSA significantly outpaces its competitors in speed, often by orders of magnitude, while improving or at least maintaining precision. We have implemented FSA in two open-source R packages: hdsvm for high-dimensional SVM and hdqr for high-dimensional quantile regression.

paragraphs: Support vector machines and quantile regression become computationally challenging with high-dimensional data partly because their loss functions are not smooth. This lack of smoothness limits the use of efficient coordinate-descent techniques. The paper introduces the finite smoothing algorithm, or FSA, to make those optimization problems easier to compute.

FSA replaces the non-smooth losses with smooth counterparts so that efficient computation becomes possible. The key theoretical point is that smoothing does not necessarily restrict the method to an approximate answer: the authors show that FSA can yield exact solutions. This matters because improving the convenience of optimization would be less useful if it necessarily changed the solution being sought.

In simulations and benchmark tests, FSA runs substantially faster than competing methods, often by orders of magnitude, while maintaining or improving precision. The authors implement the approach in two open-source R packages, hdsvm and hdqr. Together, the theory and evaluations support smoothing as a practical route to faster high-dimensional optimization without an unavoidable loss of solution accuracy.
summary.tldr: FSA smooths difficult loss functions to accelerate high-dimensional SVM and quantile-regression optimization while retaining the ability to obtain exact solutions.

title: Finite Smoothing Algorithm for High-Dimensional Support Vector Machines and Quantile Regression

abstract: Conformal prediction is a distribution-free method that wraps a given machine learning model and returns a set of plausible labels that contain the true label with a prescribed coverage rate. In practice, the empirical coverage achieved highly relies on fully observed label information from data both in the training phase for model fitting and the calibration phase for quantile estimation. This dependency poses a challenge in the context of online learning with bandit feedback, where a learner only has access to the correctness of actions (i.e., pulled an arm) but not the full information of the true label. In particular, when the pulled arm is incorrect, the learner only knows that the pulled one is not the true class label, but does not know which label is true. Additionally, bandit feedback further results in a smaller labeled dataset for calibration, limited to instances with correct actions, thereby affecting the accuracy of quantile estimation. To address these limitations, we propose Bandit Class-specific Conformal Prediction (BCCP), offering coverage guarantees on a class-specific granularity. Using an unbiased estimation of an estimand involving the true label, BCCP trains the model and makes set-valued inferences through stochastic gradient descent. Our approach overcomes the challenges of sparsely labeled data in each iteration and generalizes the reliability and applicability of conformal prediction to online decision-making environments.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction returns a set of plausible labels with a prescribed coverage rate. Its practical use usually depends on observing true labels for model training and calibration. This paper addresses online settings with bandit feedback, where the learner only discovers whether its chosen label was correct. An incorrect choice rules out that label without revealing the correct one.

This feedback creates two connected difficulties: incomplete information for learning and sparse labeled data for estimating calibration quantiles. Bandit Class-specific Conformal Prediction, or BCCP, tackles both through an unbiased estimate of a quantity involving the true label. It uses that estimate within stochastic gradient descent to train the model and produce prediction sets.

BCCP provides coverage guarantees at the level of individual classes, making the reliability target more specific than a single overall coverage figure. The contribution extends set-valued prediction to an online environment where complete labels are unavailable at each step. Its significance lies in connecting limited correctness feedback to learning and calibration within one approach.
summary.tldr: BCCP enables online prediction sets with class-specific coverage guarantees when feedback reveals only whether the chosen label was correct.

title: Efficient Online Set-valued Classification with Bandit Feedback

abstract: Effectively extracting motions from video is a critical and long-standing problem for action recognition. This problem is very challenging because motions (i) do not have an explicit form, (ii) have various concepts such as displacement, velocity, and acceleration, and (iii) often contain noise caused by unstable pixels. Addressing these challenges, we propose the Taylor video, a new video format that highlights the dominate motions (e.g., a waving hand) in each of its frames named the Taylor frame. Taylor video is named after Taylor series, which approximates a function at a given point using important terms. In the scenario of videos, we define an implicit motion-extraction function which aims to extract motions from video temporal block. In this block, using the frames, the difference frames, and higher-order difference frames, we perform Taylor expansion to approximate this function at the starting frame. We show the summation of the higher-order terms in the Taylor series gives us dominant motion patterns, where static objects, small and unstable motions are removed. Experimentally we show that Taylor videos are effective inputs to popular architectures including 2D CNNs, 3D CNNs, and transformers. When used individually, Taylor videos yield competitive action recognition accuracy compared to RGB videos and optical flow. When fused with RGB or optical flow videos, further accuracy improvement is achieved. Additionally, we apply Taylor video computation to human skeleton sequences, resulting in Taylor skeleton sequences that outperform the use of original skeletons for skeleton-based action recognition.

paragraphs: Recognizing actions requires extracting motion from video, but motion has several aspects and can be obscured by unstable pixels. This paper introduces Taylor videos, a representation whose frames emphasize dominant movements, such as a waving hand. The goal is to make the motion information useful for recognition more explicit in the input.

The construction starts with an implicit motion-extraction function over a short temporal block. Frames, frame differences, and higher-order differences are used in a Taylor expansion around the starting frame. The findings support the representation across multiple recognition architectures and input types.
summary.tldr: Taylor videos use higher-order temporal differences to highlight dominant motion and improve action recognition when combined with existing video representations.

title: Taylor Videos for Action Recognition

abstract: Detecting weaknesses in cryptographic algorithms is of utmost importance for designing secure information systems. The state-of-the-art soft analytical side-channel attack (SASCA) uses physical leakage information to make probabilistic predictions about intermediate computations and combines these "guesses" with the known algorithmic logic to compute the posterior distribution over the key. This attack is commonly performed via loopy belief propagation, which, however, lacks guarantees in terms of convergence and inference quality. In this paper, we develop a fast and exact inference method for SASCA, denoted as ExSASCA, by leveraging knowledge compilation and tractable probabilistic circuits. When attacking the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), the most widely used encryption algorithm to date, ExSASCA outperforms SASCA by more than 31% top-1 success rate absolute. By leveraging sparse belief messages, this performance is achieved with little more computational cost than SASCA, and about 3 orders of magnitude less than exact inference via exhaustive enumeration. Even with dense belief messages, ExSASCA still uses 6 times less computations than exhaustive inference.

paragraphs: Soft analytical side-channel attacks combine physical leakage with knowledge of a cryptographic algorithm. Leakage supplies uncertain predictions about intermediate computations, and the algorithm’s logic helps combine them into probabilities over the secret key. A common inference method, loopy belief propagation, lacks guarantees about convergence and the quality of its resulting inference.

ExSASCA replaces that inference procedure with knowledge compilation and tractable probabilistic circuits. The goal is to compute the relevant probabilities exactly while keeping the computation practical. Exactness here concerns the inference over the probabilistic information supplied to the attack; the physical leakage still provides uncertain evidence about intermediate values.

In the reported AES evaluation, ExSASCA improves top-1 success rate by more than 31 percentage points over SASCA. With sparse belief messages, its computational cost is only slightly higher than SASCA’s and roughly three orders of magnitude below exhaustive exact inference. Even with dense messages, it uses six times fewer computations than exhaustive inference. The results show substantial gains in attack success without requiring exhaustive enumeration.
summary.tldr: ExSASCA makes side-channel inference exact with probabilistic circuits, improving reported AES attack success at far less cost than exhaustive inference.

title: Exact Soft Analytical Side-Channel Attacks using Tractable Circuits

abstract: Medical Visual Question Answering (Med-VQA) interprets complex medical imagery using user instructions for precise diagnostics, yet faces challenges due to diverse, inadequately annotated images. In this paper, we introduce the Universal Instruction-Vision Navigator (Uni-Med) framework for extracting instruction-to-answer relationships, facilitating the understanding of visual evidence behind responses. Specifically, we design the Instruct-to-Answer Clues Interpreter (IAI) to generate visual explanations based on the answers and mark the core part of instructions with "real intent" labels. The IAI-Med VQA dataset, produced using IAI, is now publicly available to advance Med-VQA research. Additionally, our Token-Level Cut-Mix module dynamically aligns visual explanations with image patches, ensuring answers are traceable and learnable. We also implement intention-guided attention to minimize non-core instruction interference, sharpening focus on ’real intent’. Extensive experiments on SLAKE datasets show Uni-Med’s superior accuracies (87.52% closed, 86.12% overall), outperforming MedVInT-PMC-VQA by 1.22% and 0.92%. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/zhongzee/Uni-Med-master.

paragraphs: Medical visual question answering must connect a user’s instruction to relevant evidence in a medical image. Diverse imagery and inadequate annotations make this difficult. Uni-Med addresses the connection between instructions, visual evidence, and answers, with the aim of making the basis for a response easier to trace.

summary.tldr: Uni-Med connects instruction intent with image evidence to improve medical visual question answering and make answers more traceable.

title: Detecting Any instruction-to-answer interaction relationship:Universal Instruction-to-Answer Navigator for Med-VQA

abstract: Despite their dominance in modern DL and, especially, NLP domains, transformer architectures exhibit sub-optimal performance on long-range tasks compared to recent layers that are specifically designed for this purpose. In this work, drawing inspiration from key attributes of longrange layers, such as state-space layers, linear RNN layers, and global convolution layers, we demonstrate that minimal modifications to the transformer architecture can significantly enhance performance on the Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark, thus narrowing the gap with these specialized layers. We identify that two key principles for long-range tasks are (i) incorporating an inductive bias towards smoothness, and (ii) locality. As we show, integrating these ideas into the attention mechanism improves results with a negligible amount of additional computation and without any additional trainable parameters. Our theory and experiments also shed light on the reasons for the inferior performance of transformers on long-range tasks and identify critical properties that are essential for successfully capturing long-range dependencies.

paragraphs: Transformers can underperform specialized architectures on tasks requiring long-range dependencies. This paper investigates what attention can learn from long-range layers, including state-space models, linear recurrent layers, and global convolutions. Its central question is whether small architectural changes can recover some of their advantages without introducing a substantially larger or more expensive model.

The authors identify smoothness and locality as two key principles for these tasks. They incorporate biases toward both into the attention mechanism. These modifications add no trainable parameters and require only negligible additional computation, making the changes a way to alter how the architecture approaches the task without increasing its learned parameter count.

On the Long Range Arena benchmark, the modified transformers improve substantially and narrow the gap with specialized long-range layers. Theory and experiments also examine why conventional transformers perform less well in this setting. The findings support the importance of architectural biases for capturing long-range relationships: useful changes can come from how attention is organized, even when the number of trainable parameters stays the same.
summary.tldr: Adding smoothness and locality biases to attention improves long-range benchmark performance without adding trainable parameters.

title: Viewing Transformers Through the Lens of Long Convolutions Layers

abstract: Machine unlearning methods aim to remove sensitive or unwanted content from trained models, but typically demand extensive model updates at significant computational cost while potentially degrading model performance on both related and unrelated tasks. We propose Single Layer Unlearning Gradient (SLUG) as an efficient method to unlearn targeted information by updating a single critical layer using a one-time gradient computation. SLUG uses layer importance and gradient alignment metrics to identify the optimal layer for targeted information removal while preserving the model utility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SLUG for CLIP, Stable Diffusion, and vision-language models (VLMs) in removing concrete (e.g., identities and objects) and abstract concepts (e.g., artistic styles). On the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, SLUG achieves comparable unlearning performance to existing methods while requiring significantly less computational resources. Our proposed approach offers a practical solution for targeted unlearning that is computationally efficient and precise. Our code is available at https://github.com/CSIPlab/SLUG

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove unwanted information from an already trained model. Broad model updates can be computationally expensive and can damage performance on both related and unrelated tasks. This paper investigates whether targeted removal can be achieved through a much more localized change, reducing the amount of model updating required.

Single Layer Unlearning Gradient, or SLUG, updates one critical layer using a one-time gradient computation. It selects the layer through measures of layer importance and gradient alignment, with the aim of removing the target information while preserving model utility. Layer selection is therefore central to the method’s combination of efficiency and targeted intervention.

The authors demonstrate SLUG on CLIP, Stable Diffusion, and vision-language models, covering concrete concepts such as identities and objects as well as abstract concepts such as artistic styles. On UnlearnCanvas, it achieves unlearning performance comparable to existing methods with substantially fewer computational resources. These findings support selective single-layer updates as a practical approach to the evaluated unlearning tasks.
summary.tldr: SLUG targets unwanted concepts through a single-layer update, matching reported unlearning performance with substantially less computation.

title: Targeted Unlearning with Single Layer Unlearning Gradient

abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) have revolutionized the field of machine learning, demonstrating exceptional performance across a wide range of tasks. However, their robustness remains vulnerable to the spurious-correlation problem. Existing works often involve fine-tuning the model with labeled data or relying on large language models (LLMs) to generate more complex prompts. Although effective to some extent, these methods introduce new challenges, including additional computational costs and dependence on the quality of prompts without fully utilizing the vision modality. To address these limitations, we propose a novel method named ERICT to Enhance model Robustness by Identifying Concept Tokens. ERICT mitigates spurious correlation directly in the inference stage and comprises two key steps: (1) Identify concept tokens capturing invariant features through auxiliary prompts to generate a token-level mask. (2) Apply the mask to the attention weights of the CLS token in the vision encoder to help the model focus on the relevant image region. Extensive experiments show that ERICT significantly improves the overall performance including that of the worst group, and achieves new state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can rely on spurious correlations, associating a prediction with image features that are incidental to the intended concept. Existing approaches often use labeled fine-tuning or increasingly elaborate prompts generated by language models. ERICT addresses the problem during inference by using concept information to guide the model’s visual attention.

The method first uses auxiliary prompts to identify concept tokens that capture invariant features and builds a token-level mask. It then applies this mask to attention weights associated with the vision encoder’s CLS token. This directs the model toward image regions relevant to the concept, putting the visual representation at the center of the robustness intervention.

The experiments report significant gains in overall performance and in performance for the worst-performing group, alongside new state-of-the-art results. The group-level finding matters because an aggregate improvement alone can leave poorly served groups behind. ERICT’s contribution is an inference-stage mechanism that connects identifying relevant concepts with changing where the vision encoder attends.
summary.tldr: ERICT uses concept-based attention masks during inference to reduce spurious correlations and improve overall and worst-group vision-language performance.

title: ERICT: Enhancing Robustness by Identifying Concept Tokens in Zero-Shot Vision Language Models

abstract: Emotion recognition systems face significant challenges in real-world applications, where novel emotion categories continually emerge and multiple emotions often co-occur. This paper introduces multi-label fine-grained class incremental emotion decoding, which aims to develop models capable of incrementally learning new emotion categories while maintaining the ability to recognize multiple concurrent emotions. We propose an Augmented Emotional Semantics Learning (AESL) framework to address two critical challenges: past- and future-missing partial label problems. AESL incorporates an augmented Emotional Relation Graph (ERG) for reliable soft label generation and affective dimension-based knowledge distillation for future-aware feature learning. We evaluate our approach on three datasets spanning brain activity and multimedia domains, demonstrating its effectiveness in decoding up to 28 fine-grained emotion categories. Results show that AESL significantly outperforms existing methods while effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChangdeDu/EmoGrowth.

paragraphs: An emotion recognition system may need to learn new emotion categories over time while still recognizing several emotions in the same example. These requirements interact: extending the label set should not erase recognition of earlier categories or force a single emotion choice. The paper introduces a learning task that explicitly combines fine-grained emotions, multiple labels, and incremental category growth.

Its Augmented Emotional Semantics Learning framework addresses partial labels involving both past and future categories. An augmented Emotional Relation Graph supplies soft labels, using relationships among emotions to support learning when labels are incomplete. A second component transfers knowledge through affective dimensions to develop features with future categories in mind. Together, these mechanisms address the changing label space as well as knowledge retention.

The authors evaluate the framework on three datasets covering brain activity and multimedia, with as many as 28 emotion categories. They report substantial improvements over existing methods and reduced catastrophic forgetting. The findings support using emotional relationships and knowledge transfer to sustain recognition as the system’s emotion vocabulary expands.
summary.tldr: AESL uses emotional relationships and knowledge distillation to learn new emotion categories while retaining recognition of multiple existing emotions.

title: EmoGrowth: Incremental Multi-label Emotion Decoding with Augmented Emotional Relation Graph

abstract: The sustainable performance improvements of integrated circuits (ICs) drive the continuous advancement of nearly all transformative technologies. Since its invention, IC performance enhancements have been dominated by scaling the semiconductor technology. Yet, as Moore’s law tapers off, a crucial question arises: How can we sustain IC performance in the post-Moore era? Creating new circuit topologies has emerged as a promising pathway to address this fundamental need. This work proposes AnalogGenie-Lite, a decoder-only transformer that discovers novel analog IC topologies with significantly enhanced scalability and precision via lightweight graph modeling. AnalogGenie-Lite makes several unique contributions, including concise device-pin representations (i.e., advancing the best prior art from $O\left(n^2\right)$ to $O\left(n\right)$), frequent sub-graph mining, and optimal sequence modeling. Compared to state-of-the-art circuit topology discovery methods, it achieves $5.15\times$ to $71.11\times$ gains in scalability and 23.5% to 33.6% improvements in validity. Case studies on other domains’ graphs are also provided to show the broader applicability of the proposed graph modeling approach. Source code: https://github.com/xz-group/AnalogGenie-Lite.

paragraphs: AnalogGenie-Lite addresses the search for new analog integrated-circuit topologies: the patterns of connections that define a circuit. The motivation is that improvements from shrinking semiconductor technology are slowing, making new circuit structures an increasingly important route to better performance. The paper focuses on making automated topology discovery more scalable and more likely to produce valid results.

The method uses a decoder-only transformer with a lightweight graph representation. Its contributions include a concise representation of device pins, mining frequently occurring subgraphs, and sequence modeling. The device-pin representation changes the stated complexity from quadratic to linear. This representation change is central to the approach because it reduces how quickly the description grows as the represented structure becomes larger.

Compared with existing leading topology-discovery methods, the authors report scalability gains of 5.15 to 71.11 times and validity improvements of 23.5% to 33.6%. These findings support the value of changing how circuit graphs are represented for generation. Additional case studies on graphs from other domains suggest broader applicability of the graph-modeling approach.
summary.tldr: AnalogGenie-Lite uses compact graph modeling to improve the scalability and validity of transformer-based analog circuit topology discovery.

title: AnalogGenie-Lite: Enhancing Scalability and Precision in Circuit Topology Discovery through Lightweight Graph Modeling

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on domain-specific data is the dominant approach for adapting foundation models to specialized tasks. However, it has been observed that SFT models tend to forget knowledge acquired during pretraining. In vision models, ensembling a pretrained model with its fine-tuned counterpart has been shown to mitigate this issue. In this work, we demonstrate that the same holds for language models, and, more strikingly, we observe an overadaptation phenomenon: the ensemble model not only retains general knowledge from the foundation model but also outperforms the fine-tuned model even on the fine-tuning domain itself. Despite the empirical success of ensembling, a theoretical understanding of its benefits remains underexplored. We develop a formal theoretical analysis of the overadaptation phenomenon. Ensembling mitigates this by balancing two primary sources of error: bias, caused by insufficient fine-tuning, and variance, introduced by overfitting to fine-tuning data. While regularization techniques aim to address this trade-off, we show that ensembling provides a more effective solution. We analyze this phenomenon in over-parameterized linear settings and demonstrate that interpolating between pretrained and fine-tuned weights significantly improves performance. These findings offer theoretical justification for the observed advantages of model ensembling, supported by empirical experiments consistent with our analysis.

The findings provide theoretical support for the observed ensemble benefits while locating the formal analysis in a specific model setting, connecting the practical phenomenon to an explicit bias-variance explanation.
summary.tldr: Combining pretrained and fine-tuned models can counter overadaptation and improve performance even on the fine-tuning domain.

title: Understanding Overadaptation in Supervised Fine-Tuning: The Role of Ensemble Methods

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) on graph-structured data has attracted considerable attention recently. Masked graph autoencoder, as one promising generative graph SSL approach that aims to recover masked parts of the input graph data, has shown great success in various downstream graph tasks. However, existing masked graph autoencoders fail to consider the degree of difficulty of recovering the masked edges that often have different impacts on the model performance, resulting in suboptimal node representations. To tackle this challenge, in this paper, we propose a novel curriculum based self-supervised masked graph autoencoder that is able to capture and leverage the underlying degree of difficulty of data dependencies hidden in edges, and design better mask-reconstruction pretext tasks for learning informative node representations. Specifically, we first design a difficulty measurer to identify the underlying structural degree of difficulty of edges during the masking step. Then, we adopt a self-paced scheduler to determine the order of masking edges, which encourages the graph encoder to learn from easy to difficult parts. Finally, the masked edges are gradually incorporated into the reconstruction pretext task, leading to high-quality node representations. Experiments on several real-world node classification and link prediction datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over state-of-the-art graph self-supervised learning baselines. This work is the first study of curriculum strategy for masked graph autoencoders, to the best of our knowledge.

paragraphs: Masked graph autoencoders learn representations by hiding parts of a graph and reconstructing them. The paper argues that edges differ in how difficult they are to recover, and that treating masking choices without regard to this difficulty can weaken the learned node representations. It introduces a curriculum that organizes reconstruction tasks according to the graph's underlying structural difficulty.

First, a difficulty measurer assesses edges during masking. A self-paced scheduler then determines their masking order so the encoder learns from easier parts before progressing to harder ones. Masked edges are gradually incorporated into the reconstruction task. This makes the progression of self-supervised training depend on the dependencies represented by graph edges.

Experiments on real-world node-classification and link-prediction datasets report improvements over leading graph self-supervised learning baselines. The findings support task ordering as a useful design choice for masked graph learning: the training signal depends on which edges are hidden and when they enter reconstruction. The resulting curriculum is intended to produce more informative node representations for downstream graph tasks.
summary.tldr: A structure-aware curriculum improves graph representations by gradually introducing edge-reconstruction tasks from easy to difficult.

title: Self-supervised Masked Graph Autoencoder via Structure-aware Curriculum

abstract: We propose a gradient-free deep reinforcement learning algorithm to solve high-dimensional, finite-horizon stochastic control problems. Although the recently developed deep reinforcement learning framework has achieved great success in solving these problems, direct estimation of policy gradients from Monte Carlo sampling often suffers from high variance. To address this, we introduce the Momentum Consensus-Based Optimization (M-CBO) and Adaptive Momentum Consensus-Based Optimization (Adam-CBO) frameworks. These methods optimize policies using Monte Carlo estimates of the value function, rather than its gradients. Adjustable Gaussian noise supports efficient exploration, helping the algorithm converge to optimal policies in complex, nonconvex environments. Numerical results confirm the accuracy and scalability of our approach across various problem dimensions and show the potential for extension to mean-field control problems. Theoretically, we prove that M-CBO can converge to the optimal policy under some assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper considers stochastic control problems with many dimensions and a finite decision horizon. A policy must choose actions despite randomness in how the system evolves. Deep reinforcement learning can address these problems, but estimating policy gradients from Monte Carlo samples often produces high variance, making the direction of improvement difficult to determine reliably.

The authors introduce Momentum Consensus-Based Optimization and Adaptive Momentum Consensus-Based Optimization. These frameworks optimize policies using Monte Carlo estimates of the value function rather than estimates of its gradients. They also include adjustable Gaussian noise to support exploration in complex, nonconvex settings. This changes the information used to guide optimization while retaining sampled evaluations of policy quality.

Numerical experiments support the approach’s accuracy and scalability across different problem dimensions. They also suggest potential extensions to mean-field control problems. On the theoretical side, the paper proves that the momentum framework can converge to an optimal policy under assumptions. The convergence claim is therefore conditional, while the broader scalability evidence comes from the reported numerical evaluations.
summary.tldr: Two gradient-free control algorithms optimize sampled policy values, with numerical scalability evidence and a conditional convergence result for the momentum method.

title: Consensus Based Stochastic Optimal Control

abstract: Tailoring treatments to individual needs is a central goal in fields such as medicine. A key step toward this goal is estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (HTE)—the way treatments impact different subgroups. While crucial, HTE estimation is challenging with survival data, where time until an event (e.g., death) is key. Existing methods often assume complete observation, an assumption violated in survival data due to right-censoring, leading to bias and inefficiency. Cui et al. (2023) proposed a doubly-robust method for HTE estimation in survival data under no hidden confounders, combining a causal survival forest with an augmented inverse-censoring weighting estimator. However, we find it struggles under heavy censoring, which is common in rare-outcome problems such as Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Moreover, most current methods cannot handle instrumental variables, which are a crucial tool in the causal inference arsenal. We introduce Multiple Imputation for Survival Treatment Response (MISTR), a novel, general, and non-parametric method for estimating HTE in survival data. MISTR uses recursively imputed survival trees to handle censoring without directly modeling the censoring mechanism. Through extensive simulations and analysis of two real-world datasets—the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Protocol 175 and the Illinois unemployment dataset we show that MISTR outperforms prior methods under heavy censoring in the no-hidden-confounders setting, and extends to the instrumental variable setting. To our knowledge, MISTR is the first non-parametric approach for HTE estimation with unobserved confounders via instrumental variables.

paragraphs: Estimating how treatment effects differ between people becomes difficult when the outcome is time until an event. Right-censoring means that some event times remain unobserved, and treating these records as fully observed can cause bias and inefficiency. The paper focuses particularly on heavy censoring, where an existing doubly-robust survival method struggles.

The proposed method, Multiple Imputation for Survival Treatment Response, or MISTR, uses recursively imputed survival trees. It handles censoring without directly modeling the censoring mechanism and provides a general, non-parametric approach to heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation. The method also extends to instrumental variables, addressing a setting that many existing approaches cannot handle.

Simulations and analyses of the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Protocol 175 and Illinois unemployment datasets support the approach. Under heavy censoring and no hidden confounders, MISTR outperforms prior methods. Its instrumental-variable extension also covers unobserved confounding. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first non-parametric method for this survival treatment-effect problem using instrumental variables.
summary.tldr: MISTR uses recursively imputed survival trees to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects under censoring and extends to instrumental-variable settings.

title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effect in Time-to-Event Outcomes: Harnessing Censored Data with Recursively Imputed Trees

abstract: Millions of abandoned oil and gas wells are scattered across the world, leaching methane into the atmosphere and toxic compounds into the groundwater. Many of these locations are unknown, preventing the wells from being plugged and their polluting effects averted. Remote sensing is a relatively unexplored tool for pinpointing abandoned wells at scale. We introduce the first large-scale Benchmark dataset for this problem, leveraging high-resolution multi-spectral satellite imagery from Planet Labs. Our curated Dataset comprises over 213,000 wells (abandoned, suspended, and active) from Alberta, a region with especially high well density, sourced from the Alberta Energy Regulator and verified by domain experts. We evaluate baseline algorithms for well detection and segmentation, showing the promise of computer vision approaches but also significant room for improvement.

paragraphs: Abandoned oil and gas wells can release methane and contaminate groundwater, yet many locations are unknown. That makes finding wells a necessary step toward plugging them and preventing further pollution. This paper introduces a large-scale benchmark for investigating whether satellite imagery can help locate wells, an application where remote sensing remains relatively unexplored.

The Alberta Wells Dataset combines high-resolution, multispectral imagery from Planet Labs with records for more than 213,000 wells. The records come from the Alberta Energy Regulator and were verified by domain experts. They cover abandoned, suspended, and active wells in Alberta, a region with particularly dense well infrastructure, so the collection extends beyond abandoned wells alone.

The authors evaluate baseline methods for detecting wells and segmenting their image regions. Their results indicate that computer vision is promising for this task while leaving substantial room for improvement. The dataset's central contribution is to make well localization a concrete benchmark problem, supporting systematic evaluation of methods intended to help identify this environmental infrastructure.
summary.tldr: A satellite-imagery benchmark covering over 213,000 Alberta wells supports research on automated well detection and segmentation.

title: Alberta Wells Dataset: Pinpointing Oil and Gas Wells from Satellite Imagery

abstract: The concept of sharpness has been successfully applied to traditional architectures like MLPs and CNNs to predict their generalization. For transformers, however, recent work reported weak correlation between flatness and generalization. We argue that existing sharpness measures fail for transformers, because they have much richer symmetries in their attention mechanism that induce directions in parameter space along which the network or its loss remain identical. We posit that sharpness must account fully for these symmetries, and thus we redefine it on a quotient manifold that results from quotienting out the transformer symmetries, thereby removing their ambiguities. Leveraging tools from Riemannian geometry, we propose a fully general notion of sharpness, in terms of a geodesic ball on the symmetry-corrected quotient manifold. In practice, we need to resort to approximating the geodesics. Doing so up to first order yields existing adaptive sharpness measures, and we demonstrate that including higher-order terms is crucial to recover correlation with generalization. We present results on diagonal networks with synthetic data, and show that our geodesic sharpness reveals strong correlation for real-world transformers on both text and image classification tasks.

paragraphs: Sharpness measures how loss changes around a model's parameters and has helped predict generalization in some neural architectures. For transformers, earlier work found weak correlations. This paper argues that attention mechanisms introduce rich symmetries: parameters can change along certain directions while the network or its loss remains identical. Such directions make ordinary parameter-space measurements ambiguous.

The authors define sharpness on a quotient manifold that removes those symmetry-related ambiguities. Using Riemannian geometry, they measure neighborhoods through geodesic balls in that corrected space. This reframes the question around meaningful changes after accounting for equivalent parameter configurations. Computing the required geodesics is difficult in practice, so the method relies on approximations.

First-order approximations recover existing adaptive sharpness measures, while the authors show that higher-order terms are crucial for recovering correlations with generalization. Experiments include diagonal networks on synthetic data and transformers on text and image classification. The reported strong correlations support the idea that transformer sharpness can be informative when its geometry accounts sufficiently for model symmetries.
summary.tldr: Accounting for transformer symmetries with geometric sharpness measures restores strong empirical correlations with generalization.

title: Hide & Seek: Transformer Symmetries Obscure Sharpness & Riemannian Geometry Finds It

abstract: In order to streamline the fine-tuning of foundation models, Low-Rank Adapters (LoRAs) have been substantially adopted across various fields, including instruction tuning and domain adaptation. The underlying concept of LoRA involves decomposing a full-rank matrix into the product of two lower-rank matrices, which reduces storage consumption and accelerates the training process. Furthermore, to address the limited expressive capacity of LoRA, the Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) has been introduced for incorporating multiple LoRA adapters. The integration of LoRA experts leads to a visible improvement across several downstream scenes. However, the mixture of LoRAs (MoE-LoRA) still exhibits its low robustness during tuning and inferring. Inspired by the Riemannian Preconditioners which train LoRA as a sub-space projector, we propose a new training strategy for MoE-LoRA, to stabilize and boost its feature learning by gate-rescaled multi-space projections. We provide both a theoretical solution as well as an alternative engineering strategy. Examinations on SGD and AdamW optimizers demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology. Source code is available at https://github.com/THUDM/MoELoRA_Riemannian.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adapters, or LoRAs, make foundation-model fine-tuning more economical by representing a matrix through two smaller matrices. Combining several LoRA adapters as a mixture of experts can increase their expressive capacity. However, the paper identifies weaknesses in the robustness of these mixtures during both tuning and inference, despite their improvements on downstream tasks.

The proposed training strategy draws on Riemannian preconditioning, which treats a LoRA adapter as a projection into a subspace. It extends this perspective to several experts through gate-rescaled multi-space projections. In plain terms, the method changes how the experts learn across their respective spaces while accounting for the gates that determine their contributions.

The authors provide both a theoretical solution and an alternative engineering strategy for applying the idea. Evaluations with SGD and AdamW support the effectiveness of the approach. The contribution is therefore a way to stabilize and strengthen feature learning in mixtures of low-rank adapters, addressing how those adapters are trained as well as how much representational capacity they provide.
summary.tldr: Gate-rescaled projections improve the stability and feature learning of mixtures of low-rank adapters.

title: A Stronger Mixture of Low-Rank Experts for Fine-Tuning Foundation Models

abstract: Motivated by empirical observations of prolonged plateaus and stage-wise progression during training, we investigate the loss landscape of transformer models trained on in-context next-token prediction tasks. In particular, we focus on learning in-context $n$-gram language models under cross-entropy loss, and establish a sufficient condition for parameter configurations to be stationary points. We then construct a set of parameter configurations for a simplified transformer model that represent $k$-gram estimators (for $k \leq n$), and show that the gradient of the population loss at these solutions vanishes in the limit of infinite sequence length and parameter norm. This reveals a key property of the loss landscape: sub-$n$-grams are near-stationary points of the population cross-entropy loss, offering theoretical insight into widely observed phenomena such as stage-wise learning dynamics and emergent phase transitions. These insights are further supported by numerical experiments that illustrate the learning dynamics of $n$-grams, characterized by discrete transitions between near-stationary solutions.

paragraphs: Transformer training can exhibit long periods of little improvement followed by discrete advances. This paper investigates a possible explanation through in-context next-token prediction with n-gram language models. It studies the population cross-entropy loss landscape to understand why solutions corresponding to simpler prediction rules can form plateaus along the learning process.

The authors establish a sufficient condition for parameter configurations to be stationary points. For a simplified transformer, they then construct configurations representing k-gram estimators with k no greater than n. At these configurations, the population-loss gradient approaches zero as both sequence length and parameter norm become infinite. This gives a precise limiting account of near-stationary sub-n-gram solutions.

Numerical experiments support the connection to staged learning, showing discrete transitions between near-stationary solutions. The findings offer a theoretical explanation for why training may pause around partial solutions before progressing. Their force is specific: the stationary-point condition is sufficient, and the vanishing-gradient result uses a simplified model and an infinite-limit argument.
summary.tldr: Simplified transformers have near-stationary solutions representing shorter n-gram rules, offering an explanation for training plateaus and staged progress.

title: Learning In-context $n$-grams with Transformers: Sub-$n$-grams Are Near-Stationary Points

abstract: Multi-Modal Learning (MML) aims to learn effective representations across modalities for accurate predictions. Existing methods typically focus on modality consistency and specificity to learn effective representations. However, from a causal perspective, they may lead to representations that contain insufficient and unnecessary information. To address this, we propose that effective MML representations should be causally sufficient and necessary. Considering practical issues like spurious correlations and modality conflicts, we relax the exogeneity and monotonicity assumptions prevalent in prior works and explore the concepts specific to MML, i.e., Causal Complete Cause ($C^3$). We begin by defining $C^3$, which quantifies the probability of representations being causally sufficient and necessary. We then discuss the identifiability of $C^3$ and introduce an instrumental variable to support identifying $C^3$ with non-exogeneity and non-monotonicity. Building on this, we conduct the $C^3$ measurement, i.e., $C^3$ risk. We propose a twin network to estimate it through (i) the real-world branch: utilizing the instrumental variable for sufficiency, and (ii) the hypothetical-world branch: applying gradient-based counterfactual modeling for necessity. Theoretical analyses confirm its reliability. Based on these results, we propose $C^3$ Regularization, a plug-and-play method that enforces the causal completeness of the learned representations by minimizing $C^3$ risk. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made significant strides in code translation tasks. However, ensuring both the correctness and readability of translated code remains a challenge, limiting their effective adoption in real-world software development. In this work, we propose F2STrans, a function-to-style guiding paradigm designed to progressively improve the performance of LLMs in code translation. Our approach comprises two key stages: (1) Functional learning, which optimizes translation correctness using high-quality source-target code pairs mined from online programming platforms, and (2) Style learning, which improves translation readability by incorporating both positive and negative style examples. Additionally, we introduce a novel code translation benchmark that includes up-to-date source code, extensive test cases, and manually annotated ground-truth translations, enabling comprehensive functional and stylistic evaluations. Experiments on both our new benchmark and existing datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves code translation performance. Notably, our approach enables Qwen-1.5B to outperform prompt-enhanced Qwen-32B and GPT-4 on average across 20 diverse code translation scenarios.

paragraphs: Code translation must preserve what a program does while producing code that people can read. F2STrans approaches these requirements through a staged training process. It treats functional correctness and style as distinct learning goals, giving each an explicit role in improving a language model’s translations between programming languages.

The first stage learns functionality from high-quality source and target code pairs gathered from online programming platforms. The second stage learns style from both positive and negative examples. This progression is designed to improve readability after establishing translation correctness. The authors also introduce a benchmark containing recent source code, extensive tests, and manually annotated reference translations so that both aspects can be evaluated.

Experiments on that benchmark and existing datasets show significant improvements in translation performance. With this approach, Qwen-1.5B outperforms prompt-enhanced Qwen-32B and GPT-4 on average across twenty translation scenarios. The finding demonstrates the value of targeted training for this task, with the reported comparison applying to the average across those evaluated scenarios.
summary.tldr: F2STrans trains code translation first for correctness and then for style, substantially improving performance across the evaluated translation scenarios.

title: Function-to-Style Guidance of LLMs for Code Translation

abstract: Image steganography hides multiple images for multiple recipients into a single cover image. All secret images are usually revealed without authentication, which reduces security among multiple recipients. It is elegant to design an authentication mechanism for isolated reception. We explore such mechanism through sufficient experiments, and uncover that additional authentication information will affect the distribution of hidden information and occupy more hiding space of the cover image. This severely decreases effectiveness and efficiency in large-capacity hiding. To overcome such a challenge, we first prove the authentication feasibility within image steganography. Then, this paper proposes an image steganography network collaborating with separate authentication and efficient scheme. Specifically, multiple pairs of lock-key are generated during hiding and revealing. Unlike traditional methods, our method has two stages to make appropriate distribution adaptation between locks and secret images, simultaneously extracting more reasonable primary information from secret images, which can release hiding space of the cover image to some extent. Furthermore, due to separate authentication, fused information can be hidden in parallel with a single network rather than traditional serial hiding with multiple networks, which can largely decrease the model size. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves more secure, effective, and efficient image steganography. Code is available at https://github.com/Revive624/Authentication-Image-Steganography.

paragraphs: Image steganography can hide several recipients' secret images inside one cover image, but revealing all secrets without authentication undermines separation between recipients. Adding authentication creates its own difficulty: the extra information consumes hiding capacity and changes how hidden information is distributed. The paper studies this tension between separate access and effective, efficient high-capacity hiding.

After proving authentication feasibility within image steganography, the authors propose a network that generates multiple lock-key pairs during hiding and revealing. A two-stage method adapts the relationship between locks and secret images while extracting their primary information more effectively. This releases some of the cover image's hiding space, addressing the capacity cost that the authors observed when authentication information is added.

Separate authentication also allows fused information to be hidden in parallel through a single network, reducing model size compared with serial hiding through multiple networks. Experiments report improved security, effectiveness, and efficiency. The contribution combines recipient-specific authentication with a hiding architecture designed to accommodate the additional information and computational demands that authentication introduces.
summary.tldr: A two-stage steganography network combines separate recipient authentication with more efficient hiding and a smaller parallel architecture.

title: Efficient and Separate Authentication Image Steganography Network

abstract: The factors driving the performance of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models (LLMs) remain poorly understood despite ICL’s surprising effectiveness, enabling models to adapt to new tasks from only a handful of examples. To clarify and improve these capabilities, we characterize how the statistical properties of the pretraining distribution (e.g., tail behavior, coverage) shape ICL. We develop a theoretical framework that encompasses generalization and task selection and show how distributional properties govern sample efficiency, task retrieval, and robustness. To this end, we generalize existing concentration results to heavy-tailed priors and dependent sequences, better reflecting the structure of LLM pretraining data. Our framework reveals a fundamental design trade-off: heavy-tailed pretraining distributions facilitate robust task selection under distribution shifts but are detrimental to generalization, especially in low-data regimes. We then empirically evaluate our predictions by studying how ICL performance varies with the pretraining distribution on challenging tasks such as stochastic differential equations and stochastic processes with memory. Together, these findings suggest that controlling key statistical properties of the pretraining distribution is essential for building ICL-capable and reliable LLMs.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model adapt to a task from a small set of examples. This paper examines how that ability depends on the statistical structure of pretraining data. Its framework connects properties such as tail behavior and coverage to task selection, generalization, sample efficiency, and robustness.

Selecting an appropriate task and generalizing well within it therefore need not benefit from the same distributional choices.

The authors empirically investigate these predictions using tasks involving stochastic differential equations and stochastic processes with memory. They study how changing the pretraining distribution changes in-context learning performance. The resulting perspective makes distribution design a substantive modeling decision: statistical properties that support robustness can also carry a generalization cost, so improving in-context learning requires considering both effects.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies a trade-off in which heavy-tailed pretraining distributions improve robust task selection but hinder generalization, especially with little data.

title: How Does the Pretraining Distribution Shape In-Context Learning? A Fundamental Trade-Off

abstract: Imbalanced Domain Generalization (IDG) focuses on mitigating both domain and label shifts, both of which fundamentally shape the model’s decision boundaries, particularly under heterogeneous long-tailed distributions across domains. Despite its practical significance, it remains underexplored, primarily due to the technical complexity of handling their entanglement and the paucity of theoretical foundations. In this paper, we begin by theoretically establishing the generalization bound for IDG, highlighting the role of posterior discrepancy and decision margin. This bound motivates us to focus on directly steering decision boundaries, marking a clear departure from existing methods. Then, we technically propose a novel Negative-Dominant Contrastive Learning (NDCL) for IDG to enhance discriminability while enforce posterior consistency across domains. Specifically, inter-class decision-boundary separation is enhanced by placing greater emphasis on negatives as the primary signal in our contrastive learning, naturally amplifying gradient signals for minority classes to avoid the decision boundary being biased toward majority classes. Intra-class compactness is encouraged through a re-weighted cross-entropy strategy, and posterior consistency across domains is enforced through a prediction-central alignment strategy. Finally, rigorous yet challenging experiments on benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our NDCL. The code is available at https://github.com/Alrash/NDCL.

paragraphs: Imbalanced domain generalization concerns models that face both changing domains and unequal class frequencies. These shifts interact: a class may be common in one domain and rare in another, influencing where the model places its decision boundaries. The paper first derives a generalization bound that highlights differences in predicted class probabilities across domains and the separation provided by decision margins.

That analysis motivates Negative-Dominant Contrastive Learning, which emphasizes examples from different classes as the main contrastive signal. The method strengthens separation between classes and amplifies gradient signals for minority classes, countering decision boundaries biased toward majority classes. A reweighted cross-entropy component encourages examples from the same class to form compact groups.

A further alignment strategy operates around predictions to encourage consistent class probabilities across domains. Together, the components address class separation, within-class compactness, and cross-domain consistency. Benchmark experiments validate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution connects the theoretical quantities in the bound with training mechanisms that directly influence decision boundaries under the combined pressures of domain shift and class imbalance.
summary.tldr: NDCL emphasizes negative contrastive examples and prediction alignment to improve generalization across domains with uneven class frequencies.

title: Negatives-Dominant Contrastive Learning for Generalization in Imbalanced Domains

abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning (RL) methods have achieved remarkable success in improving the performance of large language models (LLMs) and have been rapidly extended to agentic tasks. However, their credit assignment relies heavily on coarse-grained trajectory-level attribution according to final outcomes, making it difficult to capture the contribution of individual steps, such as valuable steps obscured within failed trajectories. To uncover latent information and enable more faithful step-level credit assignment, we propose Graph-based Group Policy Optimization (GraphGPO), which first aggregates all rollout trajectories into a unified state-transition graph and then estimates the distance from each state to the task goal using the global information encoded in the graph. Finally, GraphGPO assigns credit to each edge by estimating a graph-based advantage, based on how much the transition reduces the distance to the task goal. In this way, GraphGPO significantly improves training efficiency and achieves state-of-the-art performance across a range of challenging benchmarks.

paragraphs: When an agent learns from complete attempts at a task, its final outcome can obscure the value of individual actions. A failed attempt may contain useful progress, yet assigning credit mainly from overall success or failure makes that progress difficult to recognize. This paper develops a more detailed training signal for language-model agents.

GraphGPO combines rollout trajectories into one graph of states and transitions. It uses information across that graph to estimate how far each state is from the task goal. Each transition then receives a graph-based advantage according to how much it reduces the estimated distance. This makes the training signal depend on a step’s contribution to progress, informed by the other collected trajectories.

The authors report substantially improved training efficiency and state-of-the-art performance across challenging benchmarks. The approach matters because it reuses relationships among collected attempts to extract information that final outcomes alone do not provide. In particular, a useful transition can receive credit even when the trajectory containing it ultimately fails, addressing the specific attribution problem that motivates the method.
summary.tldr: GraphGPO combines agent trajectories into a graph and rewards individual transitions for reducing their estimated distance to the goal.

title: Beyond Trajectory-Level Attribution: Graph-Based Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern enterprises generate vast streams of time series metrics when monitoring complex systems, known as observability data. Unlike conventional time series from domains such as climate, observability data are zero-inflated, highly stochastic, and exhibit minimal temporal structure. Despite their importance, observability datasets remain underrepresented in public benchmarks due to proprietary restrictions and privacy concerns. Existing datasets are often anonymized and normalized, removing scale information and limiting their use for tasks such as anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and multi-modal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TelecomTS, a large-scale observability dataset derived from a 5G telecommunications network. TelecomTS features heterogeneous, de-anonymized covariates with explicit absolute scale information and provides a diverse suite of downstream tasks, including anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and multi-modal question-answering. Benchmarking state-of-the-art time series, language, reasoning, and multi-modal foundation models reveals that existing approaches struggle with the abrupt, noisy, and high-variance dynamics characteristic of observability data. Our experiments further underscore the importance of preserving covariates’ absolute scale, emphasizing the need for foundation time series models that natively leverage scale information for practical real-world observability applications. The code is available at: https://github.com/Ali-maatouk/TelecomTS.

paragraphs: Operational monitoring produces time series that can contain many zeros, abrupt changes, and substantial randomness with little temporal structure. Public datasets underrepresent these signals, partly because of proprietary restrictions and privacy concerns. This paper introduces TelecomTS to support evaluation on the kinds of data generated by a complex operational system.

Derived from a 5G telecommunications network, TelecomTS includes heterogeneous covariates with meaningful identities and explicit absolute scales. It supports anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and question answering that combines language with time series. Preserving scale addresses a problem with normalized datasets: they can remove information useful for interpreting operational measurements.

Benchmarking time series, language, reasoning, and multimodal foundation models reveals difficulty handling the dataset’s noisy, abrupt, high-variance behavior. The experiments also show the importance of retaining absolute scale. The dataset therefore contributes both a testing resource and evidence about a modeling need: observability models should be able to use measurement scale directly when it carries information relevant to practical monitoring tasks.
summary.tldr: TelecomTS benchmarks operational time series and language tasks using 5G network data that preserves meaningful covariates and absolute measurement scales.

title: TelecomTS: A Multi-Modal Observability Dataset for Time Series and Language Analysis

abstract: The scalable solution of large sparse linear systems is a bottleneck in scientific computing and graph analysis. While algebraic multigrid (AMG) offers optimal linear scaling, its performance is severely constrained by the trade-off between the sparsity and convergence quality of coarse-grid operators. Classical AMG heuristics struggle to balance these objectives, often sacrificing stability or performance for sparsity. We propose RAPNet, a graph neural network (GNN) framework that resolves this trade-off by learning to generate sparse, robust coarse operators directly from the sparse algebraic system. Key to our approach is a level-wise training strategy that enables learning from small subgraphs and generalization to million-node domains, bypassing the bottlenecks of prior neural AMG attempts. RAPNet executes exclusively during the solver setup phase, ensuring that the solve phase retains its favorable computational properties. We show that our method outperforms classical non-Galerkin baselines on diverse PDE discretizations and graph Laplacians, making it particularly effective for multi-query tasks such as eigenproblems, time-dependent simulations, and inverse or design problems.

title: RAPNet: Accelerating Algebraic Multigrid with Learned Sparse Corrections

abstract: Recent research has established that the impact of context in a vanilla transformer can be represented implicitly by forming a token-dependent, rank-1 patch to its MLP weights. This work extends that foundational theory to the diverse architectures of modern Large Language Models. We first demonstrate a precise, analytical solution for a Gemma-style transformer block, proving that the entire effect of a context can be perfectly mapped to rank-1 patches on its MLP weight matrices and a patch to the RMSNorm scale. We then generalize this result, providing a constructive proof and algorithm for multi-layer models. To unify these findings, we introduce a general framework centered on two core properties: input controllability and output controllability. We prove that a perfect implicit weight patch is possible for any MLP block where the inner function is input-controllable and the outer function is output-controllable. This provides a simpler and more powerful lens for understanding how transformer models transmute prompts into effective weights. This setup generalizes to a wide range of modern LLM architectures including gating, pre-/post-norm, mixture of experts and sequential/parallel transformer blocks.

paragraphs: A transformer’s output changes when its context changes, even though its stored parameters remain fixed. Earlier theory represented this contextual effect through token-dependent rank-one changes to a vanilla transformer’s MLP weights. This paper extends that mathematical correspondence to the more varied blocks used in modern language models.

For a Gemma-style block, the authors give an analytical construction that exactly reproduces the context’s effect using rank-one patches to MLP weight matrices and a patch to the RMSNorm scale. They then provide a constructive proof and algorithm for multilayer models. The result describes an implicit parameter representation of contextual behavior.

The broader framework uses two properties called input controllability and output controllability. A perfect implicit patch is possible when the MLP’s inner function has the former property and its outer function has the latter. This is a sufficient condition supporting extensions across gating, normalization layouts, mixture-of-experts designs, and sequential or parallel blocks. It offers a common mathematical language for understanding how prompts act like effective weight changes.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs implicit weight patches that exactly reproduce contextual effects in modern transformer blocks under stated controllability conditions.

title: Equivalence of Context and Parameter Updates in Modern Transformer Blocks

abstract: Low-precision arithmetic is pervasive in neural network training and deployment, yet its effect on prediction confidence, not just accuracy, remains unexamined. We show that the softmax function amplifies logit-space quantization errors in an input-dependent manner: confidence distortion scales with the product of precision-dependent error bound $\epsilon$ and logit norm, peaking when the model is confident but not saturated. This explains why identical models report different confidence values across precisions, a phenomenon we term Precision Split. During training, the same mechanism causes gradient underflow: when logit margins exceed a precision-dependent threshold, gradients vanish and samples silently stop contributing to learning. Since logit norm serves as a computable proxy for precision-induced risk, we propose Precision-Aware Confidence Scaling (PACS), which applies sample-adaptive temperature inversely related to this risk, with sub-one-percent overhead and no full-precision computation required. On ImageNet with mixed-precision ResNet-50, PACS reduces Expected Calibration Error from 5.82% to 1.92% while maintaining accuracy, with consistent improvements across architectures, precision formats, and modalities.
