paragraphs: Using fewer numerical bits can change a neural network's reported confidence even when its accuracy remains similar. The paper explains this through softmax amplification of quantization errors in logits, the scores converted into prediction probabilities. Confidence distortion scales with a precision-dependent error bound multiplied by logit norm, and peaks when predictions are confident but not yet saturated.

The authors call the resulting differences across numerical precisions Precision Split. They also connect the same mechanism to training: once logit margins exceed a precision-dependent threshold, gradient underflow can cause examples to stop contributing to learning. Logit norm therefore becomes a computable indicator of exposure to precision-induced distortion.

Precision-Aware Confidence Scaling uses that indicator to apply a sample-adaptive temperature inversely related to the estimated risk. It requires no full-precision computation and adds less than one percent overhead. On ImageNet with mixed-precision ResNet-50, it reduces Expected Calibration Error from 5.82% to 1.92% while maintaining accuracy. Reported improvements across architectures, precision formats, and modalities support correcting confidence as a distinct concern in low-precision deployment.
summary.tldr: PACS corrects input-dependent confidence distortion from low-precision arithmetic, improving calibration with less than one percent overhead.

title: Precision-Induced Miscalibration: Understanding and Correcting Confidence Distortion in Quantized Neural Networks

abstract: Speculative reasoning has recently been proposed as a means to accelerate reasoning-intensive generation in large multimodal models, but its effectiveness is often constrained by misalignment between speculative drafts and target-verified reasoning. In this work, we introduce DREAM-R, a framework that substantially improves the performance of speculative reasoning. At its core, DREAM-R employs Speculative Alignment Policy Optimization (SAPO), a reinforcement-learning objective that trains draft models to generate reasoning steps that are both faithful to target trajectories and concise. We further propose a Threshold-based Verification Mechanism (TBVM) that uses a ratio-based criterion to provide stable and interpretable acceptance of speculative steps only when positive evidence clearly dominates, thereby preventing error propagation. Building on these components, we develop a Fully Parallel Speculative Reasoning (FPSR) framework that parallelizes draft generation, target-side reasoning, and verification across multi-step reasoning, enabling early stopping and clean fallback. Experiments on reasoning-heavy benchmarks demonstrate up to $2.49\times$ speedup while preserving target-model accuracy, yielding substantial efficiency gains without compromising reasoning quality.

paragraphs: Speculative reasoning accelerates multimodal reasoning by proposing draft steps that a target model verifies. Its usefulness depends on how well those drafts match the target’s reasoning: misaligned proposals can waste work or introduce errors. DREAM-R coordinates draft training, verification, and execution to make more of this speculative work useful.

Its reinforcement-learning objective, SAPO, trains the draft model to produce concise steps that remain faithful to target reasoning trajectories. A threshold-based verifier then uses a ratio criterion to accept steps only when positive evidence clearly dominates. The execution framework runs drafting, target reasoning, and verification in parallel across multiple steps, with support for early stopping and fallback when speculative progress cannot be used.

The result links efficiency to three complementary choices: better-aligned drafts, selective acceptance, and overlapping computation. It demonstrates that speculative reasoning can deliver substantial measured acceleration when these components work together, with the reported accuracy preservation applying to the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: DREAM-R combines aligned drafts, selective verification, and parallel execution for up to 2.49 times faster multimodal reasoning at preserved target accuracy.

title: DREAM-R: Multimodal Speculative Reasoning with RL-Based Refined Drafting, Precise Verification, and Fully Parallel Execution

abstract: Modeling the learning curve is critical for cost-effective data collection in deep learning systems. Most prior approaches assume a specific parametric learning curve, but these can be inappropriate when no reliable parametric form can be assumed for the learning curve. While Gaussian processes offer flexible nonparametric modeling, existing GP approaches that enforce monotonicity typically introduce intractable factors or require derivative observations. To address this, we propose a Monotonic Variational Gaussian Process for Efficient Data Collection (MOVE), which (i) introduces a novel monotonic variational GP formulation with virtual-derivative factors to enable tractable posterior inference, and (ii) develops an expected shortfall based objective for target-driven data collection. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis shows that expected shortfall provides non-vanishing gradient signals that enable reliable gradient-based optimization. Extensive experiments on classification, segmentation, and detection benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over the prior method.

paragraphs: Planning data collection requires estimating how a model’s performance will change as more data becomes available. A fixed mathematical curve can be a poor fit when its shape is uncertain. Gaussian processes offer greater flexibility, but existing ways of making their curves monotonic can complicate inference or require observations of derivatives.

MOVE introduces a monotonic variational Gaussian process that uses virtual-derivative factors to keep posterior inference tractable. These factors incorporate information about the direction of change into the model. The method pairs this learning-curve formulation with an expected-shortfall objective for collecting data toward a target, connecting uncertainty about future performance to the data-collection decision.

The theoretical analysis shows that expected shortfall supplies non-vanishing gradient signals, supporting reliable gradient-based optimization of that objective. Experiments on classification, segmentation, and detection benchmarks show consistent improvements over the prior method. Together, the modeling and decision components address both parts of the problem: estimating a flexible monotonic learning curve and using it to guide target-driven data collection.
summary.tldr: MOVE combines tractable monotonic Gaussian-process modeling with an expected-shortfall objective to guide data collection toward a performance target.

title: Monotonic Variational Gaussian Process for Efficient Data Collection

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning capabilities, their deployment as embodied agents still faces fundamental challenges in long-horizon planning. Unlike open-ended text generation, embodied agents must decompose high-level intents into actionable sub-goals while adhering to the constraints of a dynamic environment. Standard LLM planners frequently fail to maintain strategy coherence over extended horizons due to context window limitations or hallucinate state transitions that violate environment constraints. We propose GiG, a planning framework that structures embodied agents’ memory using a Graph-in-Graph architecture. Our approach employs a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to encode environmental states into embeddings, organizing these embeddings into action-connected execution trace graphs within an experience memory bank. GiG enables retrieval of structurally-similar priors, allowing agents to ground current decisions in relevant past structural patterns. Furthermore, we introduce a bounded lookahead module that leverages symbolic transition logic to enhance the agent’s planning capabilities through grounded action projections. We evaluate our framework on three embodied planning benchmarks—Robotouille Synchronous, Robotouille Asynchronous, and ALFWorld. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving Pass@1 performance gains of up to 22% on Robotouille Synchronous, 37% on Asynchronous, and 15% on ALFWorld while maintaining comparable or lower computational cost.

paragraphs: An embodied agent must turn a broad goal into actions that remain valid as its environment changes. Over long tasks, language-model planners can lose strategic consistency or imagine state changes that the environment does not permit. GiG addresses these problems by giving planning a structured memory of previous execution and a grounded way to examine possible next steps.

Reported Pass@1 gains reach up to 22%, 37%, and 15%, respectively, with comparable or lower computational cost. The results support combining structural experience retrieval with limited symbolic lookahead to help language models maintain coherent plans across extended sequences of actions.
summary.tldr: GiG improves embodied planning by retrieving graph-structured experiences and checking prospective actions with symbolic transition logic.

title: Embodied Task Planning via Graph-Informed Action Generation with Large Language Models

abstract: Current deep learning models for Multispectral and Hyperspectral Image Fusion (MS/HS fusion) are typically designed for fixed spectral bands and spatial scales, which limits their transferability across diverse sensors. To address this, we propose SSA, a unified framework for MS/HS fusion with spectral-band and fusion-scale agnosticism. Specifically, we introduce Matryoshka Kernel (MK), a novel operator that enables a single model to process varying ordered spectral band counts within a supported range. Meanwhile, we build SSA upon an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) backbone that models the HS signal as a continuous function, enabling reconstruction at arbitrary spatial resolutions. Together, these two mechanisms support a single MS/HS fusion model for heterogeneous sensors and arbitrary query scales. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our single jointly trained model achieves state-of-the-art performance, generalizes to unseen spatial scales, and transfers to unseen sensors with few-step adaptation. The code can be obtained at https://github.com/vg219/SSA.

paragraphs: Multispectral and hyperspectral image fusion models commonly expect a fixed number of spectral bands and a fixed spatial scale. Those expectations make it difficult to reuse one model across sensors with different characteristics. SSA addresses both sources of rigidity within a single framework for combining these types of imagery.

Its Matryoshka Kernel operator supports varying counts of ordered spectral bands within a supported range. Separately, an implicit neural representation describes the hyperspectral signal as a continuous function. That continuous representation allows reconstruction to be queried at arbitrary spatial resolutions. Together, the two mechanisms let one model accommodate differences in spectral input and requested output scale.

The authors report that a single jointly trained model achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes to spatial scales it did not encounter during training. Transfer to unseen sensors is also demonstrated with a few adaptation steps. These qualifications matter: spectral flexibility remains within the operator's supported range, and the reported sensor transfer involves adaptation. The results support broader reuse of a fusion model across heterogeneous imaging setups.
summary.tldr: SSA combines flexible spectral-band processing with continuous spatial reconstruction to support one fusion model across scales and adaptable sensor settings.

title: Hyperspectral Image Fusion with Spectral-Band and Fusion-Scale Agnosticism

abstract: Generating human videos with realistic and controllable motions is a challenging task. While existing methods can generate visually compelling videos, they lack separate control over four key video elements: foreground subject, background video, human trajectory, and action patterns. In this paper, we propose a decomposed human motion control and video generation framework that explicitly decouples motion from appearance, subject from background, and action from trajectory, enabling flexible mix-and-match composition of these elements. Concretely, we first build a ground-aware 3D world coordinate system and perform motion editing directly in the 3D space. Trajectory control is implemented by unprojecting edited 2D trajectories into 3D with focal-length calibration and coordinate transformation, followed by speed alignment and orientation adjustment; actions are supplied by a motion bank or generated via text-to-motion methods. Then, based on modern text-to-video diffusion transformer models, we inject the subject as tokens for full attention, concatenate the background along the channel dimension, and add motion (trajectory and action) control signals by addition. Such a design opens up the possibility for us to generate realistic videos of anyone doing anything anywhere. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and real-world cases demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both element-wise controllability and overall video quality.

paragraphs: RealisMotion aims to make four parts of human video generation independently controllable: the person, the background, the path of movement, and the action being performed. Separating these elements allows them to be recombined more flexibly. The framework explicitly distinguishes motion from appearance, the subject from the surroundings, and action patterns from trajectories.

Edited 2D trajectories are converted into 3D using focal-length calibration and coordinate transformations, followed by adjustments to speed and orientation. Actions come from a motion bank or a text-to-motion method. This creates motion controls that account for movement through world space.

A text-to-video diffusion transformer then receives each control through a distinct mechanism: subject tokens participate in full attention, background information is concatenated along channels, and motion signals are added. Experiments on benchmark datasets and real-world cases report state-of-the-art element-wise controllability and overall video quality. The results support flexible composition of the evaluated elements, while the broader vision of arbitrary people, actions, and places remains a possibility enabled by the design.
summary.tldr: RealisMotion separates subject, background, trajectory, and action controls to generate human videos with editable motion in 3D world space.

title: RealisMotion: Decomposed Human Motion Control and Video Generation in the World Space

abstract: Geospatial understanding is a critical yet underexplored dimension in the development of machine learning systems for tasks such as image geolocation and spatial reasoning. In this work, we analyze the geospatial representations acquired by three model families: vision-only architectures (e.g., ViT), vision-language models (e.g., CLIP), and large-scale multimodal foundation models (e.g., LLaVA, Qwen, and Gemma). By evaluating across image clusters, including people, landmarks, and everyday objects, grouped based on the degree of localizability, we reveal systematic gaps in spatial accuracy and show that textual supervision enhances the learning of geospatial representations. Our findings suggest the role of language as an effective complementary modality for encoding spatial context and multimodal learning as a key direction for advancing geospatial AI.

paragraphs: Understanding the geographic context of an image matters for image geolocation and spatial reasoning. This paper examines how different kinds of machine learning models represent that information, focusing on the contribution of textual supervision. It compares vision-only models, vision-language models, and large multimodal foundation models.

The analysis evaluates groups of images containing people, landmarks, and everyday objects. These groups are organized according to how readily their contents can be localized geographically. That structure lets the study examine spatial accuracy across different kinds of visual evidence, rather than treating every image as equally informative about location. The compared families include ViT, CLIP, and models such as LLaVA, Qwen, and Gemma.

The authors find systematic gaps in spatial accuracy and report that textual supervision improves geospatial representations. Their findings suggest that language supplies complementary spatial context useful to visual learning. The contribution is an empirical account of differences across model families and image groups, supporting multimodal learning as a promising direction for geospatial AI.
summary.tldr: Comparisons across model families and image types show that textual supervision improves learned geospatial representations.

title: Textual Supervision Enhances Geospatial Representations in Vision-Language Models

abstract: Deep neural networks achieve impressive results across diverse applications, yet their overconfidence on unseen inputs necessitates reliable epistemic uncertainty modeling. Existing methods for uncertainty modeling face a fundamental dilemma: Bayesian approaches provide principled estimates but remain computationally prohibitive, while efficient second-order predictors lack rigorous connections between their specific objectives and epistemic uncertainty quantification. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Dirichlet-approximated possibilistic posterior predictions (DAPPr), a principled framework grounded in possibility theory. We define a possibilistic posterior over parameters, project it to the prediction space via supremum operators, and approximate the projected posterior using learnable Dirichlet possibility functions. This projection-and-approximation strategy yields a simple training objective with closed-form solutions. Despite its simplicity, extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks show that DAPPr achieves competitive or superior uncertainty quantification performance over state-of-the-art second-order predictors while maintaining both principled derivation and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Deep networks can be overconfident on unfamiliar inputs, motivating estimates of epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty associated with the model’s knowledge. This paper seeks a principled connection between an efficient training objective and that uncertainty. Its proposed framework, DAPPr, develops the connection using possibility theory.

The contribution is both methodological and empirical: it supplies a derivation for the uncertainty objective and shows that the resulting method performs well in the evaluated settings. Its central aim is practical uncertainty estimation with a clear theoretical foundation.
summary.tldr: DAPPr derives an efficient predictive uncertainty method from possibility theory and reports competitive or superior benchmark performance.

title: Possibilistic Predictive Uncertainty for Deep Learning

abstract: In many real-world settings, a centralized decision-maker must repeatedly allocate finite resources to a population over multiple time steps. Individuals who receive a resource derive some stochastic utility; to characterize the population-level effects of an allocation, the expected individual utilities are then aggregated using a social welfare function (SWF). We formalize this setting and present a general confidence sequence framework for SWF-based online learning and inference, valid for any monotonic, concave, and Lipschitz-continuous SWF. Our key insight is that monotonicity alone suffices to lift confidence sequences from individual utilities to anytime-valid bounds on optimal welfare. Building on this foundation, we propose SWF-UCB, a SWF-agnostic online learning algorithm that achieves near-optimal $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n+\sqrt{nkT})$ regret (for $k$ resources distributed among $n$ individuals at each of $T$ time steps). We instantiate our framework on three normatively distinct SWF families: Weighted Power Mean, Kolm, and Gini, providing bespoke oracle algorithms for each. Experiments confirm $\sqrt{T}$ scaling and reveal rich interactions between $k$ and SWF parameters. This framework naturally supports inference applications such as sequential hypothesis testing, optimal stopping, and policy evaluation.

paragraphs: Repeated resource allocation requires learning who benefits while deciding how to distribute a limited supply. This paper models individual benefits as stochastic utilities and aggregates their expectations through a social welfare function. Different welfare functions express different priorities for assessing the population-level outcome of an allocation.

The authors develop a confidence-sequence framework for monotonic, concave, Lipschitz-continuous welfare functions. Its central insight is narrower and particularly useful: monotonicity alone is sufficient to transfer uncertainty bounds on individual utilities into bounds on optimal welfare that remain valid throughout sequential observation. The framework also supports sequential testing, stopping decisions, and policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: A general framework learns repeated resource allocations while providing anytime-valid welfare bounds across several social welfare objectives.

title: Online Social Welfare Function-based Resource Allocation

abstract: Modern GUI agents typically rely on a model-centric and step-wise interaction paradigm, where LLMs must re-interpret the UI and re-decide actions at every screen, which is fragile in long-horizon tasks. In this paper, we propose Executable Agentic Memory (EAM), a structured Knowledge Graph (KG) that shifts GUI planning from free-form generation to a robust retrieval-and-execution process. Our approach includes a sample-efficient memory construction pipeline using state-aware DFS and action-group mining to compress multi-step routines. To ensure efficient planning, we introduce a value-guided graph search where a lightweight Q-function model steers Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) over the KG. We theoretically establish bias-consistency for the Q-model and derive sample complexity bounds for path recovery. Empirically, EAM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines like UI-TARS-7B by up to $19.6%$ on AndroidWorld, while reducing token costs $6\times$ relative to GPT-4o. With a $2.8$s average latency, EAM enables reliable, quick, and long-horizon GUI automation.

paragraphs: Graphical-interface agents often ask a language model to interpret each screen and select the next action from scratch. Repeating that process over a long task can be fragile and expensive. Executable Agentic Memory stores interface knowledge in a structured graph, allowing planning to retrieve and execute known action sequences.

The memory-building pipeline explores interfaces with state-aware depth-first search and mines groups of actions to compress multi-step routines. During planning, a lightweight Q-function estimates the value of choices and guides Monte Carlo Tree Search over the graph. These results show how executable memory can improve both task performance and interaction efficiency by making reusable routines a central part of planning.
summary.tldr: EAM turns interface experience into an executable knowledge graph, improving GUI-agent performance while reducing token costs.

title: Executable Agentic Memory for GUI Agent

abstract: While Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MMDiTs) have achieved remarkable success in high-fidelity generation, maintaining semantic faithfulness and structural consistency during the image editing process remains a fundamental challenge. DiT-based editing is primarily limited by cumulative drift and semantic leakage induced by new textual conditions. To address these challenges, we propose T-Edit, a training-free framework that formalizes consistent editing as a trajectory anchoring process. T-Edit explicitly decouples the inversion, reconstruction, and editing trajectories, leveraging the reconstruction branch as a structural reference to achieve real-time compensation for deviations in the latent manifold. To further reveal the internal regulation mechanism of DiTs, we analyze the spatio-temporal heterogeneity of their layer-wise structural sensitivity and accordingly propose a Dynamic Vital Layer (DVL) localization mechanism based on information energy. Furthermore, addressing the asymmetry of textual perturbations in the frequency domain distribution, we introduce a frequency-aware strategy based on tensor Singular Value Decomposition (t-SVD) to anchor (TA) high-rank structural components. Experiments show that T-Edit achieves state-of-the-art performance in both semantic alignment and structural fidelity, and can be seamlessly extended to multi-step editing and video scenarios, providing a new perspective for understanding and controlling the internal stability of DiTs.

paragraphs: Editing an image with a new text instruction can gradually alter structures that should remain stable. T-Edit attributes this problem in diffusion transformers to cumulative drift and semantic leakage from the new condition. It introduces a training-free framework that treats consistent editing as keeping the generation trajectory anchored to a structural reference.

The framework separates inversion, reconstruction, and editing into three trajectories. The reconstruction branch supplies a reference for correcting deviations during editing. T-Edit also analyzes how structural sensitivity varies across layers, space, and time, then uses an information-energy criterion to dynamically locate influential layers.

These mechanisms aim to preserve the source structure while allowing the requested semantic change. Experiments report state-of-the-art semantic alignment and structural fidelity, along with extensions to repeated editing and video. The results support using internal reconstruction references and selective structural control to stabilize diffusion-transformer editing.
summary.tldr: T-Edit stabilizes image editing with a reconstruction reference and selective structural anchoring, improving instruction alignment and structural fidelity.

title: T-Edit: Triple-Branch Diffusion Anchoring for Consistent Editing

abstract: Natural policy gradients improve optimization by accounting for the geometry of distribution space, but their practical use is limited by the cost of estimating and inverting the Fisher matrix. We present Randomized Advantage Transformation (RAT), a method for estimating Tikhonov-regularized natural policy gradients via direct backpropagation. By applying the Woodbury formula, we reformulate the regularized natural gradient as vanilla policy gradients with a transformed advantage. RAT computes this transformation efficiently via randomized block Kaczmarz iterations on on-policy mini-batches, avoiding explicit Fisher construction, conjugate-gradient solvers, and architecture-specific approximations. We provide convergence guarantees for RAT and demonstrate empirically that it matches or exceeds established natural-gradient methods across continuous and visual control benchmarks, while remaining simple to implement and compatible with various architectures.
originalAbstract: Natural policy gradients improve optimization by accounting for the geometry of distribution space, but their practical use is limited by the cost of estimating and inverting the Fisher matrix. By applying the Woodbury formula, we reformulate the regularized natural gradient as vanilla policy gradients with a transformed advantage. Randomized Advantage Transformation aims to retain a regularized version of this update while making it accessible through ordinary backpropagation.

Using the Woodbury formula, the authors rewrite the Tikhonov-regularized natural gradient as a standard policy gradient with a transformed advantage signal. RAT estimates that transformation through randomized block Kaczmarz iterations on on-policy mini-batches. The computational work therefore moves into transforming the learning signal, avoiding explicit Fisher-matrix construction, conjugate-gradient solvers, and approximations tied to a particular architecture.

It reports performance matching or exceeding established natural-gradient methods, together with implementation simplicity and compatibility across architectures. The contribution is a practical route to estimating regularized natural policy gradients, connecting a geometry-aware optimization objective to the familiar machinery of direct backpropagation.

title: Randomized Advantage Transformation (RAT): Computing Natural Policy Gradients via Direct Backpropagation

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have recently achieved strong mathematical and code reasoning performance through Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training. However, we show that modern reasoning post-training induces an unintended exploration collapse: temperature-based sampling no longer increases pass@$n$ accuracy. Empirically, the final-layer posterior of post-trained LRMs exhibit sharply reduced entropy, while the entropy of intermediate layers remains relatively high. Motivated by this entropy asymmetry, we propose Latent Exploration Decoding (LED), a depth-conditioned decoding strategy. LED aggregates intermediate posteriors via cumulative sum and selects depth configurations with maximal entropy as exploration candidates. Without additional training or parameters, LED consistently improves pass@1 and pass@16 accuracy by 0.61 and 1.03 percentage points across multiple reasoning benchmarks and models. Relevant code is included in the supplementary material and will made be fully public after this paper is accepted.

title: Restoring Exploration after Post-Training: Latent Exploration Decoding for Large Reasoning Models

abstract: Neural networks trained under different hyperparameter settings can fall into distinct training "regimes," with consistent behavior within regimes and qualitative differences across regimes. In this paper, we study such multi-regime behavior in scientific machine learning (SciML) models through a regime-aware diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes performance, training dynamics, and loss-landscape geometry. We identify three key findings: (i) a consistent three-regime structure emerges across many standard SciML models, different constraint enforcements, and various optimizer designs; (ii) optimization effectiveness is regime-specific, with no single method performing well across all regimes; and (iii) SciML models can exhibit fine-grained failure modes that can challenge conventional interpretations of standard loss-landscape metrics. Our results provide an approach to establish a unified, task-oblivious perspective on failure modes in SciML and to inform regime-aware guidance for improving robustness. We validate these findings across widely-used SciML models, including physics-informed neural networks, neural operators, and neural ordinary differential equations, on benchmarks spanning representative ordinary and partial differential equations.

The authors report a recurring three-regime structure across many standard scientific machine learning models, constraint-enforcement choices, and optimizer designs. They also find that optimization effectiveness depends on the regime, with no single method working well across all studied regimes. The findings are validated with physics-informed neural networks, neural operators, and neural ordinary differential equations on representative differential-equation benchmarks. The contribution is a diagnostic perspective that can organize failures across tasks and model families. Its practical implication is that guidance for improving robustness should account for the current training regime, because an optimization choice that helps one regime may not work well in another.
summary.tldr: A joint analysis of training behavior and geometry reveals three recurring SciML regimes with different failure modes and optimization needs.

title: Unveiling Multi-regime Patterns in SciML: Distinct Failure Modes and Regime-specific Optimization

abstract: Entropy serves as a critical metric for measuring the diversity of outputs generated by large language models (LLMs), providing valuable insights into their exploration capabilities. While recent studies increasingly focus on monitoring and adjusting entropy to better balance exploration and exploitation in reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT), a principled understanding of entropy dynamics during this process is yet to be thoroughly investigated. In this paper, we establish a theoretical framework for analyzing the entropy dynamics during the RFT process, which begins with a discriminant expression that quantifies entropy change under a single logit update. This foundation enables the derivation of a first-order expression for entropy change, which can be further extended to the update formula of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The corollaries and insights drawn from the theoretical analysis inspire the design of entropy control methods, and also offer a unified lens for interpreting various entropy-based methods in existing studies. We provide empirical evidence to support the main conclusions of our analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of the derived entropy-discriminator clipping methods. This study yields novel insights into RFT training dynamics, providing theoretical support and practical strategies for optimizing the exploration-exploitation balance during LLM fine-tuning. We release our code at https://github.com/agentscope-ai/Trinity-RFT/tree/main/examples/entropy.

This paper develops an analysis of how those updates change entropy.

The contribution combines an account of training dynamics with practical controls for balancing exploration and exploitation, while retaining the first-order nature of the relevant expression.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis of entropy changes during reinforcement fine-tuning motivates effective clipping methods for controlling output diversity.

title: On the Entropy Dynamics in Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce Genome-Factory, the first integrated Python library for tuning, deploying, and interpreting genomic foundation models. Our core contribution is to simplify and unify the workflow for genomic model development: data collection, model tuning, inference, benchmarking, and interpretability. For data collection, Genome-Factory offers an automated pipeline to download genomic sequences and preprocess them. For model tuning, Genome-Factory supports both full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning across diverse genomic models. For inference, Genome-Factory enables both embedding extraction and DNA sequence generation. For benchmarking, we include two existing benchmarks and provide a flexible interface to incorporate additional benchmarks. For interpretability, Genome-Factory introduces an open-source biological interpreter based on a sparse auto-encoder. We validate the utility of Genome-Factory across three dimensions: (i) Compatibility with diverse models and fine-tuning methods; (ii) Benchmarking downstream performance using two open-source benchmarks; (iii) Biological interpretation of learned representations with DNABERT-2. These results highlight its practical value for real-world genomic analysis. GitHub: https://github.com/WeiminWu2000/Genome_Factory.

summary.tldr: Genome-Factory unifies genomic model data preparation, fine-tuning, inference, benchmarking, and representation interpretation in one Python library.

title: Genome-Factory: A Library for Tuning, Deploying, and Interpreting Genomic Foundation Models

abstract: As Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are increasingly deployed, auditing their chain-of-thought (CoT) traces for safety becomes critical. Recent work has reported that monitorability—the degree to which CoT faithfully and informatively reflects internal computation—can appear as a "free gift" during the early stages of Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). We make this observation concrete through a systematic evaluation across model families and training domains. Our results show that this effect is not universal: monitorability improvements are strongly data-dependent. In particular, we demonstrate the critical role of data diversity and instruction-following data during RLVR training. We further show that monitorability is orthogonal to capability—improvements in reasoning performance do not imply increased transparency. Through mechanistic analysis, we attribute monitorability gains primarily to response distribution sharpening (entropy reduction) and increased attention to the prompt, rather than stronger causal reliance on reasoning traces. We also reveal how monitorability dynamics vary with controlled training and evaluation difficulty. Together, these findings provide a holistic view of how monitorability emerges under RLVR, clarifying when gains are likely to occur and when they are not.

paragraphs: Visible reasoning traces can be useful for monitoring a model only if they reveal meaningful information about its computation. Early reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards sometimes appears to improve this monitorability automatically. This paper tests when that effect occurs and whether improved reasoning accuracy explains it.

Across model families and domains, monitorability gains depend strongly on training data, especially diversity and instruction-following examples. Capability improvements do not reliably predict transparency improvements. Mechanistic analysis attributes much of the observed gain to sharper response distributions and greater attention to the prompt, rather than stronger causal dependence on the written reasoning trace.

Controlled changes in training and evaluation difficulty further reveal different monitorability dynamics. The contribution is a qualified account of an apparently beneficial training effect. It cautions against treating stronger task performance or more readable explanations as sufficient evidence that a model’s chain of thought faithfully exposes the computation producing its answer.
summary.tldr: RLVR can improve monitorability, but the effect depends on data and does not necessarily reflect more causally faithful reasoning traces.

title: Monitorability as a Free Gift: How RLVR Spontaneously Aligns Reasoning

abstract: Solving complex geometric problems inherently requires interleaved reasoning: a tight alternation between constructing diagrams and performing logical deductions. Although recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in visual generation and plotting, we identify a counter-intuitive and underexplored phenomenon. Naively applying Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on interleaved plot–solution data leads to a substantial degradation in reasoning performance compared to text-only baselines. We argue that this failure stems from a fundamental limitation of SFT, which primarily induces distributional alignment: the model learns to reproduce the surface format of interleaved plotting but fails to internalize the causal dependency between the generated plot and reasoning steps. To overcome this limitation, we propose Faire (Functional alignment for interleaved reasoning), a reinforcement learning framework that enforces three casual constraints to move beyond superficial imitation toward functional alignment. Extensive experiments show that Faire induces a qualitative shift in model behavior in which the plotting is effectively internalized, yielding competitive performance on challenging geometric reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Geometric problem solving can require alternating between drawing a diagram and making logical deductions. This paper investigates why teaching a multimodal model that alternating format does not necessarily improve reasoning. The authors find that naive supervised fine-tuning on interleaved plots and solutions substantially reduces performance relative to text-only baselines.

Their explanation is that supervised training can teach the appearance of the workflow without teaching how a plot should influence subsequent deductions. A model may reproduce the expected sequence of drawing and text while failing to use their causal relationship. Faire addresses this with reinforcement learning and three constraints intended to make plotting functionally connected to reasoning.

The result supports the paper’s distinction between reproducing an interleaved format and learning to use it productively. Its contribution is a training framework aimed at making visual construction serve the reasoning process, rather than assuming that interleaved examples alone achieve that connection.
summary.tldr: Faire uses reinforcement learning to connect plotting with geometric reasoning after naive interleaved supervised training degrades performance.

title: How RL Unlocks the Aha Moment in Geometric Interleaved Reasoning

abstract: Designing sparse attention for 2D image data in diffusion and vision-language models requires reconciling spatial locality with hardware-efficient execution: handcrafted 2D sparsity patterns preserve spatial structure but often induce uncoalesced memory access, limiting practical speedups on modern GPUs. We present HilbertA, a 2D-aware sparse attention mechanism that reorders image tokens along a Hilbert curve, converting local spatial neighborhoods into contiguous memory segments for efficient GPU execution. To enable communication beyond local tiles, HilbertA shifts attention windows along the Hilbert-ordered sequence across layers and uses a small central shared region, preserving contiguous access while supporting cross-tile information flow. Across diffusion and vision-language models, HilbertA delivers consistent efficiency gains while maintaining competitive quality, achieving up to 4.16$\times$ attention acceleration and 1.44$\times$ end-to-end speedup on Flux.1-dev, and up to 2.30$\times$ attention acceleration with 1.57$\times$ faster time-to-first-token on Qwen3-VL-8B inference.

title: HilbertA: Hilbert-Curve–Aligned Sparse Attention for 2D Structured Data

abstract: Current data-driven scientific modeling struggles with a functional dichotomy: neural operators exhibit spectral bias in high-frequency regimes, while physics-constrained paradigms suffer from optimization pathologies. To bridge this gap, we propose Adaptive Physics-Informed Computing (APIC), a neuro-symbolic meta-architecture designed with structural reconfigurability to encode diverse domain priors. Crucially, APIC integrates a gradient isolation strategy that reduces interference between the optimization paths of parameter identification and residual correction, effectively mitigating gradient conflicts. By instantiating this framework for nonlinear dissipative systems, we derive the Generalized Kuramoto-Sivashinsky-Cahn-Hilliard (G-KSCH) kernel, providing a unified representation for sparse dynamic identification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that APIC establishes new benchmarks in 3D compressible supersonic shock wave prediction, surpassing diverse architectures (e.g., CNNs and Transformers) by substantial margins in predictive accuracy. Notably, APIC achieves Pareto-optimal performance, delivering superior precision with reduced computational overhead compared to SOTA models, while exhibiting strong cross-task adaptability across meteorological and urban traffic datasets.

APIC combines neural and symbolic modeling in a reconfigurable architecture, allowing different kinds of domain knowledge to be built into the model.

title: APIC: Orthogonalized Neuro-Symbolic Modeling for Nonlinear Dissipative Dynamics

abstract: Pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP achieve strong zero-shot generalization, but their performance degrades sharply under adversarial perturbations. Existing test-time adaptation methods typically rely on sample-level confidence heuristics, overlooking the intrinsic distributional structure of the data. This sample-centric approach limits robustness, as it fails to distinguish confident adversarial mispredictions from true semantic consistency. In this work, we observe that adversarial distortion is structurally brittle: while holistic representations are corrupted, semantic integrity is often preserved in the distribution of augmented views. Motivated by this insight, we propose $\texttt{RITA}$, a $\textbf{R}$obust test-t$\textbf{I}$me promp$\textbf{T}$ $\textbf{A}$daptation framework that shifts from sample-level estimates to distribution-level alignment. Specifically, $\texttt{RITA}$ employs optimal transport to align the distribution of augmented visual features with textual prototypes, mitigating adversarial outliers and rectifying cross-modal semantic misalignment. Furthermore, we introduce a dynamic cache to progressively accumulate reliable cues from the test stream for online refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $\texttt{RITA}$ significantly improves adversarial robustness without compromising clean accuracy.

paragraphs: RITA improves the adversarial robustness of pretrained vision-language models through prompt adaptation at test time. The paper identifies a weakness in approaches that trust individual high-confidence predictions: an adversarially corrupted prediction can still be confident. Its motivating observation is that semantic structure often survives across a distribution of augmented image views even when the overall representation is corrupted.

RITA uses optimal transport to align these augmented visual features with textual prototypes. Looking at the distribution allows the method to reduce the influence of adversarial outliers and correct misalignment between visual and textual semantics. A dynamic cache then accumulates reliable cues from the incoming test stream to support continued online refinement.

The authors report substantial robustness improvements without sacrificing accuracy on clean inputs. These results support using consistency across augmented views as a stronger adaptation signal than confidence in a single sample. The approach rests on the observed preservation of semantic information across views, which the paper describes as frequent rather than universal.
summary.tldr: RITA improves adversarial robustness by aligning distributions of augmented visual features with text during test-time prompt adaptation.

title: Robustifying Vision-Language Models via Test-Time Prompt Adaptation

abstract: Active vision, also known as active perception, refers to actively selecting where and how to look in order to gather task-relevant information. It is a critical component of efficient perception and decision-making in humans and advanced embodied agents. With the rise of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) as central planners in robotic systems, the lack of methods for equipping MLLMs with active perception has become a key gap. We first provide a systematic definition of MLLM-based active perception tasks and show that GPT-o3’s zoom-in strategy can be viewed as a special case, though it suffers from low efficiency and inaccurate region selection. To address these issues, we propose Active-o3, a reinforcement learning framework built on GRPO that equips MLLMs with active perception capabilities. Leveraging a modular sensing-action design and a dual-form reward, Active-o3 autonomously learns efficient and stable region selection strategies without explicit supervision. We further establish a comprehensive benchmark covering both open-world tasks (small/dense-object grounding) and domain-specific scenarios (remote sensing, autonomous driving, interactive segmentation). Experimental results demonstrate that Active-o3 significantly enhances active perception capabilities compared to Qwen2.5-VL-CoT. Moreover, we show that our RL framework not only preserves the model’s general understanding ability but can also serve as a proxy task for leveraging perception data, further improving performance on benchmarks such as RealWorldQA. We hope that our work can provide a simple codebase and unified evaluation protocol to facilitate future research on active perception with MLLMs.

Moreover, we show that our RL framework not only preserves the model’s general understanding ability but can also serve as a proxy task for leveraging perception data, further improving performance on benchmarks such as RealWorldQA. We hope that our work can provide a simple codebase and unified evaluation protocol to facilitate future research on active perception with MLLMs.

paragraphs: Active-o3 addresses how a multimodal language model chooses where to look for useful information. The paper defines active perception tasks for these models and treats zooming into an image as one instance. Its motivation is that effective perception requires selecting informative regions efficiently, especially when relevant objects are small or densely packed.

The proposed framework uses Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, to learn region selection through reinforcement learning. A modular sensing-action design and a reward with two forms guide this learning without explicit supervision of the selection strategy. This makes choosing what to inspect part of the model’s learned behavior, rather than simply requiring it to interpret a fixed view.

The authors introduce a benchmark spanning object grounding, remote sensing, autonomous driving, and interactive segmentation. They report substantially better active perception than Qwen2.5-VL-CoT while preserving general understanding. They also find that active perception training can provide a way to use perception data that improves broader evaluation performance, including RealWorldQA.
summary.tldr: Active-o3 uses reinforcement learning to teach multimodal models efficient region selection while preserving their general understanding.

abstract: Many supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms are very sensitive to the choice of an appropriate distance metric. Whileclassification tasks can make use of class label information for metriclearning, such information is generally unavailable in conventional clusteringtasks. Some recent research sought to address a variant of the conventionalclustering problem called semi-supervised clustering, which performsclustering in the presence of some background knowledge or supervisoryinformation expressed as pairwise similarity or dissimilarity constraints. However, existing metric learning methods for semi-supervised clusteringmostly perform global metric learning through a linear transformation. Inthis paper, we propose a new metric learning method which performs nonlineartransformation globally but linear transformation locally. In particular, weformulate the learning problem as an optimization problem and present twomethods for solving it. Through some toy data sets, we show empirically thatour locally linear metric adaptation (LLMA) method can handle some difficultcases that cannot be handled satisfactorily by previous methods. We alsodemonstrate the effectiveness of our method on some real data sets.

paragraphs: Clustering depends heavily on how distance is measured. In semi-supervised clustering, some background knowledge is available as pairs of examples that should be treated as similar or dissimilar. This paper uses those constraints to learn a distance representation, addressing the limitations of methods that apply one global linear transformation.

The proposed locally linear metric adaptation method uses transformations that are linear within local regions but nonlinear across the dataset as a whole. This gives the learned representation more flexibility than a single global linear change. The authors formulate the learning task as an optimization problem and present two methods for solving it.

Experiments on toy datasets show that the method can handle some difficult configurations that previous methods do not handle satisfactorily. Tests on real datasets also demonstrate its effectiveness. The findings support local adaptation as a useful way to express supervisory relationships when one global linear transformation is insufficient for the studied data, without establishing that it is preferable in every clustering setting.
summary.tldr: Locally linear metric adaptation learns a globally nonlinear representation that handles some clustering cases poorly served by global linear methods.

title: Locally linear metric adaptation for semi-supervised clustering

abstract: Low-rank matrix decompositions are essential tools in the application of kernel methods to large-scale learning problems. These decompositions have generally been treated as black boxes—the decomposition of the kernel matrix that they deliver is independent of the specific learning task at hand— and this is a potentially significant source of inefficiency. In this paper, we present an algorithm that can exploit side information (e.g., classification labels, regression responses) in the computation of low-rank decompositions for kernel matrices. Our algorithm has the same favorable scaling as state-of-the-art methods such as incomplete Cholesky decomposition—it is linear in the number of data points and quadratic in the rank of the approximation. We present simulation results that show that our algorithm yields decompositions of significantly smaller rank than those found by incomplete Cholesky decomposition.

Our algorithm has the same favorable scaling as state-of-the-art methods such as incomplete Cholesky decomposition—it is linear in the number of data points and quadratic in the rank of the approximation. We present simulation results that show that our algorithm yields decompositions of significantly smaller rank than those found by incomplete Cholesky decomposition.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the use of low-rank matrix approximations to make kernel methods practical for large learning problems. Conventional decomposition procedures typically work independently of the prediction task. The authors identify this separation as a potential source of inefficiency: an approximation may be constructed without considering the information the learner is trying to predict.

Their algorithm incorporates side information, such as classification labels or regression responses, into the decomposition of the kernel matrix. This makes the approximation sensitive to the learning task. The computational scaling remains favorable: it is linear in the number of data points and quadratic in the chosen approximation rank, matching the stated scaling of incomplete Cholesky decomposition.

Simulation results show that the proposed algorithm produces decompositions with significantly smaller rank than incomplete Cholesky decomposition. That result matters because rank is a direct component of the method’s computational scaling. The work supports using prediction information during matrix approximation, with the reported simulations demonstrating more compact decompositions.
summary.tldr: A task-aware kernel decomposition uses labels or responses to obtain smaller-rank approximations while retaining favorable computational scaling.

title: Predictive low-rank decomposition for kernel methods

abstract: Chord progressions are the building blocks from which tonal music is constructed. Inferring chord progressions is thus an essential step towards modeling long term dependencies in music. In this paper, a distributed representation for chords is designed such that Euclidean distances roughly correspond to psychoacoustic dissimilarities. Parameters in the graphical models are learnt with the EM algorithm and the classical Junction Tree algorithm. Various model architectures are compared in terms of conditional outof-sample likelihood. Both perceptual and statistical evidence show that binary trees related to meter are well suited to capture chord dependencies.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent and learn chord progressions, which help organize tonal music over time. Its starting point is that a useful model should account for how chords sound in relation to one another. The authors design a distributed representation in which ordinary geometric distances roughly track perceived differences between chords.

This representation gives graphical models a musically motivated space in which to describe chord dependencies. Model parameters are learned using expectation maximization together with the Junction Tree algorithm. The authors compare several model architectures using conditional likelihood on examples outside the training data, assessing how well the learned dependencies carry over to unseen examples.

Both the perceptual evidence and the statistical comparisons favor binary tree structures related to musical meter. These structures organize chord relationships hierarchically around the rhythmic organization of music. The finding supports meter as a useful guide for modeling chord dependencies, while the approximate correspondence between distance and perceived dissimilarity supplies a connection between the representation and musical listening.
summary.tldr: A perceptually motivated chord representation and graphical-model comparisons support meter-related binary trees for capturing chord dependencies.

title: A graphical model for chord progressions embedded in a psychoacoustic space

abstract: We study the problem of simultaneously estimating several densities where the datasets are organized into overlapping groups, such as a hierarchy. For this problem, we propose a maximum entropy formulation, which systematically incorporates the groups and allows us to share the strength of prediction across similar datasets. We derive general performance guarantees, and show how some previous approaches, such as hierarchical shrinkage and hierarchical priors, can be derived as special cases. We demonstrate the proposed technique on synthetic data and in a realworld application to modeling the geographic distributions of species hierarchically grouped in a taxonomy. Specifically, we model the geographic distributions of species in the Australian wet tropics and Northeast New South Wales. In these regions, small numbers of samples per species significantly hinder effective prediction. Substantial benefits are obtained by combining information across taxonomic groups.

paragraphs: Estimating several probability distributions becomes difficult when each dataset contains few observations. This paper considers datasets organized into overlapping groups, including hierarchies, and uses those relationships to share predictive information. The aim is to estimate the distributions jointly while making systematic use of similarities among datasets.

The authors develop a maximum-entropy formulation that incorporates the grouping structure. They derive general performance guarantees and show that hierarchical shrinkage and hierarchical priors arise as special cases. This makes the framework a connection among existing approaches as well as a proposed method for sharing information across related estimation problems.

The method is demonstrated on synthetic data and on geographic distributions of species grouped by taxonomy. The real-world application covers the Australian wet tropics and Northeast New South Wales, where limited observations per species hinder prediction. Combining information across taxonomic groups produces substantial benefits. The result illustrates why group structure can be valuable: related datasets can contribute evidence when separate estimates would each have little data to draw on.
summary.tldr: A maximum-entropy framework shares information across overlapping groups, improving species-distribution estimation when observations per species are scarce.

title: Hierarchical maximum entropy density estimation

abstract: Deep learning has been successfully applied to learn non-linear feature mappings and to perform dimensionality reduction. In this paper, we present supervised embedding techniques that use a deep neural network to collapse classes. The network is pre-trained using a stack of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), and finetuned using approaches that try to collapse classes. The finetuning is inspired by ideas from Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA), but it uses a Student t-distribution to model the probabilities of pairwise data points belonging to the same class in the embedding. We investigate two types of objective functions: deep t-distributed MCML (dt-MCML) and deep t-distributed NCA (dt-NCA). Our experiments on two handwritten digit datasets reveal the strong performance of dt-MCML in supervised parametric data visualization, whereas dt-NCA outperforms alternative techniques when embeddings with more than two or three dimensions are constructed, e.g., to obtain good classification performances. Overall, our results demonstrate the advantage of using a deep architecture and a heavy-tailed t-distribution for measuring pairwise similarities in supervised embedding.

The finetuning is inspired by ideas from Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA), but it uses a Student t-distribution to model the probabilities of pairwise data points belonging to the same class in the embedding. We investigate two types of objective functions: deep t-distributed MCML (dt-MCML) and deep t-distributed NCA (dt-NCA). Our experiments on two handwritten digit datasets reveal the strong performance of dt-MCML in supervised parametric data visualization, whereas dt-NCA outperforms alternative techniques when embeddings with more than two or three dimensions are constructed, e.g., to obtain good classification performances. Overall, our results demonstrate the advantage of using a deep architecture and a heavy-tailed t-distribution for measuring pairwise similarities in supervised embedding.

paragraphs: This paper learns low-dimensional representations using both a deep neural network and class labels. The aim is to bring examples from the same class together in the learned space. Because the representation is produced by a network, the method learns a nonlinear mapping that can be used to generate embeddings.

Training begins with a stack of restricted Boltzmann machines and then fine-tunes the network using class-based objectives. Inspired by Neighborhood Components Analysis, the fine-tuning models pairwise class similarities with a Student t-distribution. The authors investigate two objectives, dt-MCML and dt-NCA, combining the deep mapping with this heavy-tailed treatment of similarities.

Experiments on two handwritten-digit datasets show different strengths for the objectives. The authors report strong supervised visualization performance for dt-MCML, while dt-NCA outperforms alternatives for embeddings with more than two or three dimensions, including representations used for classification. Together, the results support the combination of a deep architecture and t-distributed similarities for the supervised embedding tasks studied.
summary.tldr: Deep supervised embeddings with t-distributed similarities show complementary strengths for digit visualization and higher-dimensional classification representations.

title: Deep Supervised t-Distributed Embedding

abstract: In this paper we present an approach to inference in graphical models with mixture of discrete and bounded continuous variables. In particular, we extend convex max-product to deal with these hybrid models and derive the conditions under which our approach is guaranteed to produce the MAP assignment. When dealing with continuous variables the messages are functions. We investigate a multi-grid approach which can be viewed as a piecewise constant representation of these messages. While this approach provides the theoretical guarantees it is not very practical. Inspired by this, we further propose a particle convex max-product algorithm that significantly outperforms existing particle methods in the task of protein folding and performs comparable to the state-of-the art while using a smaller amount of prior knowledge.

In particular, we extend convex max-product to deal with these hybrid models and derive the conditions under which our approach is guaranteed to produce the MAP assignment. When dealing with continuous variables the messages are functions. We investigate a multi-grid approach which can be viewed as a piecewise constant representation of these messages. While this approach provides the theoretical guarantees it is not very practical. Inspired by this, we further propose a particle convex max-product algorithm that significantly outperforms existing particle methods in the task of protein folding and performs comparable to the state-of-the art while using a smaller amount of prior knowledge.

paragraphs: Graphical models can contain both discrete choices and continuous quantities restricted to bounded ranges. This paper extends convex max-product inference to such hybrid models. The target is the maximum a posteriori assignment: the combination of variable values with the greatest posterior probability. The authors derive conditions under which their approach is guaranteed to find it.

Continuous variables create a representation problem because the messages passed during inference are functions. The paper investigates a multigrid method that represents these functions through piecewise constant values. This approach provides the theoretical guarantees, but the authors describe it as impractical, motivating a more usable algorithm inspired by the same development.

That practical proposal is a particle convex max-product method. On protein folding, it significantly outperforms existing particle methods and achieves performance comparable to the state of the art while using less prior knowledge. The guarantee-bearing multigrid construction and the empirically evaluated particle algorithm play distinct roles: one establishes the theoretical approach, while the other demonstrates its practical promise.
summary.tldr: Hybrid convex max-product inference leads to conditional MAP guarantees and a practical particle algorithm with strong protein-folding results.

title: Convex Max-Product over Compact Sets for Protein Folding

abstract: The contractive auto-encoder learns a representation of the input data that captures the local manifold structure around each data point, through the leading singular vectors of the Jacobian of the transformation from input to representation. The corresponding singular values specify how much local variation is plausible in directions associated with the corresponding singular vectors, while remaining in a high-density region of the input space. This paper proposes a procedure for generating samples that are consistent with the local structure captured by a contractive auto-encoder. The associated stochastic process defines a distribution from which one can sample, and which experimentally appears to converge quickly and mix well between modes, compared to Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Deep Belief Networks. The intuitions behind this procedure can also be used to train the second layer of contraction that pools lower-level features and learns to be invariant to the local directions of variation discovered in the first layer. We show that this can help learn and represent invariances present in the data and improve classification error.

paragraphs: A contractive auto-encoder learns more than a compact representation of an input: it captures directions in which nearby inputs can vary while remaining plausible. The paper uses this local geometric information to construct a sampling procedure, turning the learned representation into a source of generated examples.

The key information comes from the Jacobian, which describes how the representation changes when the input changes. Its leading singular vectors identify local directions of variation, while the associated singular values indicate how much variation is plausible. The proposed stochastic process generates samples consistent with this structure and defines a distribution from which samples can be drawn.

In experiments, the process appears to converge quickly and move effectively between modes compared with Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Deep Belief Networks. The same intuition also guides training a second layer that pools features and becomes insensitive to local variations found by the first layer. The authors show that this can improve the representation of invariances and reduce classification error.
summary.tldr: The paper uses local structure learned by a contractive auto-encoder to generate samples and learn representations that can improve classification.

title: A Generative Process for Contractive Auto-Encoders
